items.title: Feature-flag AI-suggested UI before it hits every user
items.snippet: The first time we shipped an agent-written settings panel straight to main , it looked fine in staging. Then support got three tickets in an hour: a toggle that did nothing for free plans, a “Save” that double-fired on slow networks, and a new empty state that
items.content: The first time we shipped an agent-written settings panel straight to main , it looked fine in staging. Then support got three tickets in an hour: a toggle that did nothing for free plans, a “Save” that double-fired on slow networks, and a new empty state that hid the only CTA half our users needed. CI was green. Visuals looked close. The bug was product judgment the model never had — and we gave 100% of traffic that judgment on day one. So we stopped treating “agent UI merged” as “agent UI live.” Feature flags became the default release valve for anything an agent touched in the UI layer. The failure mode: merge = rollout Agent PRs tempt you to skip the usual caution: Diff is “just UI” Screenshots look right Playwright clicked through the happy path Reviewer approved the code shape None of that answers: does this layout work for the cohort that never sees premium fields? Does the new empty state break the onboarding funnel? Does the regenerated form still respect the old keyboard path power users rely on? Those are traffic questions. Feature flags are how you ask them without a full revert. What I flag (and what I don’t) I flag user-visible surfaces the agent authored or heavily rewrote : New panels, modals, empty / error / loading states Regenerated forms and settings sections Agent-refactored navigation / IA changes Copy-heavy UI where tone or CTA placement shifted I usually don’t flag: Pure token / lint / type cleanup with no layout change Test-only or Storybook-only diffs Internal admin tools with a tiny known audience (still stage them; just don’t burn a flag name) Rule of thumb: if a stranger on the free plan could hit it tomorrow, it gets a flag. The default pattern we use Keep it boring. One boolean (or percentage) per agent UI surface, named after the ticket, not the model: // flags.ts — names are product, not “gpt-panel-v3” export const flags = { settingsBillingV2 : booleanFlag ( ' settings-billing-v2 ' , false ), emptyProjectsAgentCopy : booleanFlag ( ' empty-projects-agent-copy ' , false ), } as const ; In the route / component: export function SettingsBilling () { const enabled = useFlag ( ' settings-billing-v2 ' ); if ( ! enabled ) { return SettingsBillingLegacy />; } return SettingsBillingV2 />; // agent-authored surface } Kill switch lives next to the flag definition, not in a Slack thread: // ops: set settings-billing-v2 = false → instant revert without redeploy If your stack is LaunchDarkly / Unleash / Statsig / a homegrown % cookie — sa

items.title: Claude Desktop vs Claude Code CLI: Two Different Gateway Setups
items.snippet: Changing a terminal environment variable can route Claude Code CLI through a gateway. It does not configure the Code tab inside the Claude desktop app. Those are separate configuration paths, and confusing them can leave you using the wrong account. Disclosure
items.content: Changing a terminal environment variable can route Claude Code CLI through a gateway. It does not configure the Code tab inside the Claude desktop app. Those are separate configuration paths, and confusing them can leave you using the wrong account. Disclosure: this tutorial comes from the ModelFold team. It uses our gateway as the example. The Windows screenshots document configuration and the Gateway state; they are not evidence of a completed paid coding session. Choose the right surface This guide covers the desktop app's Code tab and the CLI. It does not add third-party API keys to ordinary claude.ai web chat or the mobile app. For the desktop app, use the third-party inference form. For the CLI, use environment variables. ModelFold's Windows walkthrough now includes real screenshots of the relevant menus. Configure the desktop app on Windows Install the official Claude desktop app using the download link in the walkthrough. You will also need your own ModelFold API key from Console → API Keys . Open the application menu at the top left. Choose Help → Troubleshooting → Enable Developer Mode. Let the app restart. Open Developer → Configure Third-Party Inference. Under Connection, choose Gateway and enter: Inference provider: Gateway Gateway base URL: https://modelfold.ai/anthropic Credential kind: Static API key Gateway API key: Gateway auth scheme: bearer Click Apply Changes and allow the app to relaunch. Follow a Save & Restart prompt if it appears. These are application settings; putting the same information in a terminal does not configure this desktop surface. The screenshot uses a Chinese application UI. The field values above provide the English equivalents. Keep the base URL at /anthropic . The client appends /v1/messages ; adding /v1 yourself can produce an incorrect path. Paste the key without Bearer because the selected authentication scheme adds that prefix. After restarting, the Code page should identify the connection as Gateway. This checks the selected configuration, not whether every model request will succeed. Configure the CLI separately If you use Claude Code in a terminal, the configuration is different. The following PowerShell example assumes you have already set MODELFOLD_API_KEY privately in that shell. Do not paste a real key into an article, repository, or screenshot. # These variables affect the CLI launched from this PowerShell session. $ env : ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL = "https://modelfold.ai/anthropic" $ env : ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOK

items.title: Shop MCP Shows Why AI Shopping Agents May Choose Different Products From the Same Catalog
items.snippet: Shopify’s Shop MCP gives AI agents a new way to search product data, build carts and complete Shop Pay checkout through a single connection. That matters because product discovery in this environment is not simply a matter of where a merchant ranks in a catalo
items.content: Shopify’s Shop MCP gives AI agents a new way to search product data, build carts and complete Shop Pay checkout through a single connection. That matters because product discovery in this environment is not simply a matter of where a merchant ranks in a catalog or in Google. An agent also interprets the available product information and decides what to recommend. A hands-on experiment reported by Search Engine Journal illustrates how consequential that decision layer can be. Three Claude models received the same fixed set of 20 products retrieved through Shop MCP, yet they did not select the same top product in any of six searches. For merchants, the result is an early indication that catalog presentation, review signals and prompt fit may shape unpaid AI shopping discovery alongside established SEO and ecommerce optimization work. What Shop MCP adds to agentic commerce Shopify announced Shop MCP on October 13, 2026. According to Shopify’s Shop MCP announcement , the connection enables an agent to search the Shopify Catalog, create carts and use Shop Pay checkout. Shopify said catalog search does not require an API key and that the catalog covers more than one billion products. The significance is not merely that an AI assistant can point a shopper to a product page. An agent can use structured product information during a shopping interaction, narrow the choices, make a recommendation and potentially take the shopper through checkout. This places a model-mediated selection process between the buyer’s request and the merchant’s listing. That process is distinct from a conventional search result page. Traditional organic visibility still depends on crawling, indexing, ranking and search-result presentation. In an agent-enabled shopping flow, visibility can additionally depend on whether the agent receives the item in its candidate set, how the catalog describes it, and how a particular model evaluates those details against the shopper’s request. Same products, different AI decisions The Search Engine Journal test used three Claude models: Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 5 and Opus 5. Researchers gave each model the same 20 products obtained via Shop MCP and ran six searches. Each model made 50 selections per search, producing 1,980 total picks. The models never agreed on the leading product across those searches. Their reported top-product agreement rates were 8% for Haiku, 0% for Sonnet and 20% for Opus. items.title: Fix Fetch Race Conditions in a Market Price Widget
items.snippet: A user selects EURUSD, then immediately switches to GBPUSD. The second request finishes first. The widget displays GBPUSD correctly until the slower EURUSD response arrives and replaces it. Both requests can succeed. The bug is that the screen accepts a result
items.content: A user selects EURUSD, then immediately switches to GBPUSD. The second request finishes first. The widget displays GBPUSD correctly until the slower EURUSD response arrives and replaces it. Both requests can succeed. The bug is that the screen accepts a result after the user has stopped asking for it. A reliable selector needs a simple rule: only the latest selection may update the widget. Use an AbortController to stop unnecessary fetch work where possible, and a request counter to decide which completion still owns the screen. Two safeguards with different jobs Passing an abort signal to fetch() lets the browser cancel the request or response-body consumption. Calling abort() normally causes the affected operation to reject with AbortError . See MDN's cancellation reference . Cancellation does not undo work already performed by your server. Treating it as a transaction rollback would be a separate bug. A price lookup should be a read operation, and its server may still finish processing after the browser loses interest. The request counter protects the interface even when an asynchronous adapter ignores cancellation, or when additional processing cannot be interrupted. Increment it for every selection, including an empty selection and a refresh of the same symbol. Comparing symbol strings alone is insufficient. If someone selects EURUSD, switches away, and returns to EURUSD, the first request still belongs to an older interaction. Give each request ownership of its state Save this function as devto-price-loader.mjs . It accepts a price-fetching function and a synchronous renderer. The small response contract, { price: number } , belongs to this example. export function createPriceLoader ( fetchPrice , render ) { let latest = 0 ; let active = null ; return async function selectPrice ( symbol ) { const id = ++ latest ; active ?. abort (); active = null ; if ( ! symbol ) { render ({ status : " idle " , symbol : "" }); return ; } const controller = new AbortController (); active = controller ; render ({ status : " loading " , symbol }); try { const data = await fetchPrice ( symbol , controller . signal ); if ( id !== latest ) return ; if ( ! data || ! Number . isFinite ( data . price )) { throw new Error ( " Invalid price " ); } render ({ status : " ready " , symbol , price : data . price }); } catch ( error ) { if ( id !== latest ) return ; render ({ status : " error " , symbol , error : error ?. name === " AbortError " ? items.title: Controls to add before an AI agent takes action
items.snippet: An agent that can call tools or move money fails in a different place than a chatbot that only replies. I assume most builders start with software permissions, an API key, and a policy sitting in the prompt. I would not stop there. Four episodes each hand you
items.content: An agent that can call tools or move money fails in a different place than a chatbot that only replies. I assume most builders start with software permissions, an API key, and a policy sitting in the prompt. I would not stop there. Four episodes each hand you one decision: how you patch, how you bound a tool, where governance lives, and when hardware has to sign the action. What changes if an attacker needs no human? In The First Fully Autonomous AI Attack is Coming , Kris Lovejoy, Global Head of Strategy at Kyndryl, predicts a fully autonomous attack that takes an enterprise network down with no human driving it, inside 18 months. Her reasoning runs through attackers chaining low-risk vulnerabilities. That changes the patching math. A bug you scored as low risk is still a step in a chain an agent can walk without a person at the keyboard. She separates individual productivity use from mission-critical business transformation. The same episode notes that 62% of enterprise AI initiatives are stuck in pilots, and that agentic AI still needs a real control plane. I would read those together. A productivity assistant can live in a pilot. A workflow that can take a network down should not borrow that pilot's missing controls. I would not point an autonomous agent at a mission-critical system while that control plane is still undefined. Practical move: when you triage, ask whether a low-risk finding becomes useful once something can chain it with others. Patch and segment for that case, even when each item looks small on its own. How do you keep a bad prompt from using a strong tool? Malte Ubl, CTO of Vercel , describes agents as a new type of software for solving flexible tasks. The security lesson he says people get wrong most often is prompt injection. Teams treat it like SQL injection and filter what goes in. He argues for constraining what the tool can do. My inference is that flexible tasks are why the tool list grows. The agent is supposed to pick a path. That is also why a filter on the inbound text is a weak control. Text that gets past the filter still meets every function you exposed. I would write the constraint on the tool before spending time on the filter. This sketch is mine, for illustration. It is not a vendor SDK, and it is not a policy Malte spelled out. type Effect = " read " | " draft " | " send " | " pay " ; const allowed : Record string , Effect [] > = { inbox : [ " read " , " draft " ], billing : [ " read " ], }; function permit ( tool :

items.title: Why iBird Settles Social on HCS: The Protocol Comparison (Nostr, AtProto, ActivityPub)
items.snippet: Decentralized social has four live answers in 2026: Nostr relays, AT Protocol's app view, ActivityPub's server federation, and Hedera Consensus Service settlement. A first-party comparison of identity, permanence, operator risk, and cost — and why we chose con
items.content: Decentralized social has four live answers in 2026: Nostr relays, AT Protocol's app view, ActivityPub's server federation, and Hedera Consensus Service settlement. A first-party comparison of identity, permanence, operator risk, and cost — and why we chose consensus timestamps over relay trust. Four Answers to One Question Where does a social post actually live? Ask four communities and you'll get four architectures. This month the question got unusually loud — a Nostr-vs-fediverse-vs-Bluesky comparison and a NIP-05 identity explainer both drew large Hacker News discussions in the same week — so it's a good moment to lay out where iBird fits, from a first-party point of view and without pretending the alternatives are strawmen. The four live answers in 2026: Nostr — clients sign events; relay servers store and forward them. Simple, censorship-resistant at the client level, but permanence depends entirely on which relays choose to keep what. AT Protocol (Bluesky) — DIDs and portable identity, with data repos mirrored through relayer infrastructure and a company-operated app view that turns raw data into the feed users actually see. ActivityPub (the fediverse) — each server hosts its users and federates by mutual trust. Mature, huge, and human-scale, but content is bound to the server that hosts it. Consensus settlement (iBird) — every social action is a message on the Hedera Consensus Service , timestamped and sequenced by public infrastructure no single company operates. Identity: Where Does Your Name Come From? Nostr identity is a keypair. The NIP-05 convention maps keys to human-readable names, but the mapping lives on a web server — trust meanders back to DNS and whoever hosts the mapping file. Bluesky issues DIDs and resolves handles through DNS or operator infrastructure. ActivityPub identity is a URL on your home server; when the server folds, the identity and the graph around it fold too. iBird uses Hedera accounts surfaced through HCS-14 UAIDs — verifiable identifiers rooted in a council-governed ledger. Every message is signed by the account that produced it, and provenance is checkable on-chain rather than recon­structed from a naming convention hosted somewhere. Permanence: Trust Me vs. Consensus The honest framing is who you're trusting . On Nostr you trust relay operators to keep storing your events. items.snippet: n8n News Monitoring Workflow: Build a Free Daily Web Digest An n8n news monitoring workflow checks the web for you: every morning it searches your topics, drops anything it already showed you, has a model summarize what's new, and emails you the digest. This g
items.content: n8n News Monitoring Workflow: Build a Free Daily Web Digest An n8n news monitoring workflow checks the web for you: every morning it searches your topics, drops anything it already showed you, has a model summarize what's new, and emails you the digest. This guide builds it with the free n8n-nodes-agentsearch community node, with no search API key and an importable workflow JSON. Install the node first (self-hosted n8n, then restart): cd ~/.n8n/nodes && npm install n8n-nodes-agentsearch Or use Settings > Community Nodes > Install and enter n8n-nodes-agentsearch . Here's the whole pipeline: Schedule Trigger -> Topics (Code) -> AgentSearch (Free Search, split) -> Only New URLs (Remove Duplicates) -> Build Digest Prompt (Code) -> Summarize (Basic LLM Chain + chat model) -> Send Email What we checked: every AgentSearch parameter and output field below comes from the n8n-nodes-agentsearch 0.2.4 package (npm latest on November 2, 2026). Core node types and parameters come from n8n's docs and node source. We ran one real free search against the endpoint the node calls and ran both Code node scripts in Node.js against that output. We didn't run the full workflow inside n8n. Want a chat agent that decides when to search? See n8n AI agent web search . This post is the scheduled version. What the AgentSearch node gives you Version 0.2.4 has one node, AgentSearch (type n8n-nodes-agentsearch.agentSearch ), and one operation, Free Search ( freeSearch ). Because it sets usableAsTool , n8n also offers it to the AI Agent node as AgentSearch Tool ( n8n-nodes-agentsearch.agentSearchTool ). A digest doesn't need an agent, so we use the plain node: Query ( query , required). Expressions work, so {{ $json.topic }} searches one topic per input item. Max Results ( maxResults , 1 to 5, default 5). Split Results Into Items ( split , default off). On means one output item per result. No credentials. The free tier allows up to 25 searches per day per IP, each returning up to 5 results. With split on, every item carries query , title , url and content . items.title: Only 6 of 45 Odds APIs Cover All 8 Big US Sportsbooks
items.snippet: If you build a betting app, the first question is which sportsbooks the odds API carries. Pricing pages promise "all the major books". We counted what you get. We track 45 odds APIs and 135 books. For 10 of the APIs, we call the API with our own key every 3 da
items.content: If you build a betting app, the first question is which sportsbooks the odds API carries. Pricing pages promise "all the major books". We counted what you get. We track 45 odds APIs and 135 books. For 10 of the APIs, we call the API with our own key every 3 days and record what comes back. For the other 35, we read the provider's docs. This is the snapshot from 1 November 2026. The big US books Sportsbook APIs that list it (of 45) Verified by probe (of 10) DraftKings 23 5 FanDuel 20 4 BetMGM 20 5 BetRivers 19 4 theScore Bet 18 5 Caesars 16 4 Fanatics 16 4 Hard Rock Bet 16 4 25 APIs list at least one of these 8 books. Only 6 list all 8. If your app needs every one of them, you have a shortlist of 6 before you compare a single price. One more pattern: every API that lists FanDuel also lists DraftKings. Three list DraftKings without FanDuel. Prediction markets match the majors Kalshi ties DraftKings at 23 APIs. Novig, a US sports exchange, is on 18, two more than Caesars. In total, 25 APIs list at least one prediction market or exchange, the same number that list a big US book. If you devig sportsbook lines against exchange prices, check that one API carries both. Two feeds with different timestamps add error that is hard to spot. Book count and market depth The API with the most books in our probes did not return the most markets. One API with about a fifth as many books returned twice as many markets. For a props product, depth can matter more than breadth. Check your own case List the books, leagues and markets you cannot ship without. Filter for them in a coverage tool, and prefer verified matches over docs claims. Test on a free tier before you pay. The full tables, the method and a free CSV (CC BY 4.0) are in the Odds API Coverage Report .

items.title: MiniMax H3 Video Upscaling in ComfyUI: Five H3 Routes and One LTX 2.5 Detailer
items.snippet: There are two ways to make a video bigger. You can resample it and hope the detail holds, or you can regenerate the detail with a diffusion model while keeping the motion and composition. This episode ships six ComfyUI graphs for the second approach: five Mini
items.content: There are two ways to make a video bigger. You can resample it and hope the detail holds, or you can regenerate the detail with a diffusion model while keeping the motion and composition. This episode ships six ComfyUI graphs for the second approach: five MiniMax H3 routes (first/last-frame and multi-reference, in two- and three-stage variants) plus one LTX 2.5 video-to-video detailer. No inference was run for this release. Everything below is read from the saved graphs. There is no timing, VRAM or quality claim. One attribution note before the details: several graphs keep in-file notes referencing MarkDKBerry.com (YouTube/Patreon). Those indicate the source material is adapted from third-party public workflows. The notes are preserved in the distributed JSONs and this article does not claim to be the original author of those graphs. # Route Nodes / links Passes 01 LTX 2.5 V2V detailer 20 / 26 single pass + tiled VAE 02 FL2VA three-stage 2K 72 / 98 8/1 → 0.65 → 0.65 03 FL2VA two-stage 59 / 68 8/1 → 0.65 04 Ref2VA three-stage 2K 75 / 109 8/1 → 0.65 → 0.65 05 Ref2VA two-stage 63 / 80 8/1 → 0.65 06 Universal single-pass 26 / 34 one 4-step pass The shared H3 pattern The five H3 graphs all run a first pass at 8 steps, CFG 1, beta scheduler, denoise 1, with sigma shift 6/3 (the "dynamic-first" setting). Then a pixel-space RTX upscale node scales the video by 1.5×, and a second pass runs at 4 steps, denoise 0.65, sigma shift 12/3, re-conditioned at the actual upscaled size. The three-stage files repeat that upscale-and-refine once more. Two practical traps are baked into these files and worth calling out: The RTX node title and its saved multiplier disagree in several files. The title says ×1.5 while the widget is 2.0. Check the widget before queueing; the label is not the value. One scheduler title is stale. In the two-stage FL2VA file, a PASS 2 scheduler is titled "8 steps / denoise 0.30" but its saved widgets are 4 steps / 0.65. Quote the widgets. There are also loader differences worth knowing: the Ref2VA routes use a MiniMaxH3HybridLoader (H25 + LightX2V 8) as the active model path, and the universal single-pass file uses a DiffusionModelLoaderKJ — it has no UNETLoader node at all. If you search these JSONs for a UNETLoader to confirm the model, you will not find one in file 06. 01 — LTX 2.5 V2V detailer This is the outlier: a different model family. ltx-2.5-22b-distilled-transformer-bf16 , a Gemma 4 12B text encoder with type ltxv, and the LTX 2.5 video VAE

items.title: Building a Custom Node.js Service for Secure OTP Validation with an External SMS API
items.snippet: Use a small Node.js OTP service with an external SMS API when a healthtech marketplace needs to notify a seller about a new order and then protect the seller's 2FA login. The important decision is the integration boundary: keep randomness, expiry, attempt limi
items.content: Use a small Node.js OTP service with an external SMS API when a healthtech marketplace needs to notify a seller about a new order and then protect the seller's 2FA login. The important decision is the integration boundary: keep randomness, expiry, attempt limits, and verification in your backend, and make the SMS provider responsible for delivery rather than security policy. The invariant is simple: a code is generated with a cryptographic random source, stored only as a short-lived record, and marked consumed after one successful verification. The failure boundary is equally important. A successful API response means the provider accepted a send request; it does not prove that the phone received the message. Delivery status, abuse controls, and account recovery remain application concerns. What should the service own? For an order notification flow, I would keep an order event and an authentication challenge separate. The marketplace can notify a seller about order ord_8124 , while the login service creates an OTP challenge for that seller's verified phone number. Mixing those records makes retries dangerous: a repeated order event should never create a fresh login code, and a repeated login request should not invalidate a code that is already in flight. Store a hash of the OTP, not the plaintext. Save the user identifier, purpose, creation time, expiry time, attempt count, and a consumed timestamp. A five- or six-digit code has limited entropy, so the expiry and attempt ceiling are part of the security mechanism, not housekeeping. Hashing does not rescue an unlimited online guesser. The code is disposable. Five attempts is a policy, not a law. Here is the critical path in compact Python. In Node.js, use crypto.randomInt or crypto.randomBytes for the equivalent generation step; do not use Math.random . The database transaction that consumes a valid challenge must be atomic. items.title: UG25 VTOL Log Validation: A Python State Machine That Keeps Data Gaps Visible
items.snippet: A log contains a fixed observation followed by ground . A simple state-machine checker reports an invalid transition. Then somebody notices that the sequence number jumped from 17 to 24. The software has diagnosed the path between two observations without havi
items.content: A log contains a fixed observation followed by ground . A simple state-machine checker reports an invalid transition. Then somebody notices that the sequence number jumped from 17 to 24. The software has diagnosed the path between two observations without having that path in its input. This is a common failure in telemetry tooling: a correct transition table is applied to the wrong pair of records. Missing observations, repeated delivery, restarts and mixed producers can all change what adjacency means. Adding more states does not repair that mistake. The observer needs a separate model of continuity before it can evaluate a state change. This tutorial builds a small offline Python observer for that problem. It uses a fixed-wing VTOL aircraft as its application context, defines a deliberately explicit CSV contract, and produces findings that retain the distinction between unexplained transitions and missing information. You can adapt the pattern to log importers, maintenance dashboards or integration test tools without connecting it to aircraft control. Why the UG25 is a useful context The current UG25 fixed-wing VTOL product page describes vertical takeoff and transition into fixed-wing cruise. That combination gives a developer a concrete reason to distinguish vertical-lift operation, transition and fixed-wing operation in a diagnostic view. The listing does not establish the telemetry contract used below. The field names, phase labels and transition graph are tutorial definitions for a downstream adapter. Obtain the supported interface documentation and sample logs for an actual delivered configuration before mapping its reported values. A model name or product photograph cannot identify the installed controller, firmware revision or available logging fields. Check continuity before checking a transition There are two different questions. First, are these records consecutive observations from the same defined stream? Second, if they are, does their label change belong to the selected analysis graph? The first question determines whether the second is meaningful. In this example, continuity requires the same vehicle, producer and boot identifier; consecutive sequence numbers; and a strictly increasing source time whose interval does not exceed a configured threshold. items.title: The Evolution of Algorithmic Trading: How MQL5 and TradingView are Changing the Financial Markets
items.snippet: Introduction In today’s fast-paced financial markets, relying purely on manual chart analysis is no longer enough. The shift toward algorithmic trading has transformed how traders approach currency pairs, gold, and global markets. By automating execution and e
items.content: Introduction In today’s fast-paced financial markets, relying purely on manual chart analysis is no longer enough. The shift toward algorithmic trading has transformed how traders approach currency pairs, gold, and global markets. By automating execution and eliminating emotional bias, modern tools have leveled the playing field for independent analysts and developers worldwide. The Power of MQL5 in Automated Trading MetaTrader 5 (MT5) and its proprietary programming language, MQL5 , remain the backbone of custom algorithmic trading. Whether you are developing Expert Advisors (EAs), custom indicators, or automated risk management scripts, MQL5 offers multi-threaded testing and robust execution speeds. For traders operating in high-volatility environments like gold and major forex pairs, precision is everything—and MQL5 delivers the necessary depth for backtesting and optimization. TradingView: The Visual Strategy Hub While execution often happens on platforms like MetaTrader, ideation and strategy testing frequently start on TradingView . With Pine Script, traders can prototype ideas instantly, visualize market structures, and monitor multi-timeframe trends. Combining TradingView’s analytical prowess with automated execution creates a comprehensive workflow for modern algorithmic traders. Conclusion Algorithmic trading is not about removing the human element entirely; it is about refining strategy, managing risk mathematically, and scaling precision. As financial markets continue to evolve, mastering tools like MQL5 and TradingView is essential for any serious market participant. Written by **Mohammad Ali Charooseh (محمدعلی چاروسه) * — Financial Markets Analyst & Algorithmic Trading Enthusiast.*

items.title: Krea 2 Advanced Cleanup in ComfyUI: One Recipe, Three I/O Shells
items.snippet: Krea 2 cleanup graphs all share the same skeleton, and once you see it the three workflows in this episode stop looking like three different products. They are one recipe wrapped in three different I/O shells: a single image, a local folder loop, and a Running
items.content: Krea 2 cleanup graphs all share the same skeleton, and once you see it the three workflows in this episode stop looking like three different products. They are one recipe wrapped in three different I/O shells: a single image, a local folder loop, and a RunningHub ZIP batch. The recipe: reverse-prompt the input image into a Krea 2 prompt, rebuild it through three depth-structure passes with one structure LoRA, then upscale with 4x-UltraSharp. A console at the top of each graph controls the render stages, the final long edge, and which reverse-prompt route to use. No inference was run for this release. Everything below is read from the saved nodes. Variant File Nodes / links I/O Single image 01 51 / 89 one LoadImage Local batch 02 57 / 98 folder loop, local-only Online batch 03 66 / 109 RunningHub ZIP + batch nodes The shared engine All three load krea2_turbo_fp8.safetensors , encode text with qwen3vl_4b_fp8_scaled.safetensors (type krea2 ) and use qwen_image_HDR_vae_fp32_comfy.safetensors as the VAE. There is exactly one structure LoRA — a Krea2ControlLoRALoader on depth-control-lora.safetensors at strength 1.0. If you were expecting the three-strength preset trio from the later cleanup release, that is a different episode; this one uses a single shared LoRA. The depth side is three Krea2ControlImageEncode → Krea2ControlApply pairs: source-size encoding for the high-noise stage, a mid-size encoding, and a final-size encoding. The depth maps come from DA3 nodes in-graph. Sampling is three KSamplers at 8 steps, CFG 1, euler, simple. Denoise is 0.55 in the single-image file and 0.95 in the two batch files for the base pass, then 0.35 and 0.25 for the following passes. Two LatentUpscale nodes are present but saved disabled; the real upscale is UpscaleModelLoader with 4x-UltraSharp.pth plus ImageUpscaleWithModel . The reverse-prompt stage has two routes: Qwen3VLProcessor for the open-source path, and an RH_LLMAPI_Pro_Node for the closed path (its model label is GLM-4.6V). The console decides which one is active. 01 — Single image: the cleanest read The single-image file is the best place to understand the recipe. One LoadImage, the console, three depth passes, the upscale, and a save to KSK_Krea2_ReverseDepthHires . ConditioningKrea2Rebalance is saved bypassed here, and the ComfyUI-Krea2T-Enhancer patch is saved enabled. Practical dial: the graph's own note says 2048 on the long edge is the value-for-money point and that 3072/4096 increase VRAM and cost noticeab

items.title: Per-customer budget caps for Anthropic API calls (with prompt caching priced right)
items.snippet: If your product calls Claude on behalf of your customers, one heavy account can spend a month's margin in a weekend. Anthropic's console limits protect your organization. They don't know which of your customers sent the traffic, so they can't stop one of them
items.content: If your product calls Claude on behalf of your customers, one heavy account can spend a month's margin in a weekend. Anthropic's console limits protect your organization. They don't know which of your customers sent the traffic, so they can't stop one of them without stopping everyone. This post builds a per-customer monthly cap for the Anthropic Messages API in TypeScript: Price each call correctly, including prompt-cache reads and writes . Check the budget before the call, in a way that holds up under concurrent requests. Switch to a cheaper model near the cap, and refuse at the cap. It uses @anthropic-ai/sdk and Redis ( ioredis ). The ideas carry over to any store with atomic operations. 1. Pricing a Messages API call A Claude response's usage has four token counts that matter for cost: Field What it is Billed at input_tokens input after the last cache breakpoint base input price cache_read_input_tokens prefix read from the prompt cache 0.1x base for most models (0.05x for Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5) cache_creation_input_tokens prefix written to the cache this call 1.25x base (5-minute TTL), 2x (1-hour TTL) output_tokens generated tokens, including thinking output price The trap is that input_tokens is not the total input. Total input is input_tokens + cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens . If you only price input_tokens , a cached chat app looks almost free. And if you ignore cache writes, you under-count the first call of every conversation by 25% or more on its prefix. When the 1-hour TTL is in play, usage.cache_creation splits writes into ephemeral_5m_input_tokens and ephemeral_1h_input_tokens , so you can price them separately. // prices.ts: USD per 1M tokens, standard tier. // From https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/about-claude/pricing, read 2026-11-02. Check before relying on these. type Price = { input : number ; output : number ; cacheRead : number ; cacheWrite5m : number ; cacheWrite1h : number }; export const PRICES : Record string , Price > = { " claude-sonnet-5-5 " : { input : 2.0 , output : 10.0 , cacheRead : 0.1 , cacheWrite5m : 2.5 , cacheWrite1h : 4.0 }, // Haiku 5.5 has a higher price for prompts over 100K tokens; this is the up-to-100K tier. " claude-haiku-5-5 " : { input : 0.1 , output : 0.5 , cacheRead : 0.01 , cacheWrite5m : 0.125 , cacheWrite1h : 0.2 }, }; export interface ClaudeUsage { input_tokens : number ; output_tokens : number ; cache_read_input_tokens ?: number | null ; cache_creation_input_tokens ?: number |

items.title: Tracking LLM cost per customer in Node.js with AsyncLocalStorage
items.snippet: Your OpenAI invoice tells you what you spent. It doesn't tell you which customer you spent it on. If you sell a flat-price plan on top of an LLM, that second number is the one that decides whether a customer is profitable. The usual first attempt is to add a c
items.content: Your OpenAI invoice tells you what you spent. It doesn't tell you which customer you spent it on. If you sell a flat-price plan on top of an LLM, that second number is the one that decides whether a customer is profitable. The usual first attempt is to add a customerId parameter to every function that might end up calling the model. That works until the call sits five layers down, inside a retry helper, a summarizer, and a background job. This post shows a smaller approach: Put the customer on the request's async context once, in middleware. Wrap the OpenAI client once, so every call reads that context and logs its cost. Store one row per call and use SQL for the questions you actually have. Everything here is plain Node 18+ and the official openai package. No proxy, no extra service. 1. Put the customer on the async context Node's AsyncLocalStorage carries a value through every await , timer and promise that starts inside a run() call. That's exactly the scope of "this HTTP request". // context.ts import { AsyncLocalStorage } from " node:async_hooks " ; export interface CostContext { customerId : string ; plan ?: string ; feature ?: string ; // "chat", "summarize", "search"... useful later } export const costContext = new AsyncLocalStorage CostContext > (); export function currentCostContext (): CostContext | undefined { return costContext . getStore (); } In Express (any framework with middleware works the same way): app . use (( req , res , next ) => { const user = req . user ; // whatever your auth sets if ( ! user ) return next (); costContext . run ({ customerId : user . id , plan : user . plan }, next ); }); To tag a feature, nest another run() around the code that implements it: export function withFeature T > ( feature : string , fn : () => Promise T > ): Promise T > { const parent = currentCostContext (); if ( ! parent ) return fn (); return costContext . run ({ ... parent , feature }, fn ); } // in a route handler const summary = await withFeature ( " summarize " , () => summarizeThread ( thread )); Background jobs don't go through your middleware, so start a context there too, using the customer the job belongs to: queue . process ( async ( job ) => costContext . run ({ customerId : job . data . customerId , feature : " nightly-digest " }, () => runDigest ( job . data ), ), ); 2. items.title: The Seed Decides Everything: fold() vs reduce() in Production Kotlin on Android
items.snippet: fold() and reduce() look like twins. Both walk a collection, both hand you an acc and the next element, and both collapse everything into one value. Most developers pick whichever name comes to mind first, and for a long time nothing bad happens. Then a Room q
items.content: fold() and reduce() look like twins. Both walk a collection, both hand you an acc and the next element, and both collapse everything into one value. Most developers pick whichever name comes to mind first, and for a long time nothing bad happens. Then a Room query returns zero rows, a Flow emits its first empty list, and a screen crashes in production with UnsupportedOperationException . Or a "harmless" reduce quietly rewrites the first item in your UI state. Or a total of cached bytes wraps around to a negative number on a device with a big cache. All of these trace back to one question: where does the accumulator start? This post walks through the mechanics, the type rules that follow from them, and the failure modes I would flag in a code review. The examples use a download and sync domain, so none of it is tied to a particular app. The one difference that matters fold(initial) starts from a value you provide, then processes every element. reduce starts from the first element and processes the remaining ones. Here is the same sum written both ways: data class DownloadPart ( val index : Int , val bytes : Long , val error : String ? = null , ) val parts = listOf ( DownloadPart ( index = 0 , bytes = 4_096 ), DownloadPart ( index = 1 , bytes = 8_192 ), DownloadPart ( index = 2 , bytes = 2_048 ), ) // reduce needs elements that are already the accumulator's type, so we map first. val viaReduce : Long = parts . map { it . bytes } . reduce { acc , bytes -> acc + bytes } // fold starts from 0L, so it can read the field directly and skips the intermediate list. val viaFold : Long = parts . fold ( 0L ) { acc , part -> acc + part . bytes } Both give 14_336 . Look at what each version had to do to get there, though. The reduce version had to turn DownloadPart into Long first, because the accumulator and the elements share a type. The fold version was free to bring its own seed type. (For a plain sum you would normally write parts.sumOf { it.bytes } . I'm using fold here because it is the simplest case that shows the mechanics.) Type freedom: why fold builds state and reduce merges values Because fold takes an explicit seed, its result type R is independent of the element type T : inline fun T , R > Iterable T >. fold ( initial : R , operation : ( acc : R , T ) -> R , ): R reduce has no seed to infer anything from. Its signature ties the accumulator to the elements: inline fun S , T : S > Iterable T >. reduce ( operation : ( acc : S , T ) -> S , ): S S has to be a s

items.title: Starting My DSA Journey with C++ — Learning One Problem at a Time 🚀
items.snippet: I've decided to take my Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA) preparation more seriously and, instead of just solving problems privately, I want to start documenting my learning journey here. I'm currently practising DSA using C++, with a simple goal: build str
items.content: I've decided to take my Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA) preparation more seriously and, instead of just solving problems privately, I want to start documenting my learning journey here. I'm currently practising DSA using C++, with a simple goal: build strong problem-solving skills, understand the logic behind solutions, and become better at writing efficient code. Why I started this journey One thing I've realised is that knowing programming syntax and actually solving problems are two different things. You might know loops, conditions, arrays, and functions, but applying them to solve a problem requires a different level of understanding. That's what I want to improve through consistent practice. What I'm currently working on I'm starting with basic logic-building problems, particularly star patterns. At first, these problems might look simple, but they are a great way to understand nested loops and how program execution works. For example, consider this pattern: * While solving it, I explored how the outer loop controls the rows and the inner loop controls the number of stars printed in each row. One interesting thing I learned was how the expression 2 * i - 1 can generate an increasing odd number of stars without manually specifying the count for every row. It's a small concept, but understanding the mathematics behind the logic makes a difference. How I plan to document my progress I'm planning to follow a consistent approach: Practise problems regularly. Understand the logic before looking at solutions. Maintain notes about concepts and mistakes. Complete problems in batches of five. Push my solutions and progress updates to GitHub. I'll also share what I learn, the problems I find challenging, and the concepts that become clearer along the way. My goal I don't want this to become just another repository filled with solutions. I want it to reflect my actual learning process — including the mistakes, confusion, improvements, and progress. I know consistency matters more than speed, so I'm taking it one problem at a time. This is Day 1 of documenting my DSA journey. Let's see how far consistent effort can take me! GitHub Repository: DSA #CPP #CPlusPlus #Programming #LearningInPublic #100DaysOfCode #ProblemSolving #DeveloperJourney

items.title: How I turn Hacker News, GitHub and npm into product ideas every 3 hours
items.snippet: Picking what to build was my slowest step, so I built a pipeline for it. Here is how it works. 1. Collect Every 3 hours a collector pulls from 23 sources. The builder sources are Hacker News, Lobsters, new GitHub repos, trending npm packages, Product Hunt, r/S
items.content: Picking what to build was my slowest step, so I built a pipeline for it. Here is how it works. 1. Collect Every 3 hours a collector pulls from 23 sources. The builder sources are Hacker News, Lobsters, new GitHub repos, trending npm packages, Product Hunt, r/SideProject, r/microsaas, TLDR and Changelog. Wider signals come from Google Trends, Google News, Bluesky, Mastodon and a few others. 2. Filter A trend only enters the feed when at least two builder sources mention it. One viral post is noise; the same thing showing up on HN and in new GitHub repos is a signal. 3. Turn signals into ideas, with your own agent The Mac app sends the feed and the pages behind each trend to the coding agent you already use (Claude Code, Codex, opencode, Gemini CLI and others). The agent runs read-only, in an empty temp folder , so it never touches your files. It writes ranked ideas, each with who would pay, a price, a 7-day plan and source links. 4. Check in code, not with AI Pulsar checks the shape of the answer in code (every idea needs a plan and links) and retries once if it is off. No AI grades the AI. Try it Pulsar is a Mac app, $9 one-time, one free preview per computer: https://getpulsar.web.app . It launched on Product Hunt today. I'd like to hear how you decide what to build next.

items.title: We rebuilt our Kalshi AI trading bot from its own prompt twice: it bought a filled order again
items.snippet: Originally published on BotCookery , free build recipes for AI-built trading and prediction-market bots. Written with AI assistance. Every log line below is from real runs on Oct 24 and Oct 27, 2026, with live market data from Kalshi's demo exchange and a mock
items.content: Originally published on BotCookery , free build recipes for AI-built trading and prediction-market bots. Written with AI assistance. Every log line below is from real runs on Oct 24 and Oct 27, 2026, with live market data from Kalshi's demo exchange and a mock broker: no keys, and no order was sent anywhere. Nothing here is financial advice, and the strategy in this bot is a placeholder. Our Kalshi AI trading bot recipe is a prompt. You paste it into your AI coding tool in an empty folder and it builds a small Python bot that runs on Kalshi's demo environment by default: it watches a few markets, applies your rule, checks hard limits in code, and places 1-contract limit orders inside an order group, with a kill switch and an optional LLM research step that only ever sees public market text. The interesting part of a bot like this isn't the strategy. It's everything around the order: what happens on restart, after a fill, when a market closes, when the API is slow. So we tested exactly that. Twice, we pasted the published prompt into a clean folder, built it as written, and ran it against live demo markets with a mock broker. The first pass (Oct 24) found three bugs. The second pass (Oct 27) built the fixed Oct 24 prompt exactly as written and found five more. The prompt is now fixed for all eight. None of them was a crash. Each one was the bot quietly doing the wrong thing with orders, limits or retries. The Kalshi side in one paragraph Orders go to POST /portfolio/events/orders (Create Order V2; Kalshi says the legacy /portfolio/orders will be deprecated no earlier than May 6, 2026). The body has ticker , side ( bid or ask ), count as a string, price as a fixed-point dollar string like "0.5600" , time_in_force , self_trade_prevention_type , and optional client_order_id , post_only , reduce_only and cancel_order_on_pause . Order groups ( POST /portfolio/order_groups/create ) auto-cancel every resting order in the group if fills exceed a contracts limit in a rolling 15-second window. DELETE /portfolio/events/orders cancels everything. Demo lives at https://external-api.demo.kalshi.co/trade-api/v2 , with separate keys. Kalshi's order book lists bids only, so the implied YES ask is 1.00 minus the best NO bid; no NO bids means no ask, and the bot doesn't trade. items.title: Building a Delivery Dispatch Backend: The Decisions That Actually Mattered
items.snippet: Most backend portfolio projects are CRUD with extra steps. I wanted to build something with actual teeth, a system where the interesting work isn’t the endpoints but the handful of places where a naive implementation would quietly break under real conditions.
items.content: Most backend portfolio projects are CRUD with extra steps. I wanted to build something with actual teeth, a system where the interesting work isn’t the endpoints but the handful of places where a naive implementation would quietly break under real conditions. So I built a scaled-down version of what sits behind an app like Uber Eats or Chowdeck: a backend that coordinates customers, vendors, and riders through the full order lifecycle, live rider matching, atomic assignment under concurrency, idempotent payment webhooks, and automatic reassignment when nobody’s available. This article isn’t a tour of every endpoint. It’s a discussion of questions I had to answer with code and why I answered them the way I did. “What happens when two orders want the same rider at the same instant?” This is the core of the whole dispatch problem. A customer’s order gets accepted by a vendor, and the system needs to find the nearest available rider and lock them in. Still, if two vendors accept orders within milliseconds of each other, and the pool of available riders near both is the same three people, you will get a collision eventually. The naive fix would be to “check if the rider is available, then assign them.” But that has a race condition baked directly into its two steps. Both requests can pass the check before either one writes. I used two atomic Redis operations instead of application-level locking: SET order:lock:{orderId} riderId NX EX 10 : an atomic compare-and-set with a self-expiring TTL, so a crashed process doesn’t leave an order permanently locked. SREM riders:available riderId : Redis’s set-remove command returns exactly how many elements it removed. Only the caller that gets 1 back actually claimed the rider. Everyone else, even if they got there “at the same time” from the application’s perspective, gets 0 and moves to the next candidate. “What happens when a payment provider retries a webhook?” Payment providers don’t trust a single delivery attempt. If they don’t get a fast 200 response back, they resend, sometimes more than once. Any webhook handler that isn’t explicitly idempotent will eventually double-process a payment. I handle this by inserting the event’s event_id into a table with a UNIQUE constraint inside the same database transaction as the status update. A duplicate delivery hits that constraint; the transaction rolls back cleanly, and the response is still a 200 (so the provider stops retrying), so it just reports duplicate: true instead o

items.title: Next.js Open Graph Image Missing? Your Page Replaced It
items.snippet: My homepage had a share image. Fourteen other pages on my site didn't, and nothing told me. I only found out when I ran my own pages through a metadata checker I'd just built. Lighthouse hadn't flagged it: pages with no og:image still scored 100 for SEO. The c
items.content: My homepage had a share image. Fourteen other pages on my site didn't, and nothing told me. I only found out when I ran my own pages through a metadata checker I'd just built. Lighthouse hadn't flagged it: pages with no og:image still scored 100 for SEO. The cause Here's the setup almost every Next.js site starts with. The layout holds the shared tags, and each page adds its own title. // app/layout.tsx export const metadata : Metadata = { metadataBase : new URL ( " https://example.com " ), openGraph : { type : " website " , siteName : " Example " , images : [ " /og-image.jpg " ], }, }; // app/pricing/page.tsx export const metadata : Metadata = { title : " Pricing " , openGraph : { title : " Pricing " , url : " /pricing " }, }; It reads as if the page adds to the layout's Open Graph tags. It doesn't. Next.js merges metadata shallowly, so nested fields like openGraph are "overwritten by the last segment to define them". The page's object replaces the layout's whole object. That pricing page ships with no og:image , no og:type and no site name. The homepage usually looks fine because it never sets its own openGraph , which is why this is so easy to miss. Why it stays hidden Nothing fails. An openGraph object without images is valid, so my build gave no error or warning. The page renders and can rank as normal. The only symptom is in a shared link, which appears without an image in chat apps and social feeds. And you probably test sharing with your homepage, the one page that works. The fix Keep the shared fields in one object and spread it into every openGraph . The Next.js docs suggest the same pattern. // lib/metadata.ts export const OG_DEFAULTS = { type : " website " as const , locale : " en_US " , siteName : " Example " , images : [{ url : " /og-image.jpg " , width : 1200 , height : 630 , alt : " Example " }], }; // app/pricing/page.tsx export const metadata : Metadata = { title : " Pricing " , openGraph : { ... OG_DEFAULTS , title : " Pricing " , url : " /pricing " }, }; Put page-specific values after the spread, such as type: "article" on a blog post or a different image on a case study. If one page deserves its own image, add an opengraph-image.jpg file to that page's folder. Next.js generates the tags for you, and file-based metadata takes priority over the metadata object. items.title: Your CI is red because of code you didn't write
items.snippet: TL;DR: Added a markdownlint check to 33 repos at once — and woke up to ~100 CI failure emails about code I didn't write. The fix: lint only the files changed in the PR, never the whole backlog. Grandfather existing violations; enforce the standard on new chang
items.content: TL;DR: Added a markdownlint check to 33 repos at once — and woke up to ~100 CI failure emails about code I didn't write. The fix: lint only the files changed in the PR, never the whole backlog. Grandfather existing violations; enforce the standard on new changes. I maintain a GitHub org with 33 open-source repos . Last month I decided to do the responsible thing: add a default markdownlint check to every repo so our docs stay consistent. By the next morning I had ~100 failure emails in my inbox. Here's what went wrong — and the rollout playbook I'd use instead. What happened The lint workflow ran against every markdown file in each repo — READMEs, changelogs, and contributor guides written years ago by people who had never heard of markdownlint. Upstream markdown, as it turns out, has never passed a linter in its life. Trailing spaces, inconsistent heading levels, bare URLs — the works. My inbox became a firehose of red X's on code I didn't write, in files I'd never touched, for rules nobody on those projects had agreed to. The noise-vs-signal problem This is the classic failure mode of adopting tooling across many repos at once: Signal: "the file you just edited violates the style guide" Noise: "a README from 2021 has trailing whitespace" When 95% of failures are noise, people stop reading CI results entirely — and then the 5% that matter get ignored too. A check everyone ignores is worse than no check at all. The fix: scope linting to the files you own Instead of linting the whole repo, I changed the workflow to lint only files changed in the PR : - uses : actions/checkout@v4 - name : Get changed files id : changed uses : tj-actions/changed-files@v44 with : files : | **/*.md - name : Lint changed markdown if : steps.changed.outputs.any_changed == 'true' run : npx markdownlint-cli ${{ steps.changed.outputs.all_changed_files }} Overnight the emails stopped. CI went green on every repo, and the check still catches every new violation — which is the only thing it was ever supposed to do. The broader lesson: a playbook for rolling out tooling across many repos Never lint the backlog on day one. Grandfather existing violations; enforce the standard on new changes only. Scope every check to what the PR touches. Changed-files linting, diff-aware tests, incremental type checks — same principle everywhere. Disable noisy upstream workflows you don't own rather than letting them train everyone to ignore red. Keep the checks you own green. A green build people trust

items.content: This article provides a step by step guide to running Gemma 4 E2B with the model written in Rust and every operation executed by TorchTPU, on a Colab v5e-1 runtime: one TPU v5e chip. A Rust crate reads the checkpoint, unpacks the 4-bit weights, runs the 35 layers and the ring cache, and drives the decode loop. Python hosts the backend and starts the engine. No JAX is involved. https://github.com/xbill9/torchtpu-dev/tree/main/colab/rust Rust writes the same tokens as compiled Python at about half the streaming speed and less than half the peak memory. Same chip, same checkpoint, same 19-token prompt, 64 greedy tokens, 33,024-token context: One Colab v5e-1 chip Streamed tok/s Batched tok/s First call Peak memory Rust, defer-and-fuse 14.7 to 15.7 15.2 to 16.0 82 to 84 s 7.75 GB Rust, strict eager 4.8 to 5.0 4.8 23 to 25 s 8.62 GB Python torch.compile 33.4 to 33.5 45.1 to 45.2 98 to 101 s 16.91 GB Both Rust ways match the compiled Python model on all 64 tokens and on all three long-prompt answers. What Is Being Measured? TorchTPU ( torch_tpu ) is a PyTorch backend for TPUs. The question here is how far a model can move out of Python and still run on it. The Rust ways run on PyTorch 2.13.0 and the Python baseline on 2.14.1. The notebook swaps versions between them, for a reason Step 3 covers. The model is Gemma 4 E2B in the W4A16 repack xbill9/gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-q4_0-w4a16-ct-text , with the per-layer table from its -text-emb4 twin. The Python baseline comes from notebook 05, the ring cache in PyTorch on TPU: Hands On With Colab . Versions on the Colab image: Python 3.13.18, torch_tpu 0.2.0, libtpu 0.0.50, Transformers 5.20.2, compressed-tensors 0.19.0, rustc 1.99.1. SKAdNetwork 4.0 postback windows and why treating them identically breaks your measurement 2. A production-ready coarse conversion value mapping calibrated to LTV tiers 3. The unit economics spreadsheet that tells you whether to press scale or fix your funnel first Let me show you a pattern I use in every project: anchor your MMP as the source of truth before you touch campaign structure. Everything downstream depends on it. --- ## Prerequisites - An iOS app live on the App Store with SKAdNetwork integrated - An MMP account (Adjust, AppsFlyer, or equivalent) with postback forwarding configured - A Meta Ads account running or planning Advantage+ App Campaigns - At least 60 days of cohort revenue data (you will need this for LTV calibration) - Basic familiarity with mobile attribution concepts (postbacks, conversion values, cohort ROAS) --- ## Step 1 — Understand the Three Postback Windows SKAdNetwork 4.0 introduced three distinct measurement windows. Most teams misconfigure these by treating them identically, which is the single most common cause of MMP-to-Meta reporting discrepancies above 20%. | Window | Lookback | Conversion Value Type | Typical Signal | |--------|----------|-----------------------|----------------| | 1 | Day 0–2 | Fine (0–63) + Coarse | Early engagement, tutorial completion | | 2 | Day 3–7 | Coarse only (low/medium/high) | First purchase, subscription trial | | 3 | Day 8–35 | Coarse only (low/medium/high) | Repeat purchase, D30 LTV proxy | The docs do not emphasize this enough, but fine-grained values in window 1 are only returned when your campaign clears Apple's crowd anonymity threshold. Plan for coarse values as your **baseline** , not your fallback. items.title: How I Built a Mac Cleaner in Rust
items.snippet: CleanMyMac wanted $40 to renew. I cancelled, looked for a free alternative, and didn't find one that felt like a real Mac app. So I spent a few weeks writing my own. This is the story of SweepMac — and the parts that were genuinely interesting to build. What i
items.content: CleanMyMac wanted $40 to renew. I cancelled, looked for a free alternative, and didn't find one that felt like a real Mac app. So I spent a few weeks writing my own. This is the story of SweepMac — and the parts that were genuinely interesting to build. What it does SweepMac is a native macOS cleaner. The usual surface: caches, logs, trash, leftover app data, browser privacy data, a disk-usage map, startup audit. Plus a menu-bar health monitor (RAM, CPU, disk, network, thermals) and malware scanning via ClamAV. Free, open-source (BSD-3), no telemetry, no accounts, no subscription. ~3.2 MB app. The safety model (the part I'm most proud of) Cleaning apps are dangerous software. One wrong click and you've trashed ~/Library. So before writing a single scanner, I spent time reverse-engineering CleanMyMac's guardrails using REA (a reverse-engineering toolchain). Here's what I found and rebuilt: Trash-first, always. The only remover in CleanMyMac is MoveToTrashFileRemover — everything goes to Trash, nothing is hard-deleted. SweepMac does the same: trash_paths() moves files to Trash, and the UI says "Undo from the Trash if needed." SIP check everywhere. CleanMyMac calls isFileProtectedByRootlessAtPath: from 10 different frameworks. I traced it — it forwards to Apple's own NSFileManager isFileProtectedByRootless:. SweepMac uses the public equivalent: stat flags & SF_RESTRICTED (0x80000). Every scanner walk skips restricted paths. Verified live against /System/Library/CoreServices → protected. Ignore list. CleanMyMac has an IgnorableNodeType framework with live publishers. SweepMac has a persisted set at ~/.sweepmac/ignored — per-item "Ignore" button, skipped by all scans. Pre-clean snapshots. CleanMyMac has SnapshotsStorage with makeSnapshot/restore. SweepMac writes a JSON manifest (~/.sweepmac/snapshots/.json) of every item before cleaning — and aborts the clean if the snapshot fails to save. Never clean what you didn't record. System-app data is never "orphan." CleanMyMac's orphan sweep flags any reverse-DNS folder over 1 MB under Library whose bundle ID isn't in the installed-apps set. But that set is built only from /Applications + ~/Applications — Apple's system apps live in /System/Applications and are never in the set. So com.apple.mediaanalysisd (428 MB), com.apple.Maps (13 MB) all qualified as "orphan" and were preselected for deletion. One click trashed live system data. Fix: skip com.apple.* keys (the same rule CleanMyMac's Protection module already uses

items.title: Canadian Developers Face Job Market Slowdown: Strategies to Navigate the Changing Landscape
items.snippet: Analytical Breakdown: Unraveling the Slowdown in Canada's Developer Job Market The Canadian developer job market has witnessed a pronounced slowdown, particularly in recent months, driven by a complex interplay of economic policies, global events, and structur
items.content: Analytical Breakdown: Unraveling the Slowdown in Canada's Developer Job Market The Canadian developer job market has witnessed a pronounced slowdown, particularly in recent months, driven by a complex interplay of economic policies, global events, and structural shifts in work dynamics. This analysis dissects the key mechanisms behind this trend, with a focus on the impact of trade tensions with the United States, and explores the broader implications for Canada's tech sector. Mechanisms Driving the Slowdown The perceived slowdown is underpinned by several interconnected processes, each amplifying the effects of the others. Below is a detailed examination of these mechanisms and their observable consequences: 1. Job Market Dynamics Influenced by Economic Policies and Global Events Trade Tensions with the USA: Impact: Escalating trade tensions between Canada and the United States have curtailed cross-border tech projects and investments. Internal Process: Uncertainty in trade relations prompts companies to defer or cancel projects, directly reducing job creation in tech sectors. Observable Effect: A noticeable decline in job postings within sectors heavily reliant on cross-border collaborations, signaling a contraction in opportunities. Global Economic Slowdowns: Impact: Global economic downturns have led to reduced funding for tech sectors, affecting Canadian companies disproportionately. Internal Process: Diminished investment forces tech companies to implement budget cuts and hiring freezes. Observable Effect: A scarcity of job opportunities and prolonged hiring cycles, further dampening market activity. Changes in Immigration Policies: Impact: Stricter immigration policies have restricted the influx of international talent, a critical resource for Canada's tech industry. Internal Process: Companies struggle to fill specialized roles due to a shrinking talent pool, exacerbating workforce gaps. Observable Effect: Prolonged hiring processes and an increasing number of unfilled positions, hindering operational efficiency. Remote Work and Global Competition: Impact: The rise of remote work has opened Canadian tech positions to global competition. Internal Process: International developers now compete for roles traditionally reserved for local talent, inflating applicant pools. Observable Effect: Intensified competition reduces job acquisition rates for Canadian developers, compounding the slowdown. Seasonal Fluctuations in Hiring: Impact: Seasonal variations

items.snippet: Introduction I recently completed the ShipIt Weekend: Deploy Your First App to Azure lab. It has three missions: Build it: write a small web app, package it in a Docker image and run it locally. Ship it: publish the image to GitHub Container Registry (GHCR) an
items.content: Introduction I recently completed the ShipIt Weekend: Deploy Your First App to Azure lab. It has three missions: Build it: write a small web app, package it in a Docker image and run it locally. Ship it: publish the image to GitHub Container Registry (GHCR) and run it on Azure Container Apps with a public HTTPS URL. Automate it: add a GitHub Actions pipeline that builds, pushes and deploys on every push to main . I worked through everything from a Linux terminal (Ubuntu on WSL, on a Windows laptop). This is not a polished "everything worked first time" tutorial. I made a few mistakes along the way: I named my repository differently from what the lab expected, my pipeline failed on its first run, and my first credential claim was rejected. I've kept those moments in, because that is where most of the learning happens. What you'll need: A GitHub account An Azure account with an active subscription Docker, Git and the Azure CLI installed in a Linux-style terminal (WSL works well on Windows) A note on screenshots: I blurred subscription IDs, tenant IDs and secrets in the images below. I also deleted the token, the service principal and the Azure resources after finishing, so nothing shown here can be used. Do the same, and never publish real credentials. Mission 1: Build it, containerise a web app Step 1: Create the project and a Git repository mkdir -p ~/shipit-app && cd ~/shipit-app git init -b main mkdir -p creates the folder (and doesn't complain if it already exists), and && runs cd only if that succeeded. git init -b main turns the folder into a Git repository and names the first branch main . Step 2: Write the web app The app uses only Python's standard library, so there is nothing to install and less that can break. cat > app.py ' EOF ' import os from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer MESSAGE = "Hello from ShipIt Weekend!" class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler): def do_GET(self): body = f" {MESSAGE} Built with Docker, shipped to Azure, automated with GitHub Actions. ".encode() self.send_response(200) self.send_header("Content-Type", "text/html; charset=utf-8") self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body))) self.end_headers() self.wfile.write(body) HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0", int(os.environ.get("PORT", "8080"))), Handler).serve_forever() EOF The cat > app.py pattern is a here-document: everything up to the EOF line is written into app.py . The quotes around 'EOF' stop the shell from interpreting anything inside. The server listens on p

items.title: WebAuthn errors: NotAllowedError, InvalidStateError and more
items.snippet: WebAuthn reports every failure as a DOMException with a name . The message text differs between Chrome, Safari and Firefox, so branch on err.name and log the message for yourself. This page lists each name the spec throws from navigator.credentials.create() (r
items.content: WebAuthn reports every failure as a DOMException with a name . The message text differs between Chrome, Safari and Firefox, so branch on err.name and log the message for yourself. This page lists each name the spec throws from navigator.credentials.create() (registering a passkey) and navigator.credentials.get() (signing in), what causes it in practice, and what to show the user. try { const cred = await navigator . credentials . create ({ publicKey : options }); } catch ( err ) { console . log ( err . name , err . message ); // "NotAllowedError", "The operation either timed out or was not allowed..." } Every WebAuthn error, at a glance err.name create() get() Usual cause What to do NotAllowedError Yes Yes Cancelled, timed out, no matching credential, blocked by policy Show "Try again" and a fallback sign-in. Do not count it as a failed attempt InvalidStateError Yes A credential in excludeCredentials is already on this authenticator Say the passkey is already set up SecurityError Yes Yes rp.id does not match the page's domain, or the page is not HTTPS Fix rp.id or serve the page over HTTPS NotSupportedError Yes None of the algorithms in pubKeyCredParams is supported Include -7 (ES256) and -257 (RS256) ConstraintError Yes residentKey: "required" or userVerification: "required" and no authenticator can do it Use "preferred" unless you really need it AbortError Yes Yes Your AbortSignal was aborted Expected when you cancel; ignore it TypeError Yes Yes Bad options: user.id empty or over 64 bytes, a challenge that is not a buffer Fix the options your server sends NotAllowedError This is the one you will see most, and it covers several causes on purpose. The spec makes the browser answer the same way whether the user cancelled or no credential exists, so a page cannot probe which accounts have passkeys. Causes, in the order you are likely to hit them: The user cancelled the browser or system prompt, or pressed Escape. The timeout ran out. timeout is in milliseconds and is a hint the browser may change. Five minutes ( 300000 ) is common. No credential matched (sign-in). You sent an allowCredentials list and none of those ids is on any authenticator the browser can reach: the passkey was deleted, was made on another phone that is not synced, or was made for another rpId . items.title: The checklist I run on every cloud account
items.snippet: Every account I review, I go through the same checklist Not because I need the checklist. Because the checklist makes sure I don't skip things when I'm moving fast or when something interesting distracts me early Here it is Billing and visibility Are budget al
items.content: Every account I review, I go through the same checklist Not because I need the checklist. Because the checklist makes sure I don't skip things when I'm moving fast or when something interesting distracts me early Here it is Billing and visibility Are budget alerts configured at meaningful thresholds? Is billing export set up for deep analysis? What percentage of resources have cost allocation tags? What is the tag coverage gap and what does it make invisible? Compute What is the average CPU utilization across EC2 or Compute Engine instances over the last 30 days? What is the average memory utilization? Are there instances with consistent utilization under 20 percent? Are there instances that could run on spot or preemptible capacity? Is autoscaling configured where the workload allows it? Storage What storage class is the majority of object storage using? When were the objects last accessed? Are there snapshots or backups older than the recovery requirement? Are there volumes or disks not attached to any compute resource? Databases What is the RDS or Cloud SQL utilization compared to provisioned capacity? Are automated backup retention policies aligned with actual recovery requirements? Are read replicas being used and is their utilization justified? Networking What is the data transfer cost broken down by type? Is there traffic crossing regional or AZ boundaries that doesn't need to? Are there NAT gateways or load balancers with no traffic? Forgotten resources Are there resources in regions not being actively used? Are there services that were provisioned for testing and never decommissioned? Are there reserved instances that expired and weren't renewed? Spending commitments What percentage of steady-state compute is covered by savings plans or reserved instances? Are the commitments sized based on rightsized utilization or on historical on-demand usage? This list is not complete. Every account adds something new But accounts that are clean on this list are accounts that have their costs under control

items.title: Why I Prefer Lightweight WordPress Development and Custom Code
items.snippet: I'm a self-taught developer and the owner of SJS Leo Universal LLC. My work includes HTML, CSS, PHP, WordPress, accessibility improvements, and responsive website development. Over time, I've learned that adding more tools or plugins isn't automatically the be
items.content: I'm a self-taught developer and the owner of SJS Leo Universal LLC. My work includes HTML, CSS, PHP, WordPress, accessibility improvements, and responsive website development. Over time, I've learned that adding more tools or plugins isn't automatically the best solution to a website problem. When working with WordPress, I prefer to evaluate the existing structure first. Sometimes native blocks and custom CSS provide everything a project needs. My development approach Understand the existing website Before rebuilding anything, I review the structure, navigation, content, and existing functionality. Choose the appropriate solution I use native WordPress features and custom code when they fit the requirements. The goal is maintainability rather than unnecessary complexity. Consider accessibility Navigation, readable content, responsive layouts, and keyboard usability are important parts of the development process. Evaluate performance Images, scripts, stylesheets, and unnecessary dependencies can all affect how a website performs. Explain the changes Clients should understand what was changed, why it matters, and how it affects their website. Examples of my work I've developed operating websites, WordPress demonstrations, custom PHP projects, dashboards, and interactive application concepts. You can explore my public technical work here: https://gist.github.com/sjsleodigitalblueprintco I plan to share more project breakdowns, development decisions, and practical examples from my work.
