items.title: Deleting a Transaction Should Be Surgical — Here's How to Do It Right
items.snippet: In software development, "delete" sounds simple: remove the row from the database and move on. In a relational personal finance application, however, deleting a transaction is a major architectural operation. A single transaction record often has tentacles rea
items.content: In software development, "delete" sounds simple: remove the row from the database and move on. In a relational personal finance application, however, deleting a transaction is a major architectural operation. A single transaction record often has tentacles reaching into multiple subsystems: It altered account balances that must now be refunded. It may have been an inter-account transfer connecting two completely separate bank entities. It may have had a receipt photo stored in private app storage. It may have been a companion record generated by a loan repayment or a split expense. If you simply execute DELETE FROM transactions WHERE id = ? , you leave behind accounting scars : orphaned files consuming device storage, desynchronized loan balances, and corrupted account totals. Here is how FinLedger designs safe, zero-leak transaction deletion across all connected subsystems. The Web of Dependencies Consider what happens when a user deletes a single transfer transaction of 15,000 rupees sent from checking to a savings account six months ago. flowchart TD subgraph Dependencies["The Dependency Web of a Single Transaction"] direction TB Tx["Transaction Record (ID: 502)"] Source["Source Account (Checking: Deducted 15,000)"] Dest["Destination Account (Savings: Credited 15,000)"] Receipt["Receipt Attachment (File: receipt_502.jpg on Disk)"] Lending["Companion Lending Record (Debt Repayment Sync)"] Tx --- Source Tx --- Dest Tx --- Receipt Tx --- Lending end If the deletion logic only removes the row from the transactions table: The checking account balance remains permanently under-reported by 15,000 rupees. The savings account balance remains permanently over-reported by 15,000 rupees. The receipt photo image file receipt_502.jpg remains abandoned in /data/user/0/com.finance.app/files/receipts/ , silently consuming device disk space forever. If this transaction was linked to a loan repayment, the friend's outstanding debt is now permanently desynchronized from the actual ledger. items.content: Introduction In our previous series of articles , we explored the architecture of PDF.js, as well as technical topics such as the rendering layer and message communication. However, while writing those articles, we identified a few problems: The articles could not be connected to one another and failed to form a complete knowledge system. They could not be mapped back to the PDF.js source code, so following along carried a heavy mental burden. Therefore, we decided to start a new series that begins with demo code and gradually follows the call chain deep into the internals of PDF.js. We will explain the principles behind the code from two perspectives: Demo interpretation: case-by-case interpretation, linked from shallow to deep, exploring in depth. Repository interpretation: generalized interpretation that can be read in chunks, each standing on its own as an article. Come on, let's start from the beginning. items.content: Most football clubs I know run their website on whatever a volunteer set up years ago. So when I made a free template for them, I set two rules. It has to work as a folder of static files you can upload anywhere. And someone who knows a bit of HTML has to be able to change it without learning a framework. The result is Golden Team, a one-page site for a made-up club: the next match, latest results, fixtures, the league table, player of the month, the squad, news, a join form and the club's partners, in light and dark mode. Live demo Code on GitHub Ready-to-upload zip These are the parts that took some thought. Includes without a framework A club page repeats itself a lot: four result cards, six fixture rows, eight player cards, each with different data. Copying the markup eight times is how templates rot, so the page is put together at build time from small pieces, by a Node script with no dependencies. items.title: How to schedule OCI instance stop and start after hours
items.snippet: Stopping OCI instances after hours has a native answer today: Resource Scheduler, an Oracle Cloud Infrastructure service that, according to its release notes, shipped on May 21, 2024. Before that, the recipe was a cron job running the OCI CLI on some server. O
items.content: Stopping OCI instances after hours has a native answer today: Resource Scheduler, an Oracle Cloud Infrastructure service that, according to its release notes, shipped on May 21, 2024. Before that, the recipe was a cron job running the OCI CLI on some server. Oracle still documents both options. This post covers what a stopped instance stops billing, how each option is set up, which permissions it needs and when something else makes sense. What a stopped OCI instance stops billing Before the schedule, the math. According to the "Resource Billing for Stopped Instances" page of the OCI documentation, it depends on the shape: Standard shapes: stopping the instance pauses billing. The stopped instance still counts toward your service limits. The table in Oracle's Compute FAQ includes the standard flexible shapes, billed per OCPU and per GB of memory. Dense I/O and HPC: the stopped instance keeps billing, because it preserves its NVMe storage. To end the charge you have to terminate it. GPU: the VM.GPU.A10 series pauses billing when stopped; every other GPU shape keeps billing, because it preserves its GPU resources. Optimized: on VMs, stopping pauses billing; on bare metal it keeps billing. Two details change the number. Shutting the instance down from inside the operating system does not stop billing: the documentation asks you to stop it from the Console or the API as well. And the boot volume still exists while the instance is stopped: Oracle's Block Volumes FAQ states that it is billed at standard Block Volume pricing, on top of the instance price. With an 8am to 8pm weekday window, a standard-shape instance stays stopped for 108 of the 168 hours in a week: 64% of the compute. The formula for any schedule, and what does not drop with everything off, is in shutting down dev after hours . The savings calculator does the math with your VMs. Option 1: Resource Scheduler, the native scheduler Resource Scheduler stops and starts resources according to the schedules you create from the Console, the CLI or the API. The "About Resource Scheduler" page lists the supported types: Compute instances, instance pools, Autonomous AI Database, Functions and Base DB Systems. What to know before creating the first one: One action per schedule. The CLI command accepts START_RESOURCE, STOP_RESOURCE or BACKUP_RESOURCE, so a working-hours window takes two schedules: one that stops at night and one that starts in the morning. The recurrence is written in UNIX cron format or in iCa

items.title: DSPM implementation checklist: a practical rollout for cloud data
items.snippet: Most teams do not decide to buy data security posture management in the abstract. Something forces the question. An auditor asks for a map of where customer data lives. A data export turns up in a bucket nobody remembers creating. A new analytics platform arri
items.content: Most teams do not decide to buy data security posture management in the abstract. Something forces the question. An auditor asks for a map of where customer data lives. A data export turns up in a bucket nobody remembers creating. A new analytics platform arrives and nobody can say which identities can read it. DSPM is the discipline of answering those questions continuously instead of once, in a panic, the week before an audit. Prefer to watch? A short Q&A on the same topic: This post is the checklist we would use to roll it out. It is deliberately tool-neutral until the last section. The problem DSPM exists to solve Cloud data does not stay where it was put. A single production database becomes read replicas, warehouse copies, nightly exports to object storage, a staging copy for testing, and a cache that outlived the feature it served. Each copy is created by a different team for a good reason, and each one inherits whatever access and encryption settings were convenient on the day. Three things go wrong at once: Nobody has a complete inventory. The data stores the security team knows about are a subset of the ones that exist. Sensitivity is unknown. A bucket called exports-2024 might hold marketing images or a full customer table. Access is decided elsewhere. Who can read a store is the product of identity policies, resource policies and network paths, none of which live next to the data. DSPM brings those three together: what data you have, how sensitive it is, and who or what can reach it. How teams usually handle it today Before a DSPM programme, data security is usually a mix of: A spreadsheet of "crown jewel" databases maintained by hand and out of date within a quarter. Per-service checks from the cloud provider: is this bucket public, is this volume encrypted. Periodic manual reviews of who has access to production data, often driven by a compliance deadline. None of these is wrong. The gap is that each answers one question about one resource. Exposure is usually a combination: a store that is encrypted, private, and still readable by an over-privileged role that is itself reachable from the internet. The rollout checklist Work through these in order. Each step makes the next one cheaper. 1. Define what "sensitive" means for you Before scanning anything, agree on the categories you care about. Most organisations start with: Personal data (names, emails, national identifiers, dates of birth) Health data Payment card data Secrets and credentials s

items.title: Put a 0.25 second judge in front of your AI agents
items.snippet: Originally published at omerbinsaleem.com by Omer Bin Saleem (Omer Saleem). Big models do the work. Around that work sit hundreds of small yes-or-no questions a day. A small judge model answered 116,097 of them in 20 days, in a median of 245 ms, and only acts
items.content: Originally published at omerbinsaleem.com by Omer Bin Saleem (Omer Saleem). Big models do the work. Around that work sit hundreds of small yes-or-no questions a day. A small judge model answered 116,097 of them in 20 days, in a median of 245 ms, and only acts alone above a confidence gate. What changed Model routing: the judge picks the model per message. The same report went from 137 s to 45 s. Merge request reviewer: findings on code the MR never touched score 0.19 to 0.40, real ones 0.94. 16 of 26 false majors became follow-ups. QA: it reads the page and judges 57 acceptance criteria. 94 passed, 38 went to a human, none guessed. 17% of judge calls failed in 20 days and nothing broke, because the old rule decides whenever the judge is down or unsure. How to do it List the small questions your agents answer with a full model run today: is this message asking me to stop, did this change cause this bug, which model should answer this. Each is a yes or no, a pick, or a score. Put a small judge model in front of them. It answers a typed question with a probability in about a quarter of a second, instead of 5 to 14 seconds for a big model. Set a confidence gate. Above 0.9 the judge acts alone. Below it, or when it is down, the old rule decides. Nothing new can break. Keep the dangerous words on the strong model. Merge, prod, deploy and release always go to the big model, after the judge once sent a merge-to-prod to the small one and missed that the work was already merged. Log every decision with its probability for 20 days, then read where it paid and where it was wrong before widening it. Prompt to copy Read my agent code and list every place a large model answers a yes/no, a pick-one, or a score question. For each: the question, how often it runs per day, and what a wrong answer would cost. Propose which of them a small judge model could answer with a probability, the confidence gate above which it may act alone, and the fallback rule below the gate. Keep merge, deploy, production and release decisions on the strong model, always. I am Omer Bin Saleem, a frontend chapter lead who builds with AI every day. One practical AI hack a day at omerbinsaleem.com . LinkedIn: omer-bin-saleem · Instagram: @iomerbinsaleem .

items.title: Building Raasta: Flooded-Road Detection with Satellite Images and PyTorch
items.snippet: A road can remain visible on a map even when flooding has changed what is happening on the ground. That gap interested me when choosing a deep learning project. My teacher asked us to build a model with a dataset and predictions. I wanted to use that assignmen
items.content: A road can remain visible on a map even when flooding has changed what is happening on the ground. That gap interested me when choosing a deep learning project. My teacher asked us to build a model with a dataset and predictions. I wanted to use that assignment to explore a problem I could continue working on beyond the semester. The result is "Raasta", a research prototype for detecting flooded-road pixels from paired satellite images. The idea has particular relevance to Pakistan, but there is an important distinction: the current project uses historical SpaceNet 8 data from Germany and Louisiana. Its performance in Pakistan has not yet been validated. "What the model receives" Raasta takes two georeferenced RGB satellite images of the same location: one before a flood and one after it. These cannot simply be two unrelated pictures. Their geographic coverage must overlap, and the images need to be aligned so that corresponding pixels represent the same area. The preprocessing pipeline aligns the imagery and prepares road labels for training. It then combines the two RGB images into a six-channel input. A compact U-Net, implemented in PyTorch, predicts three classes: Background Road with no flood label Flooded road This is a segmentation task: the model assigns a class to each pixel rather than giving the entire image a single label. The outputs include a prediction overlay, a flooded-road score map and georeferenced files that can be examined outside the notebook. "Where the dataset comes from" Raasta uses SpaceNet 8, a dataset developed for studying flooded roads and buildings. The notebook downloads selected imagery and annotations from the official SpaceNet dataset source. With Google Drive enabled, it stores the raw files and processed samples there, alongside the training checkpoints and results. This makes the data source and storage location explicit. It also helps make the experiment reproducible: the notebook records which files were selected. Historical data provides a starting point for developing the pipeline. It does not tell us the condition of a particular road today. "Making the project practical in Colab" One issue I regularly encountered was returning to a notebook the next day and discovering that the runtime had lost its variables and files. items.snippet: Cryptocurrency Exchange Binance blamed a compromised DevOps laptop for the loss of $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency last week, adding that it will now cover any losses faced by its customers. “Binance will cover all losses from the Secure Assets Fund for Users (
items.content: Cryptocurrency Exchange Binance blamed a compromised DevOps laptop for the loss of $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency last week, adding that it will now cover any losses faced by its customers. “Binance will cover all losses from the Secure Assets Fund for Users (SAFU) and the company’s funds,” the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange said in an update on Friday, adding that user funds are safe and that it had found no evidence of wallet private-key leakage during its investigation of the incident. It had frozen approximately $3 billion in assets on-chain, temporarily suspending withdrawals while security checks were completed, and revoking the affected address authorization. Withdrawals are now being restored in phases, initially reopening services across 15 networks, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, and XRP. Binance says it has replenished approximately 95% of the affected assets using company funds, while the remaining 5%, comprising less-liquid tokens, could take longer to source. The exchange said its preliminary investigation pointed to a compromised employee device that enabled access to a service container involved in withdrawals. “This attack, reportedly on a development engineer, highlights that security is a critical element of every operational stage and personnel level,” said Tim Rawlins , senior advisor and director of security at NCC Group. “When security failures in trusted identities and administrative access can be targeted, attackers can exploit more than just the underlying technical vulnerabilities.” The FBI has since attributed the attack to North Korean threat actors, identifying the TraderTraitor hacking group as responsible for the theft. “Given what we know about the activities of countries like North Korea in targeting cryptocurrency, it’s unsurprising that attackers are prepared to invest considerable efforts in targeting individuals who have access to the building blocks of the exchanges,” Rawlins said. A compromised laptop reaches the withdrawal pipeline Binance’s preliminary findings suggest that attackers compromised a DevOps engineer’s laptop before gaining access to a service container and submitting unauthorized withdrawals. items.snippet: Stripe only accepts businesses in about 50 countries. I'm a web developer in Tunisia, one of the countries it doesn't serve, and finding a clear answer to "how do I get paid online from here?" took me weeks. Here's what I learned: almost every working setup is
items.content: Stripe only accepts businesses in about 50 countries. I'm a web developer in Tunisia, one of the countries it doesn't serve, and finding a clear answer to "how do I get paid online from here?" took me weeks. Here's what I learned: almost every working setup is one of three things. Your goal decides which one comes first. 1. A merchant of record (the fastest start) A merchant of record (MoR) is the legal seller of your product. It charges your customers, handles VAT and sales tax worldwide, and pays you out to your bank account. ✅ No foreign company needed ✅ Best for digital products and SaaS ⚠️ Higher fees than a direct processor ⚠️ Eligibility depends on the country that issued your ID, so check the provider's accepted list first 2. A receiving account (for freelancers) If clients or marketplaces pay you, a receiving account (Payoneer, Wise) gives you account details in foreign currencies they can pay into. You then withdraw to your local bank. ✅ Simple for freelance and agency work ⚠️ Wise publishes the list of countries whose residents can hold money: check yours 3. A US company (to use Stripe itself) A US LLC unlocks Stripe from almost anywhere. Stripe sees a US business, and payouts go to the company's US account. The setup is the easy part. The yearly costs are what matter: Registered agent and state fees, every year Form 5472 every year for a foreign-owned single-member LLC. The IRS penalty for not filing is $25,000 . A US business account, which is a separate approval (Mercury, for example, doesn't serve founders living in some countries) The two services most founders abroad use are doola and Firstbase , and they're priced very differently: yearly plans that can include the IRS filing vs a cheap setup plus à-la-carte services. I compared them using only their official pricing pages: 👉 doola review: prices, what's included, who it suits 👉 Firstbase review: forming a US company from abroad 👉 Firstbase vs doola: what you really pay To move the money home afterwards, many founders use Wise Business . I wrote up what Wise asks for, including the address question that trips people up: Wise Business for a US LLC owned from abroad . Which one should you pick? Your situation Start with Selling digital products, no revenue yet A merchant of record Freelancer paid by clients or marketplaces A receiving account Steady revenue and you need Stripe A US company Check your own country Provider lists change silently. items.content: 📅 November 2, 2026 • MIT Technology Review MIT Technology Review published a feature on November 2 titled 'The agentic web is here' , written by Grace Huckins . The piece argues that the web organized around pages is being rebuilt around AI agents , programs that browse sites and carry out tasks for users as machines become a new audience online. Per MIT Technology Review, this is not a forecast about a distant future but a description of a shift already underway in how sites are built and how access to them is granted. The idea behind the agentic web is a change of audience. Pages have historically been designed for human readers, with layouts, menus and forms tuned for a person behind a screen. Agents need something different, structured ways to find products, compare options and complete actions through interfaces they can operate directly. A web rebuilt around agents treats machine access as a first class use case , and platforms start making explicit decisions about which automated visitors are welcome and what they may do once inside. The feature grounds the argument in recent events. Meta released its Muse agent in September , putting into circulation an assistant that can act across websites on a user's behalf. Amazon then blocked Muse from its site entirely, and per MIT Technology Review that decision marks a clear platform level response. The move separates browsing by people from acting by agents and sets a precedent that access to a storefront is conditional rather than assumed. Amazon, per the same feature, is pushing its own shopping agent, Alexa for Shopping , designed to handle purchasing inside its own environment. The result is an emerging fight over which agents get access to commerce platforms . If agents become a primary interface for online activity, the operator of a commerce platform holds the gatekeeping position, able to admit its own agent while restricting outside ones, and access becomes a policy lever alongside pricing and search ranking. The piece treats these events as early evidence of a structural change. The first wave of the agent discussion centered on what models are capable of, while the questions now moving forward concern permission , meaning who may run an agent on a given site and under what conditions. items.title: In my own words
items.snippet: It's eight in the morning. The coffee is still brewing. In the team channel someone asks why the pipeline is red. You already know: the runner's disk is read-only, the code is fine. You ask your agent to reply. You get an essay. It opens with "I took a look."
items.content: It's eight in the morning. The coffee is still brewing. In the team channel someone asks why the pipeline is red. You already know: the runner's disk is read-only, the code is fine. You ask your agent to reply. You get an essay. It opens with "I took a look." It has six sentences, four identifiers and the mechanism laid out step by step. It ends with "Let me know if you have any questions." Every word of it is true. None of it is you. You add three words: in my words, concise, minimal . The second version is better. You send it. The next morning you do the same. And the next. Psychology knows a man who traced a star seen in a mirror day after day, each time sure he was doing it for the first time. After brain surgery Henry Molaison could no longer form new memories of facts and events, yet his hand still learned the task. Your agent also meets you for the first time every morning. Only this time, you're the one repeating the exercise. Those three words aren't a request. They're a memory that dies every morning. The hand knows, the head doesn't Try describing your style. You'll get something like "short, to the point, human." Everyone thinks that about themselves, and everyone reads those words differently. Your "short" is two sentences. Someone else's is a paragraph without an intro. It's not your fault. Writing style lives in the same drawer as riding a bike. Your hand knows how you write; your head can't recite it. But there's a side door. Recalling something from a blank page is hard. Recognising it when it's lying in front of you is much easier. The whole method rests on that: you don't ask yourself how you write. You lay cards on the table and look. Twelve cards Here's how we did it at Kodownik. First, material: two years of messages from the team chat and a few dozen comments from the issue tracker. Bots and private matters were dropped right away. Then twelve messages went on the table, shuffled, each with one question: mine or not mine? You'd expect a simple sort. Something else happened. Among the "mine" were messages written by someone else. Among the "not mine" landed four of my own. The question was "mine or not mine", but the answer turned out to be an answer to a different one: would I sign this? The accepted ones shared a spine: the cause in one sentence, what's been done, and the next step with a named owner. The rejected ones fell into two families. Some were overloaded. Others said too little, and the shortest had two words and a question

items.snippet: 📅 November 2, 2026 • Data Center Dynamics National Grid has bought a site of more than 70 acres , about 29.5 hectares , at Dorman Point on Teesside in north east England. The land was acquired from Teesworks , the organization redeveloping the former Redcar s
items.content: 📅 November 2, 2026 • Data Center Dynamics National Grid has bought a site of more than 70 acres , about 29.5 hectares , at Dorman Point on Teesside in north east England. The land was acquired from Teesworks , the organization redeveloping the former Redcar steelworks, and is earmarked for a new electricity substation with a planned capacity of up to 3.2 GW . Once complete, the facility is set to become the largest substation in the United Kingdom . A connection of this size is core transmission infrastructure, stepping voltage so that very large volumes of power can move from the national grid into the local lines that a major computing site requires. The purpose of the new site is to supply an AI data center planned on the same Redcar grounds. The site was selected as part of the UK government's AI growth zone initiative, with planning applications for a data center spanning roughly 500,000 square meters , or 5.38 million square feet , and the wider Teesside development is described as the largest brownfield project in Europe , meaning it reuses land that industry already occupied and serviced with infrastructure. Placing the substation next to the future computing campus shortens the path between grid capacity and the racks that will eventually consume it, and it signals that the connection was treated as part of the site design from the start. Delivery of the project involves several contractors. Balfour Beatty and Steel River Power are linked to the works, with National Grid acting as the network operator that will own and run the connection. The purchase forms part of the company's Great Grid Upgrade , a broad program of reinforcement across the British transmission network that prepares the grid for new large scale demand. The program reaches beyond Teesside. Under the same upgrade, National Grid is also advancing projects at Didcot and Uxbridge Moor in southern England, and the Uxbridge Moor substation alone is expected to supply more than 12 new data centers . The three projects show a utility preparing dedicated capacity for the computing sector at several points in the country at once, pairing reinforcement work with expected demand instead of waiting for connection requests to arrive. The Teesside purchase shows how AI demand is reshaping energy planning. Data centers at this scale cannot rely on standard connection timelines, so land, permits and grid capacity are now assembled years ahead of facility completion. For the region, the deal link

items.title: The Hidden Hardware Cost of Multi-Tasking: Context Switching & TLB Flushes
items.snippet: The Hidden Hardware Cost of Multi-Tasking: Context Switching & TLB Flushes When your laptop runs hundreds of background processes on an 8-core CPU, the operating system creates the illusion of simultaneous execution through rapid Context Switching . However, c
items.content: The Hidden Hardware Cost of Multi-Tasking: Context Switching & TLB Flushes When your laptop runs hundreds of background processes on an 8-core CPU, the operating system creates the illusion of simultaneous execution through rapid Context Switching . However, context switching is not free. Beyond the few microseconds it takes to swap CPU registers, there is a massive hidden penalty: Memory Cache Coldness and TLB Invalidation . ⚡ What Happens During a Context Switch? Physical CPU Silicon ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ PC | SP | RAX | RBX | RDI | CR3 Page Dir │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ ▲ 1. SAVE to PCB(P1) 2. RESTORE from PCB(P2) ▼ │ Kernel Memory: Process Control Blocks (PCB) ┌───────────────────────┐ ┌───────────────────────┐ │ PCB for Process P1 │ │ PCB for Process P2 │ │ • State: READY │ │ • State: RUNNING │ │ • Saved CPU Registers │ │ • Saved CPU Registers │ │ • Memory Maps (CR3) │ │ • Memory Maps (CR3) │ └───────────────────────┘ └───────────────────────┘ Hardware State Preservation : The kernel saves P₁'s Program Counter (PC), Stack Pointer (SP), general-purpose registers, and flags into its Process Control Block (PCB) in kernel memory. Scheduler Execution : The scheduler decides which thread to run next based on priority or CPU burst estimates. Hardware State Restoration : The kernel loads P₂'s register state into the physical CPU silicon and updates the CR3 register to point to P₂'s page tables. 🧠 The Hidden Killers: TLB & Cache Coldness Saving 16 registers takes less than 100 nanoseconds. The real performance degradation comes from the memory subsystem: 1. TLB Invalidation (Translation Lookaside Buffer) The CPU's MMU uses the TLB to cache virtual-to-physical address mappings. Because P₁ and P₂ have completely different virtual address spaces, switching processes flushes the TLB entries. Every subsequent memory access suffers a TLB Miss , forcing the MMU into slow 4-level DRAM page table walks! 2. L1/L2 Cache Pollution P₁'s working set filled the ultra-fast L1 and L2 CPU caches (which respond in ~1–4 cycles). When P₂ begins executing, it encounters an avalanche of cache misses , stalling the CPU on main DRAM (100–300 cycles per miss). 🛠️ Why Threads Are Cheaper Than Processes Threads within the same process share the same virtual memory space (same page directory) . When the kernel switches between threads of the same process, it swaps CPU registers, but does NOT need to flush the TLB . This makes threa

How to calculate a domestic helper's monthly salary with leave, half-days and advances
items.snippet: It is the last day of the month. Your maid says she worked 26 days, you think it was 22, and somewhere in between there were two half-days, a festival holiday and a ₹2,000 advance she took for her son's school fees. Nobody is trying to cheat anyone. The two of
items.content: It is the last day of the month. Your maid says she worked 26 days, you think it was 22, and somewhere in between there were two half-days, a festival holiday and a ₹2,000 advance she took for her son's school fees. Nobody is trying to cheat anyone. The two of you are just doing the sums differently. This post sets the calculation out step by step, with a worked example in rupees and a small JavaScript function you can reuse. The point is a method that both sides can check. It is not about cutting pay. Step 1: Agree the basis before the month starts Most arguments start here. To get a per-day rate, you divide the monthly salary by some number of days, and there are three common choices: Calendar days : 30 in November, 31 in December. The rate changes a little each month. A fixed 30 : simple, and the same every month. Working days only : calendar days minus weekly offs, for example 26. All three are fine. Mixing them is not. If you divide by 26 and she expects 30, every absence costs her more than she expected. Pick one, say it out loud, and write it down. Step 2: Sort every day into a type At month-end, each day of the month should fall into exactly one bucket: Day type Paid? Present Yes Weekly off Yes, it is part of the agreed salary Holiday (festival, agreed in advance) Yes Paid leave, within the agreed allowance Yes Leave beyond the allowance No Absent without leave No Half-day Half paid The bucket counts should add up to the number of days in the month. If they don't, a day was missed or counted twice. That simple check catches most disagreements. Step 3: Count unpaid days, not paid days It is easier, and kinder, to start from the full salary and take off only what was unpaid: unpaid days = absent + leave beyond allowance + (half-days x 0.5) earned = monthly salary - (unpaid days x per-day rate) Starting from the full amount makes it clear that a normal month pays in full. The deductions are the exception, and each one can be pointed to on the calendar. Step 4: Take off advances last An advance is money already paid, not a deduction for absence. Keep it separate: payable = earned - advances given this month If the advance is bigger than what she earned, don't take her to zero. Agree how much comes off each month and carry the rest forward as a balance you both know about. A worked example Sunita works as a cook for ₹12,000 a month. items.title: The Roofline Model for LLM Inference
items.snippet: In Part 3 the Word Factory had two speed limits. The forklift brings tables from the warehouse, and the workbench does the math. Reading your question got stuck on the workbench. Typing the answer got stuck on the forklift. Today we draw both limits on one pic
items.content: In Part 3 the Word Factory had two speed limits. The forklift brings tables from the warehouse, and the workbench does the math. Reading your question got stuck on the workbench. Typing the answer got stuck on the forklift. Today we draw both limits on one picture . Engineers call it the roofline model , and it's the most useful sketch I know for LLM inference. Once you have it, you can look at any chip, any model and any batch size and say which limit you'll hit, before you run anything. The whole model fits in one line: speed = the smaller of (workbench speed) and (forklift speed × math per byte) Let's unpack that, measure it, and then use it. One number per job: math per byte Every job the factory does has a recipe : how many math steps (FLOPs) it needs, and how many bytes the forklift must bring for it. Divide one by the other and you get the job's math per byte . Engineers call it arithmetic intensity . A few jobs from earlier parts: One token through a big table. Each table number is 4 bytes and gets used for 2 FLOPs (one multiply, one add). That's 0.5 FLOPs per byte. 256 tokens through the same table. The table is fetched once and used 256 times: about 122 FLOPs per byte. Adding two lists of numbers. Fetch two numbers (8 bytes), write one (4 bytes), do 1 FLOP: about 0.08 FLOPs per byte. Same factory, same tables, numbers that are 1,500 times apart. That spread is the whole story of LLM speed. Drawing the roof Now picture a chart. Left to right is math per byte . Bottom to top is speed (FLOPs per second). The slanted roof is the forklift. If a job does 1 FLOP per byte and the forklift brings 15 billion bytes per second, the job can't go faster than 15 billion FLOPs per second, however fast the workbench is. Do 2 FLOPs per byte and the limit doubles. So this roof is a slope: forklift speed × math per byte. The flat roof is the workbench. Past a certain point the forklift keeps up easily, and the workbench's top speed is the limit. Where they meet is the ridge. It's the workbench speed divided by the forklift speed. Jobs to the left of the ridge are memory-bound . Jobs to the right are compute-bound . In code, that's all of it: def roof ( intensity ): # FLOPs per byte -> best possible FLOPs per second return min ( PEAK , BW * intensity ) I measured the two roofs the same way as in Part 3, with roofline.py : one token through a 400 MB table for the forklift, and a big multiply that fits near the workbench for the math: memory roof : 15.0 GB/s math roof

ChatGPT invented six court cases that never existed — and real lawyers filed them in a real court — and got fined $5,000. This is not a story about AI lying. It is a story about a tool that guesses beautifully when it has nothing to check. Today: why models invent facts, the Mata v. Avianca case and its $5,000 lesson, how RAG actually works, a 3-step walkthrough you can use today, and the 5-rule check-before-you-trust list. Subscribe free to Paragon AI MAG for one source-checked AI story every day. Why ChatGPT Makes Things Up — And the Fix Nobody Told You By Paragon AI MAG — one video and one podcast episode every day, every fact checked against sources several times before release. ChatGPT invented six court cases that never existed — and real lawyers filed them in a real court — and got fined $5,000. That is not a hypothetical. It is the story of Mata v. Avianca, Inc., and it is the clearest warning we have about how AI works — and how to use it safely. This is not a story about AI lying to you on purpose. It is a story about a tool that guesses beautifully when it has nothing to check. Why AI invents facts Large language models like ChatGPT are not databases. They are next-word prediction machines. They are trained to predict the most plausible next word, not to look up a fact. They have no fact book inside. And their confidence is fluency, not truth: if an answer sounds smooth and confident, it feels true — even when it is completely invented. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology prefers the term "confabulation" over "hallucination" for this reason — the AI does not literally see things that are not there. It strings together highly probable words that happen to be totally false. In its Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1, July 2024), NIST describes hallucination as the production of confidently stated but erroneous or false content. Two kinds of made-up answers Not all hallucinations look the same. There are two main types. Intrinsic hallucinations: the answer directly contradicts the source material. items.title: Polly's maintenance fee starts 16 November. Is your .NET app affected?
items.snippet: Check your solution in one command, along with MediatR, AutoMapper, MassTransit and FluentAssertions. On 14 July 2026 the Polly project announced that it's adopting the Open Source Maintenance Fee (OSMF) . Payment requests start on 16 November 2026 . Polly is
items.content: Check your solution in one command, along with MediatR, AutoMapper, MassTransit and FluentAssertions. On 14 July 2026 the Polly project announced that it's adopting the Open Source Maintenance Fee (OSMF) . Payment requests start on 16 November 2026 . Polly is everywhere in .NET. The Polly package alone has more than 1.7 billion downloads, and Microsoft's own resilience packages are built on it. So the question many teams are asking right now is simple: do we have to pay? For most teams the answer is no, but it depends on two details that are easy to miss. In this post I'll explain both, then show how to check every project in your solution in one command. What actually changes Here's what the Polly announcement says, quoted directly: Price and threshold: "The Maintenance Fee is US $20 per month and applies to any company that earns at least US $20,000 from at least one product or project that uses Polly." Which versions: "The fee applies only to the next major version of Polly released after November 16, 2026." And: "Existing versions of Polly are not subject to the fee." Which references: "Only direct references to Polly are subject to the fee. If Polly is a dependency of a different library, such as Microsoft.Extensions.Resilience or Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience, the fee does not apply." The source code stays open under its existing BSD-3-Clause licence. Individuals, students, hobbyists and organisations below the revenue threshold don't pay. The two details that decide whether you're affected 1. Version. Polly 8.x, which is what you're almost certainly using today, is not affected. The fee applies to the next major version (Polly 9) released after 16 November. So upgrading carelessly is the real risk, especially with Dependabot, Renovate or a casual dotnet add package Polly . 2. Direct vs transitive. If you only get Polly through Microsoft's resilience packages, the fee doesn't apply. A typical example is AddStandardResilienceHandler() from Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience . Your app still loads Polly.Core , but you don't reference it yourself. Both are hard to see by eye in a real solution: Using statements don't tell you. The official OSMF guidance warns about this itself: using Polly; compiles whether Polly comes in directly or through another package. References hide in many places. They can be in Directory.Build.props , in Directory.Packages.props with Central Package Management, or in one test project nobody looks at. Licence scanners

items.title: Building Cometflow Do: One Chat Interface for Everyday Utilities, With Privacy at Its Core
items.snippet: What if you didn't need to open a different app every time you wanted to perform a simple task? Compressing an image, converting a file, calculating something, checking metadata, generating a checksum, or performing everyday utility operations shouldn't requir
items.content: What if you didn't need to open a different app every time you wanted to perform a simple task? Compressing an image, converting a file, calculating something, checking metadata, generating a checksum, or performing everyday utility operations shouldn't require navigating through dozens of different screens. That's the idea behind Cometflow Do. I'm building Cometflow Do, an Android utility application designed around one simple concept: Describe what you want to do. Let the app figure out which tool you need. But there's another principle behind this project that matters even more to me: privacy should come before convenience. The Problem With Traditional Utility Apps Most utility applications follow a similar pattern: Open the application. Find the correct category. Search for the required tool. Open another screen. Configure the options. Finally perform the operation. This works, but it creates unnecessary friction. And when users need multiple utilities, they often end up installing several different applications. I wanted to explore a different approach. Introducing Cometflow Do Cometflow Do is being developed as a command-driven Android utility application. Instead of making users manually search through a large tool directory, the goal is to let them interact with utilities through a familiar chat-style interface. For example: User: Compress this image. Cometflow Do: Identifies the image compression utility and processes the selected file. User: Convert this image into PDF. Cometflow Do: Understands the request and selects the appropriate conversion utility. User: Calculate the SHA-256 checksum of this file. Cometflow Do: Routes the request to the checksum calculator. The idea is to make hundreds or eventually thousands of utilities accessible through one consistent interface. 500+ Registered Utilities and Growing One of the important development milestones has been building the initial utility registry. The current development registry contains 50 registered utilities, organized across multiple development phases. Some examples include: Image to PDF Image Compressor MIME Detector Metadata Inspector Checksum Calculator File and data utilities Everyday productivity tools The objective isn't simply to increase the number of tools. Every utility should actually work, handle errors properly, and produce a reliable result. I'd rather have 100 properly working tools than 1,000 buttons that don't do anything. items.title: Mobile App Onboarding: A UX and Development Checklist for 2026
items.snippet: Mobile app onboarding sits at the intersection of product design, authentication, permissions and application performance. A new user may need to understand the app, create an account, grant access to a device capability and complete an initial task. Poor sequ
items.content: Mobile app onboarding sits at the intersection of product design, authentication, permissions and application performance. A new user may need to understand the app, create an account, grant access to a device capability and complete an initial task. Poor sequencing can turn these steps into unnecessary friction. This article covers seven practical areas to consider when implementing an onboarding flow. 1. Define the first meaningful action Before creating screens, define what a new user should accomplish. Examples include: Searching for a product. Booking an appointment. Creating a first task. Starting a workout. Adding an initial account. Build the onboarding flow around this action instead of introducing every feature upfront. 2. Keep registration minimal Separate required account information from optional profile data. Use clear field labels, client-side feedback for usability and server-side validation for security. Handle network failures and authentication errors without losing the user's progress unnecessarily. Where account creation is not required for the core experience, consider allowing guest access. 3. Request permissions contextually Do not request every device permission during the first launch. Map permissions to the features that need them. Explain why access is required and provide a sensible alternative when the feature can still work without it. Apple's onboarding guidance and privacy guidance are useful design references. 4. Use contextual guidance A short interactive hint near an unfamiliar control can be more useful than a long tutorial. Keep guidance focused, dismissible where appropriate and available again through help or settings when users need it. 5. Optimise the first-session experience Consider initial download size, image decoding, animation cost, network requests and memory usage. Test on different screen sizes and hardware categories. Provide loading, empty, offline and retry states rather than leaving users with an unresponsive interface. Refer to the Android core app quality guidelines when planning Android quality checks. 6. Design secure returning-user experiences Onboarding also includes returning after reinstalling an app or changing devices. Plan session management, credential recovery and restoration of user progress. Avoid insecure local storage or exposing authentication tokens in logs. items.title: How to Publish a Replit App to the App Store and Google Play (2026)
items.snippet: Short answer: first check what Replit built for you. If it's a web app (most Replit Agent projects are), you need to turn it into a native app before the stores will take it. If it's a mobile app built with Expo , you can build and submit it with Expo's tools.
items.content: Short answer: first check what Replit built for you. If it's a web app (most Replit Agent projects are), you need to turn it into a native app before the stores will take it. If it's a mobile app built with Expo , you can build and submit it with Expo's tools. Either way, you need developer accounts, a few store requirements Replit doesn't add by default and, on a new personal Google Play account, a 14-day closed test. Replit makes it easy to go from an idea to a working app. Getting that app into the App Store and Google Play is a separate job, and it trips up a lot of first-time publishers. Here's the full path. Disclosure: this guide is from LetsDeployIt , where we publish AI-built apps to both stores. What did Replit build: a web app or a mobile app? Open your project and look at the files and the preview: A web app runs in the browser preview and usually uses React, Vite, Next.js or a Python or Node server. You open it with a URL. This is what most Replit Agent projects are. A mobile app uses Expo and React Native. You'll see an app.json or app.config file and expo in package.json , and you preview it on your phone with Expo Go. The path to the stores depends on which one you have. Path A: your Replit app is a web app The App Store and Google Play want native apps, so a web app needs a native version first. You have two options: Wrap it: put your website inside a native shell with a tool like Capacitor. It's quick, but Apple often rejects apps that feel like a website in a frame under Guideline 4.2 . Convert it: rebuild the screens as a React Native and Expo app that talks to the same backend. It takes longer, but it feels like a real app and passes review far more reliably. Your Replit web app keeps running either way. The store app is a separate build that uses the same data. Path B: your Replit app uses Expo If your project is already an Expo app, you're much closer. The usual route is Expo's EAS services, which build your iPhone and Android apps in the cloud and upload them to the stores, with no Mac needed: npm install -g eas-cli eas login eas build:configure eas build --platform all eas submit --platform ios eas submit --platform android Before building, check app.json has a real app name, an ios.bundleIdentifier and an android.package (like com.yourcompany.yourapp ), plus your icon and splash screen. items.title: Qu'est-ce qu'une proposition d'amélioration (EIP sur Ethereum, BIP sur Bitcoin) ?
items.snippet: Rédigé avec l’aide de l’IA Définition : de quoi parle-t-on ? Une proposition d'amélioration (EIP pour Ethereum, BIP pour Bitcoin) est un document formel décrivant une nouvelle fonctionnalité, un correctif ou une modification du protocole. Elle sert de proposit
items.content: Rédigé avec l’aide de l’IA Définition : de quoi parle-t-on ? Une proposition d'amélioration (EIP pour Ethereum, BIP pour Bitcoin) est un document formel décrivant une nouvelle fonctionnalité, un correctif ou une modification du protocole. Elle sert de proposition communautaire, rédigée dans un format standardisé, qui peut être discutée, révisée et finalement adoptée par les développeurs et les mineurs. Les EIP permettent une évolution décentralisée, garantissant que les changements sont documentés, évalués et mis en œuvre de manière transparente. À quoi cela sert-il ? L'objectif principal est de fournir un mécanisme structuré pour proposer et coordonner des modifications du réseau, en impliquant tous les acteurs concernés. Cela favorise un processus de gouvernance ouvert, où les idées peuvent être examinées, testées et intégrées selon des critères techniques et de consensus. Les EIP aident également à préserver l'interopérabilité, à éviter les fork inutiles et à maintenir un historique de développement clair, ce qui renforce la confiance et la stabilité à long terme de l'écosystème blockchain. Comment cela fonctionne, étape par étape Création de l'EIP Un contributeur écrit le document dans un modèle standardisé, incluant un titre, une motivation, une spécification technique et des implications. Le texte est partagé publiquement sur GitHub, où la communauté peut réagir, proposer des modifications et évaluer la pertinence de la proposition. Discussion et révision La communauté examine la proposition via des commentaires, des tests et des analyses. Les auteurs intègrent les retours, affinent la spécification et s'assurent de la compatibilité avec les versions antérieures. Cette phase collaborative permet d'aligner les intérêts des développeurs, des validateurs et des utilisateurs. Finalisation et adoption Une fois la proposition stabilisée, un processus de revue formelle évalue sa sécurité, son efficacité et son impact. Après approbation par les développeurs principaux et les mineurs, la spécification est fusionnée dans le code, conduisant à une mise à jour du réseau lors d'un bloc ou d'un hard fork. Documentation et déploiement La proposition adoptée est enregistrée dans les archives des EIP/BIP, devenant une référence pour les futures modifications. Les nœuds de validation intègrent le nouveau code, et les outils (portefeuilles, dApps) sont mis à jour, assurant ainsi une adoption uniforme et une interopérabilité continue. items.title: I use an LLM to check fake citations, but I don't let it decide anything
items.snippet: I'm building CiteWise, a tool that checks whether an academic reference points to a real paper. You paste a citation, it looks the work up in Crossref, DataCite, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, PubMed and arXiv, and shows you which fields match and which don't. Th
items.content: I'm building CiteWise, a tool that checks whether an academic reference points to a real paper. You paste a citation, it looks the work up in Crossref, DataCite, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, PubMed and arXiv, and shows you which fields match and which don't. The obvious way to build this in 2026 is "send the reference to an LLM and ask if it's real". I tried a version of that early on and it's a bad idea for the same reason people need this tool in the first place: LLMs are very good at producing things that look right. So the LLM is in the pipeline, but it isn't allowed to decide anything. This post is about where that line sits, and about the bug in my first version that crossed it without me noticing. The pipeline Roughly: Parse the raw string into fields (title, authors, year, journal, DOI...) with a rule-based parser. Query the scholarly sources in parallel. Score every candidate against the user's input, field by field. Pick a status: verified, ambiguous, conflicting metadata, not found, and so on. Step 3 is deterministic. Title similarity, author overlap, year, DOI equality, a penalty for contradictions. No model involved. If you run the same reference twice against the same source responses, you get the same score. Where the LLM comes in Some references are just messy. A student copies a citation out of a PDF and gets Smith J Lee K Deep learning for something 2019 Nature Methods 16 4 pp 1-9 with no punctuation. The rule parser gets half the fields, the search queries are bad, and nothing comes back. That's the only case where the LLM runs: there's no DOI, and the first pass ended as not found or insufficient evidence. The model gets the raw string and tries to fill in the missing fields. Then we search again with those fields. The bug Here's a simplified version of what my first implementation did after the second search: java var enriched = llm.completeMissingFields(candidate); var retry = resolver.resolve(enriched); if (retry.score() >= first.score()) { candidate = enriched; // resolution = retry; } Looks reasonable. If the LLM-assisted search scores at least as well, use it. The problem is what candidate means. It's the thing every candidate paper gets scored against. After this swap, the scorer was no longer comparing source records to what the user typed. It was comparing them to what the LLM thought the user meant. items.title: Week 44 shelf-price indices: UK down 0.24%, Australia up 0.48%
items.snippet: I publish two weekly indices of posted online supermarket prices, one for the UK and one for Australia. Both for 2026-W44 went out on 2 November 2026. This post covers the headline moves, what the indices do not measure, and how to read the data yourself. What
items.content: I publish two weekly indices of posted online supermarket prices, one for the UK and one for Australia. Both for 2026-W44 went out on 2 November 2026. This post covers the headline moves, what the indices do not measure, and how to read the data yourself. What the indices are Each week I read the online catalogues of the retailers, match products week on week by the retailer's own product id, and chain the geometric mean (a Jevons index) of the price ratios. Retailers get equal weights. There are no spending weights. The indices are intended weekly, normally on Monday. They are not CPI and not an official statistic. They measure posted online shelf prices, not prices paid. UK, 2026-W44 The headline for Tesco, Sainsbury's, Asda and Aldi is 99.72, down 0.24% on the week. The base is 100 at 2026-W42, when the series restarted after a skipped week 41. It rests on 74,335 matched products. Food and soft drinks is 99.81, down 0.21%. By retailer, week on week: Tesco: +0.05% Sainsbury's: +0.04% Asda: -0.17% Aldi: -0.88% I am not giving a cause for Aldi's fall. The index shows the movement only. Australia, 2026-W44 The like-for-like headline for Coles, Woolworths and Aldi Australia is 100.64, up 0.48%, from a base of 100 at 2026-W41. It rests on 21,029 matched products, in Australian dollars. Food and soft drinks is 100.23, up 0.05%. Across all matched products, by retailer: Coles +0.15%, Woolworths +1.19%, Aldi Australia -0.10%. Personal care is the class that moved most, up 7.15% on the page. Shelf prices include promotions by design, so a change in how many products are on offer can move a class even when regular prices do not. One limit matters here: Coles is a partial slice, with 6,425 products used (21.0% of the Coles lists) this week. Read the data The full UK series is a public CSV under CC BY 4.0. It is long format, with one row per vintage, record type, retailer and class. import pandas as pd url = ( " https://api.apify.com/v2/datasets/AvRCWqFinCiNjx3sP/items " " ?format=csv&clean=true " ) df = pd . read_csv ( url ) head = df [ df [ " recordType " ] == " headline " ] print ( head [[ " vintage " , " level " , " weekOnWeekPct " , " matched " ]] . sort_values ( " vintage " )) The column names come from the data dictionary. Levels from different series (base W39 and base W42) cannot be compared. Where to get it UK W44: DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23881940 , and the Hugging Face dataset yappman/uk-online-shelf-price-index . items.title: AI in my own business: how I work with AI agents
items.snippet: Anyone who advises companies on AI should use it themselves. Not for a demo, but day to day, with real data and real consequences. I run HafenPixel, my web development business in Hamburg, with my own back office in which AI agents do the groundwork. This arti
items.content: Anyone who advises companies on AI should use it themselves. Not for a demo, but day to day, with real data and real consequences. I run HafenPixel, my web development business in Hamburg, with my own back office in which AI agents do the groundwork. This article covers what they take on, what I still decide myself – and the rules I have set for it. My five rules at a glance Nothing goes out without approval – internally the AI works freely, externally I decide No figure without a source Client data only when it is cleared – the AI does not read my inbox Every project has a budget and a clear criterion The AI may disagree – and so may I What the AI takes on The agents work for me, not for themselves. Specifically: Analysis: bringing together search data, visitor numbers and keyword data and saying what matters. What used to take half a day of spreadsheets is now an overview within minutes. Research: competitors, trade media, legal changes – with sources, so I can check. Drafts: texts, posts, page concepts and, when needed, emails. A draft is always a proposal for me, never a result. Checking my own visibility: regular tests of how AI assistants such as ChatGPT or Gemini talk about my business. This has become one of my most important channels for enquiries. Tasks and reminders: whatever follows from an analysis lands in the system as a task with a date – not in my head. What I decide myself The line is simple: anything that goes outside or costs money, I decide. This is how the work is split: Task The AI Me Analysis brings data together, highlights what stands out decide what follows from it Research collects, with sources check the sources Texts and pages writes drafts cut, change, approve Marketing plans content, prepares posts, measures the effect decide topics and tone, approve every post Emails writes a draft when needed read my inbox myself and approve every email Client relationships – conversations, assessments, bad news And there is one thing no table captures: how it sounds. Whether a sentence sounds like me, I notice when I read it. No AI can do that for me. An everyday example: marketing This shows most clearly in marketing, the area that is most likely to slip alongside client projects. The agents take on much of the groundwork – and I decide what of it goes outside. items.title: Krea 2 Identity Edit v1.2: Three ComfyUI Editing Modes, One Fidelity Dial
items.snippet: Krea 2 shipped an editing model, and the interesting part is not the demo images — it is that the same LoRA now covers three different working modes, and each one changes where the model gets its reference from. Three ComfyUI graphs ship with this episode, all
items.content: Krea 2 shipped an editing model, and the interesting part is not the demo images — it is that the same LoRA now covers three different working modes, and each one changes where the model gets its reference from. Three ComfyUI graphs ship with this episode, all built on the Krea 2 Identity Edit v1.2 LoRA. They share a base model, a text encoder and a VAE; what differs is the input path and the constraint: a plain single-image editor, a masked single-image editor, and a two-image reference editor. No inference was run for this release. Everything below is read from the saved graphs, not from a benchmark I executed. Mode File Nodes / links Fidelity (ref_boost) Mask Second image Single-image editor 01 24 / 26 4 – optional group, bypassed Mask editor 02 22 / 27 3 GrowMask 6 – Two-image editor 03 22 / 31 3 – active (A + B) The shared spine All three files load krea2_turbo_fp8_scaled.safetensors through a UNETLoader , apply krea2_identity_edit_v1_2_fp16.safetensors at strength 1 through LoraLoaderModelOnly , use qwen3vl_4b_fp8_scaled.safetensors with type krea2 as the text encoder, and decode through qwen_image_HDR_vae_fp32_comfy.safetensors . The KSampler is identical in all three: 10 steps, CFG 1, euler , simple , denoise 1. That is the turbo-matched setup; the workflow's own note says switching to krea2_raw_bf16 instead of turbo means 40 steps and CFG 3–4, and then the negative prompt starts mattering. The node that carries the actual editing behaviour is Krea2EditModelPatch , and its first widget is the fidelity dial — ref_boost. The note in the graph is unusually specific about it: 1.0 is described as the old v1.1 behaviour, 4.0 as the recommended preset, and very high values are said to over-copy the reference until removals and replacements stop working. The single-image graph ships at 4; the mask and two-image graphs ship at 3. The instruction itself goes through Krea2EditGroundedEncode — a plain-English sentence, not a tag soup. The saved examples are written as direct actions ("add a pair of thin black cat-eye sunglasses", "change the outfit of the woman in Image A to the complete sporty outfit from Image B") and then explicitly list what should not change: face, hairstyle, clothing, background, lighting. 01 — Single-image editor, with a second reference hiding in plain sight The first graph looks like a single-image editor and behaves like one by default, but it ships with a whole group named "2 · SECOND REFERENCE (optional — bypassed)". items.title: Never Complain, Never Explain
5 Rules of Lightsail Static IPs — They Outlive Your Instance, and Stopped Servers Still Bill
items.snippet: Introduction I recently rebuilt two Lightsail instances (dev and production) and had my first real encounter with Static IPs. They look like EC2's Elastic IPs, but the billing and behavior differ in subtle ways. Everything I learned boils down to five rules —
items.content: Introduction I recently rebuilt two Lightsail instances (dev and production) and had my first real encounter with Static IPs. They look like EC2's Elastic IPs, but the billing and behavior differ in subtle ways. Everything I learned boils down to five rules — and one framing that makes all five obvious: a static IP is not a property of the server; it's an asset of your account. The mistake that started it — copying yesterday's choice When creating the production instance, I traced the exact steps from the dev instance I'd built the day before — and ended up on the $7 plan, even though we had decided production would be $5. Copying yesterday's choice was the mistake. Normally this would hurt: recreating an instance means a new public IP, which means re-registering the allowed source IP with our payment gateway. But because a static IP was attached, recovery took 10 minutes: delete → recreate on $5 → re-attach the same static IP. That incident became a live test of all five rules. The five rules 1. A static IP is a new address you attach, not your current one frozen Creating a static IP doesn't "pin" your current public IP. It allocates a new address, and the moment you attach it, the old dynamic public IP disappears. If the old IP is registered anywhere (DNS, external services), update it around the attach. 2. Deleting the instance does not delete the static IP The static IP belongs to your account (per region), not to the instance. Delete the instance and the IP stays, detached, ready to re-attach to a new instance. That's exactly why my $7 → $5 rebuild took 10 minutes. 3. Free while attached, billed while detached An attached static IP costs nothing. Leave it detached and hourly charges begin. Combined with rule 2, the trap is obvious: the IP that survives your deleted instance is the one that starts billing. Release it if you're done with it. 4. It cannot cross regions A static IP only works within the region it was allocated in. You cannot move a Seoul IP to a Tokyo instance — a region migration always means a new IP. 5. Stopped instances bill at full price Lightsail is a monthly bundle, so Stop does not stop the cost . The only way to stop billing is deletion. This is the biggest difference from EC2's stopped-instance pricing. Where the console fought back The re-attach dialog uses a Cloudscape custom dropdown — not a native . items.title: What a JSON converter drafts from the first object
items.snippet: I copied an API response into a blank file and started a TypeScript interface by hand. The payload was a list of two people. Each object had an id, a name, a role, and a meta object with an active flag. I typed the fields from the first person and assumed the
items.content: I copied an API response into a blank file and started a TypeScript interface by hand. The payload was a list of two people. Each object had an id, a name, a role, and a meta object with an active flag. I typed the fields from the first person and assumed the second person used the same keys. The JSON converter at https://kepttools.com/json-converter makes that rule visible. Paste the text. It runs in the browser and drafts the interface from the first object only. The same paste can also become a PHP DTO, a Laravel array, or CSV. The sample below is the array the page fills, and the TypeScript is the converter's output for that text. [ { "id" : 1 , "name" : "Ada" , "role" : "engineer" , "meta" : { "active" : true }}, { "id" : 2 , "name" : "Linus" , "role" : "founder" , "meta" : { "active" : false }} ] TypeScript stops at Ada. Linus does not add a field. meta becomes its own interface because the value is an object. The root name is Root. export interface Root { id : number ; name : string ; role : string ; meta : Meta ; } export interface Meta { active : boolean ; } The PHP DTO is drafted from that same first object. The class is always named DataTransferObject. There is no child class. meta is public array $meta , and the constructor copies $data['meta'] through as an array. Laravel still walks the whole array, so both people remain and meta stays nested. CSV keeps the top-level keys and writes meta as one cell, with the inner quotes doubled: id,name,role,meta 1,Ada,engineer,"{""active"":true}" 2,Linus,founder,"{""active"":false}" TypeScript and the PHP DTO are drafted from the first object in an array. CSV keeps top-level keys only, and a nested object becomes one cell. Invalid JSON shows the parse error and leaves the output empty. { produces Expected property name or '}' in JSON at position 1 (line 1 column 2) . The output box is cleared. Before you save the draft, read the second object. A key that exists only there will not appear on the interface or the PHP class. Put that key on the object you convert, or add the property yourself. Rename DataTransferObject before you ship the class. A missing key is assigned with ?? null , including on a property declared public int $id . The full guide, with the FAQ and the converter: https://kepttools.com/guides/json-to-typescript-php-dto-laravel

items.title: Beyond the 9 to 5: Building Something of Your Own
items.snippet: I did not write Beyond the 9 to 5 because I think a regular job is a bad thing. I wrote it because I kept meeting people who felt trapped by a single job, not because the job itself was terrible, but because they had built nothing of their own alongside it. A
items.content: I did not write Beyond the 9 to 5 because I think a regular job is a bad thing. I wrote it because I kept meeting people who felt trapped by a single job, not because the job itself was terrible, but because they had built nothing of their own alongside it. A job can pay the bills. It rarely, on its own, gives you freedom, and it can disappear faster than you expect. Building something of your own is not about quitting tomorrow. It is about starting small, with what you already know how to do, and giving yourself a second option. That is how I started. I am from Abbottabad, Pakistan, and I built my work one piece at a time. I did not begin with capital, connections, or a big launch. I began with skills I could offer to real people. That is still the advice I give first: start with what you can do for someone else. If you can write, design, edit, teach, or organise, that is a service. A service does not need a perfect brand or a large audience. It needs one person who needs help and is willing to pay for it honestly. That lesson shaped findservicenest.com, my service-based site. Selling a service first taught me something no course could: clients teach you what is actually valuable. When someone pays you, they tell you the truth about your work. They show you what to improve, what to charge fairly for, and what to stop doing. Products and media can come later, but a service keeps you close to real problems. It also keeps you honest, because you cannot hide behind big promises when a real client is waiting for real delivery. From there, I built gradually. I founded Buzz Capitol, an independent digital news and media site, in 2026, and I serve as its Founder, CEO and Editor-in-Chief. I also chair Digi Skill Pro Academy, where we offer 100 percent free online earning classes. In 2025, more than 10,000 students took part, and more than 5,000 were reported as successful. I run more than 15 YouTube channels, and across Instagram, TikTok and other platforms I have more than 10 million followers. None of that arrived in one step. Each piece grew while I kept doing the unglamorous work in front of me. The point of Beyond the 9 to 5 is not to promise wealth or overnight success. I do not believe in that story, and I do not want anyone to chase it. The point is steadiness. items.title: Dropped on the Floor: Conflation in Kotlin Flows and the UI Events You Never Saw
items.snippet: Every few hundred checkouts, a support ticket arrived with the same story: “I paid, the money left my account, and the receipt screen never showed up.” The backend logs were spotless. The ViewModel logs were spotless. The ShowReceipt effect had been sent, and
items.content: Every few hundred checkouts, a support ticket arrived with the same story: “I paid, the money left my account, and the receipt screen never showed up.” The backend logs were spotless. The ViewModel logs were spotless. The ShowReceipt effect had been sent, and nobody had received it. That bug lives in a gap between two ideas Kotlin Flow lets you mix freely: state , where only the latest value matters, and events , where every occurrence matters. The mechanism that blurs the line is conflation , and it is not the only way values vanish. This post walks through what conflation is, when it quietly becomes a data-loss bug, and how to pick a primitive that matches the meaning of what you’re sending. What conflation is Conflation means that when a producer outpaces its collector, intermediate values are discarded and the collector receives the most recent one. The collector never asks for this; it simply never gets a chance to look at the values it skipped. conflation-timeline StateFlow conflates by design. Here is a download screen that updates its progress in a tight loop: class DownloadViewModel : ViewModel () { private val _progress = MutableStateFlow ( 0 ) val progress : StateFlow Int > = _progress . asStateFlow () fun start () { viewModelScope . launch ( Dispatchers . Default ) { for ( percent in 1 .. 100 ) { _progress . value = percent // no suspension point between writes } } } } A UI that takes a few milliseconds per frame to render will see only a handful of values (the exact ones depend on dispatcher scheduling and frame timing, so the sequence is nondeterministic), not a hundred distinct values. The only guarantee is that the last value written is eventually delivered. For a progress bar this is the correct behavior: rendering stale numbers faster than the user can read them would only waste CPU. Conflation is the reason StateFlow is cheap, and it is why you can write to it from anywhere without worrying about a slow UI. Two properties of StateFlow are worth keeping in mind, because they are conflation's quieter cousins: data class Cart ( val items : MutableList String > = mutableListOf ()) val cart = MutableStateFlow ( Cart ()) cart . value . items . add ( "green tea" ) // same instance, nothing assigned: no emission cart . value = cart . value // equal to the current value: ignored StateFlow compares each new value to the current one with equals and drops it when they match. A Solar Doorbell's Battery Gauge Lies to You in Winter
items.snippet: The accessory is a chain, not a panel A solar-powered doorbell is sold on one image: a small panel that means you never charge anything again. The engineering reality is a chain of four stages, and each stage has its own weather-dependent behaviour. The panel
items.content: The accessory is a chain, not a panel A solar-powered doorbell is sold on one image: a small panel that means you never charge anything again. The engineering reality is a chain of four stages, and each stage has its own weather-dependent behaviour. The panel makes electricity in proportion to light. A charge controller decides whether and how to push that electricity into the battery. The battery stores it and has opinions about temperature. The doorbell electronics draw from the battery in bursts, every time a motion event or a live view wakes the radio. When users report that a solar doorbell "dies in winter" or "never charges", the fault is rarely in one place. It is in the way the four stages interact with cold, shade, and the way battery level is estimated. Understanding the chain turns a mysterious failure into a predictable set of behaviours. The charge controller protects the battery by refusing to charge it This is the counterintuitive core of winter behaviour, and almost nobody expects it. The lithium cells used in doorbells and small security devices must not be charged below freezing. Charging a cold lithium cell causes metallic lithium to plate onto the anode instead of intercalating, and that plating is permanent, cumulative, and eventually dangerous. Every competent charge controller therefore has a low-temperature lockout: below roughly zero degrees Celsius, it refuses to pass charging current into the cell, even with a panel sitting in full sunshine. So the winter scene that confuses owners is physically correct behaviour. The doorbell is mounted on a north-facing wall, the sky is clear, the low sun is hitting the panel, the app shows the battery percentage sliding down day after day, and the owner reasonably concludes the solar feature is fake. What is actually happening is that the panel is generating, the controller is reading the cell temperature, and the controller is correctly throwing the energy away rather than damage the battery. The doorbell still runs, on stored charge, and discharging below freezing is far more tolerant than charging below freezing. The battery drains until a warmer day unlocks charging, or until it is brought inside and topped up over USB. Owners who understand the lockout stop fighting the panel and start managing the USB fallback, which is the productive response. items.content: Think about the last online form you filled out - a government services portal, a bank application, or a simple signup page. Name, email, phone number, multi-select dropdowns, and checkboxes hidden behind tiny scrollable windows. For many of us, it's a minor inconvenience. But for the elderly, individuals with disabilities, or those who aren't tech-savvy , a complex online form isn't just annoying - it's a digital wall. Whether someone is navigating a tremor, managing low vision, using one hand, or simply trying to fill out a field while multi-tasking, these traditional interfaces often lead to frustration and abandoned pages. Accessibility on the web shouldn't be an afterthought. What if, instead of typing and clicking, you could simply talk and have the page respond? From Hackathon Idea to Reality That question originally sparked GabAI - a concept my team pitched during a hackathon. The vision was straightforward: build a voice assistant that lives in your browser side panel, filling out web forms with you in real time out loud, and confirming details before anything is submitted. At the time, building a truly responsive, low-latency Voice AI agent felt like a massive undertaking, and we didn't get to complete it during the hackathon. But with the rapid advancement of real-time conversational AI tools, revisiting this idea became a whole lot easier. Powered by Agora Using the Agora Agents SDK and Agora Skills, the heavy lifting of real-time audio orchestration and conversational state management was already handled. What used to require complex custom voice pipelines can now be wired directly into a web interface. The result is a working Chrome extension that enables hands-free, accessible form filling right inside your browser side panel. It's still a demo, and I'll be completely transparent about its current limits later in this post. But building GabAI showed me just how accessible creating Voice AI agents has become - and how much power Agora gives developers to bridge digital accessibility gaps. Let's dive into how it works!
