You need low-latency audio in both directions, speech-to-text, an LLM, text-to-speech, and turn-taking: knowing when you've finished a sentence, and stopping mid-reply if you interrupt. items.title: `shutdown -h now` destroyed 13 of our 48 Ceph OSDs. Here is how we got the data back
items.snippet: We powered a site down on purpose. Electricians needed the room dead for an hour to upgrade a panel and fit a UPS. We had a runbook, we followed it, every application database shut down cleanly and reported exit code 0. Then we turned the site back on and 13 o
items.content: We powered a site down on purpose. Electricians needed the room dead for an hour to upgrade a panel and fit a UPS. We had a runbook, we followed it, every application database shut down cleanly and reported exit code 0. Then we turned the site back on and 13 of our 48 Ceph OSDs refused to start . Not one disk had failed. Every byte of object data was intact. But each of those 13 OSDs had a destroyed RocksDB index, and without it BlueStore will not mount the object store at all. At the worst point 103 placement groups were offline, our shared filesystem was degraded, and two production object stores had data we could not reach. This is the story of how we got all of it back except a single 4MB object, and why every supported repair tool in Ceph was useless to us . First, what Ceph actually is (skip this if you run it) If you already operate Ceph, jump to the next section. If you do not, none of the rest will land without this. Ceph is distributed storage. You give it a pile of disks spread across a pile of machines, and it presents them as one system that speaks three protocols at once: block devices for VMs, a POSIX filesystem you can mount, and an S3 compatible object store. Same cluster, same disks, three front doors. The pieces you need for this story: OSD (Object Storage Daemon). One process per disk. A host that owns 21 disks runs 21 OSD processes. This is the unit of storage and the unit of failure, and how many of them sit on one host is the whole root cause. Placement group (PG) . A pool is sliced into thousands of PGs, and each PG is replicated onto a set of OSDs. Clients do not track objects, they compute a PG with a hash and then compute its OSDs with an algorithm called CRUSH . No lookup table, no metadata server in the data path. It is genuinely elegant. Failure domain . You tell CRUSH what a "thing that can die" is: a disk, a host, a rack. CRUSH then guarantees replicas land in different ones. Pick this wrong and your replication is decorative. MON (Monitor). A small quorum of daemons holding the maps that describe the cluster. They do not touch your data, but nothing works without them. BlueStore . Modern OSDs do not use a filesystem. The OSD writes objects to the raw block device itself, which is faster and avoids a whole category of double-write problems. And that last one is where this incident lives. BlueStore writes your object data straight to the disk, but it has to remember where everything went: which object is at which offset, its

items.title: How to tell a client no to extra work (and keep the client)
items.snippet: "Can you just add one small thing?" Every freelancer has heard it. The small thing is rarely small, and it's never just one. Say yes too many times and a fixed-price project quietly becomes unpaid overtime. Say no badly and you risk the relationship. The good
items.content: "Can you just add one small thing?" Every freelancer has heard it. The small thing is rarely small, and it's never just one. Say yes too many times and a fixed-price project quietly becomes unpaid overtime. Say no badly and you risk the relationship. The good news: you almost never need to say a flat "no". You need to say "yes, and here's what it costs", in a way that feels professional rather than defensive. Here's how. Why saying no feels so hard Most freelancers struggle with this for three reasons: Fear of losing the client. Especially when the pipeline is thin. The request seems tiny. Refusing a 20-minute task feels petty, until there are fifteen of them. No clear scope. If the original agreement was vague, you can't point to what's in and what's out. The fix for all three is the same. Make the scope explicit, and turn every extra request into a choice the client makes, not a favour you grant. Step 1: Know your scope before the request arrives You can't defend a boundary you never drew. Every project should have a written scope covering: The deliverables, listed specifically. How many rounds of revisions are included. What's explicitly out of scope. What happens when new work is requested, like a change order at your hourly or day rate. That last line is the most important sentence in your contract. It means that when the "small thing" arrives, you're not improvising a policy. You're following one the client already agreed to. Step 2: Don't answer immediately When a client asks for extra work on a call or in a message, the pressure is to say "sure" on the spot. Don't. A simple holding reply buys you time: "Good idea. Let me check how that fits with the current scope and timeline, and I'll come back to you today." This isn't stalling. It's what professionals do. It also gives you time to estimate the work properly. Step 3: Use "yes, and" instead of "no" The most effective way to tell a client no to extra work is to not say no at all. Offer options instead. Here are three scripts you can adapt. Script 1: The change order "Happy to add that. It's outside the original scope, so I've estimated it at 4 hours, which is $320. If you approve, I'll start after the current milestone, and it moves delivery by two days. Want me to go ahead?" Script 2: The trade-off "We can absolutely include that. items.title: Fixing Extreme Mouse Lag After Suspend in Fedora (The Dual-Boot Time Bug)
items.snippet: If you dual-boot Fedora Linux and Windows, you might have run into a bizarre and frustrating issue: you wake your laptop from sleep, and suddenly your mouse cursor is lagging severely, frames are dropping, and your system time is hours in the future. Oddly eno
items.content: If you dual-boot Fedora Linux and Windows, you might have run into a bizarre and frustrating issue: you wake your laptop from sleep, and suddenly your mouse cursor is lagging severely, frames are dropping, and your system time is hours in the future. Oddly enough, opening GNOME Settings and toggling the Automatic Date & Time switch off and on instantly cures the mouse lag. But what exactly is happening behind the scenes, and how do you fix it permanently without manually toggling settings every time you open your laptop lid? The Root Cause: A Tale of Two Clocks This issue is the perfect storm of hardware clocks, dual-boot configurations, and Wayland compositor mechanics. The Time Zone Tug-of-War: By default, Windows stores your system's hardware clock (RTC / BIOS time) in Local Time . Linux, however, expects the hardware clock to be stored in UTC . The Suspend/Resume Cycle: When you suspend your laptop, the OS relies on the hardware clock to keep track of time. If you live in a UTC+5:30 time zone (like Sri Lanka), Windows sets your hardware clock 5.5 hours ahead of UTC. When Fedora wakes up, it reads that hardware clock, incorrectly assumes it is reading UTC, and adds another 5.5 hours to it to get to your local time. Mutter's Math Breaks: GNOME's Wayland compositor (Mutter) relies heavily on precise timestamps for its internal frame-pacing loops. When the system wakes up to an instantaneous, massive time jump into the future, Mutter's frame-timing calculations completely break. This results in dropped frames and severe mouse lag. When you toggle the Automatic Date & Time switch in settings, you restart the chronyd NTP service. Chrony realizes the system time is massively wrong, does a hard "step" backward to the correct internet time, and immediately fixes Mutter's math, curing the lag. Diagnosing the Issue To verify this is happening to you, check your chronyd logs right after waking your laptop: journalctl -u chronyd -b If you see something like this, you have the bug: Forward time jump detected! System clock wrong by -19799.938 seconds (Note: 19,800 seconds is exactly 5.5 hours). You can also check your current clock configuration by running: timedatectl If Universal time and RTC time do not match, your hardware clock is holding Local Time, which will cause this bug. The Permanent Fix To solve this, we need to force both operating systems to agree on a standard. The best approach is to make both OSs use UTC for the hardware clock. Step 1: Fix the Linux

items.snippet: You ever deploy your server-rendered React or Vue app with all the fanfare, only to find a flicker, an unexpected warning, or worse, a broken interactive UI on first load? You check the markup, and it looks right. The data’s there. But the client complains abo
items.content: You ever deploy your server-rendered React or Vue app with all the fanfare, only to find a flicker, an unexpected warning, or worse, a broken interactive UI on first load? You check the markup, and it looks right. The data’s there. But the client complains about hydration mismatches or silently drops event handlers. I’ve been there, chasing these ghostly bugs that show up only in production or in certain browsers. Hydration can feel like magic , but when it breaks, it’s maddening. So what’s actually going on when your client-side JavaScript reconciles the server-rendered HTML? Hydration: The Client’s Attempt to Reuse Server HTML Modern frameworks like React, Vue, or Svelte often send fully rendered HTML from the server on the initial load. This gets your page visible asap, with meaningful content for SEO and performance. But the client still needs to hook up event listeners, internal state, and reactivity. That's where hydration comes in. Hydration is the process where the client-side JavaScript parses the existing server HTML, matches it to the virtual DOM or component tree, and attaches event listeners and internal state without throwing away the HTML and re-rendering from scratch. Imagine you sent this HTML for a button: id= "like-btn" > Like (10) When your React or Vue client script runs, it looks for that button node and "hydrates" it , meaning it attaches the click handler and syncs the internal state so that when you click, the count can update. The Fragility of Hydration: When Markup and State Don’t Match Here’s the catch. Hydration expects that the client’s initial render output exactly matches the server's HTML. If there’s any mismatch , even a minor difference in attributes, element order, or text , hydration can fail in weird ways: Warnings about mismatches in the console Missing or broken event handlers UI flickering as the client throws away server HTML and re-renders Subtle glitches because DOM nodes are reused incorrectly Why do mismatches happen? Non-deterministic rendering: Your server and client generate slightly different markup because of randomness or date/time values. State divergence: The client initializes with different default state than the server used to render. Conditional rendering differences: Some code paths run only on server or client (e.g., checking window or user agent). items.content: TL;DR : I built a language model from scratch, end to end, on free GPUs : a 125.9M-parameter model that writes in a register you choose, with slang, emoji, abbreviation, elongation and formality as five dials. The idea is simple and testable: measure the register of every training document with code, write it as five control tokens in front of the text, and the model learns p(text | register) . On 200 held-out requests the generated register lands within 0.146 of the request on average, against 0.646 for a shuffled-request baseline. Behind that number sit a dated slang lexicon, a deterministic register annotator, a data pipeline and tokenizer, a verified Llama-style model, a lease-based training relay that turns flaky free sessions into one continuous run, a regression-tested training stack, and a Llama-format export that loads in three lines of transformers . Five live sketches below let you poke each idea. items.content: How AI Chatbots Work: LLMs, Tokens, Context & Backend Explained Have you ever wondered what happens when you type a question into ChatGPT and receive an answer within seconds? It may feel like you're talking to a person, but behind the scenes, a sophisticated AI system processes your message, uses conversation context, and generates a response. In this beginner-friendly guide, we'll explore how AI chatbots work, including Large Language Models (LLMs), tokens, context windows, frontend interfaces, backend servers, and AI APIs. 1. What Is an AI Chatbot? An AI chatbot is a software application that allows users to interact with an artificial intelligence system through natural language. Modern generative AI chatbots can help with: Answering questions Explaining technical concepts Writing and summarizing content Generating programming code Brainstorming ideas Assisting with research and learning Applications such as ChatGPT use large language models to generate responses based on the input and available context. 2. What Is a Large Language Model (LLM)? A Large Language Model is a machine learning model trained to process and generate language. Many modern LLMs use an architecture called the Transformer , which helps the model process relationships between tokens. During training, a language model learns statistical patterns from large amounts of data. When you ask a question, it uses those learned patterns to generate a relevant response. Example User: What is Python? AI: Python is a high-level programming language commonly used for web development, automation, data analysis, and artificial intelligence. The model generates this response based on its training and the context provided in the conversation. 3. What Happens When You Send a Message? Let's understand the process step by step. Imagine typing: "Explain machine learning in simple words." A typical AI chatbot application follows this workflow: Step 1 — User Input You enter your message into the chat interface. Step 2 — Frontend Sends a Request The application sends your message to its backend or an AI service. Step 3 — Backend Processes the Request The backend may validate the request, check permissions, retrieve relevant information, and prepare the conversation context. Step 4 — Tokenization The model's input is represented as tokens. items.snippet: A malicious version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension distributed through the Cursor marketplace attempted to install a persistent Secure Shell (SSH) backdoor on developers’ machines, potentially giving attackers remote access to systems holding source code
items.content: A malicious version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension distributed through the Cursor marketplace attempted to install a persistent Secure Shell (SSH) backdoor on developers’ machines, potentially giving attackers remote access to systems holding source code, credentials and other sensitive information. “Between about 2:27am PT and 1:35pm PT today, a maliciously modified version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension was made available in the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace,” Cursor said in a security notice . Cursor removed the compromised versions, 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, after discovering they had been available in its VS Code extension marketplace for approximately 11 hours on October 29. The company said the malicious code attempted to add an attacker-controlled SSH key, enable local SSH access, and establish a reverse tunnel to an attacker-controlled server. “These malicious versions of the extension were not developed by Anthropic,” Cursor added in the notice. The affected versions were available for Windows and macOS. Anthropic subsequently clarified how the tampered extension had been distributed. In a post on X, Felix Rieseberg, a member of Anthropic’s technical staff, said the incident did not involve a compromise of Anthropic’s systems or employee laptops. A malicious actor had used access to Cursor’s marketplace to publish the modified extension, he said. “The versions on our official channels are not affected, and this only impacts Cursor users,” Rieseberg wrote. Anthropic said it was working with Cursor on the incident. Cursor and Anthropic had not responded to requests for comment by publication time. Malware ran without user interaction Security company Phorion, which analysed the compromised extension, found that malicious code had been inserted at the beginning of its JavaScript file. It ran as soon as the extension loaded, before its normal activation code. “The user doesn’t need to interact with the extension for the payload to fire,” Phorion said . The malware attempted to add an attacker-controlled SSH key to the user’s authorized_keys file and establish a connection to a remote server. It also created scripts and startup entries intended to keep the connection available after a system restart, the company added. Phorion identified a flaw in the macOS code. items.content: Cursor's native support for the Model Context Protocol (MCP) represents the biggest leap in developer ergonomics since the introduction of inline Copilot completions. Instead of treating the AI as an isolated text predictor that only sees what you explicitly copy-paste into chat, MCP gives Cursor active hands and eyes . With the right MCP servers configured, Cursor can autonomously inspect local SQLite databases, query your production Postgres replicas, test API endpoints, search real-time GitHub PRs, and manipulate browser sessions via Puppeteer. However, configuring MCP manually via JSON files remains one of the biggest friction points for developers. A single missing comma, an unquoted environment variable, or an incorrect executable path can cause Cursor's MCP client to fail silently. In this guide, we break down how Cursor's MCP subsystem works under the hood, provide the exact configuration schemas, solve the most common connection errors, and show how to manage your toolchain with zero friction. Understanding the mcp.json Config Schema & File Locations Cursor stores all MCP server definitions in a global configuration file named mcp.json . The location depends on your operating system: Operating System Default Config Path macOS ~/.cursor/mcp.json or ~/Library/Application Support/Cursor/User/globalStorage/mcp.json Linux ~/.cursor/mcp.json or ~/.config/Cursor/User/globalStorage/mcp.json Windows %USERPROFILE%\.cursor\mcp.json or %APPDATA%\Cursor\User\globalStorage\mcp.json The Official JSON Schema The top-level structure requires an mcpServers object containing named server keys: json { "mcpServers": { "sqlite-local": { "command": "uvx", "args": [ "mcp-server-sqlite", "--db-path", "/Users/username/projects/data/production.db" ] }, "github-tools": { "command": "npx", "args": [ "-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-github" ], "env": { "GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN": "ghp_your_secret_pat_here" } } } }

items.title: Smart Retries Are Smart About One Thing
items.snippet: Every major billing platform now advertises some version of “smart retries,” and the pitch sounds total: machine learning will fix your failed payments. Tear the capability down to what it actually does, and a narrower, more honest picture appears. Smart retri
items.content: Every major billing platform now advertises some version of “smart retries,” and the pitch sounds total: machine learning will fix your failed payments. Tear the capability down to what it actually does, and a narrower, more honest picture appears. Smart retries are genuinely smart about one thing — when to present a card again. They are not smart about why the card failed in your customer's life, whether that customer still consents to be charged, or what your business promised them last week. Confusing those layers is expensive. What the timing layer actually optimizes Start with the real strength. A large platform sees billions of payment attempts across issuers, countries, card networks, and times of day. From that firehose it can learn patterns no single merchant could ever see: which issuers process more cleanly overnight, how long an insufficient-funds decline typically needs before another attempt is worthwhile, which decline codes should never be retried at all. It can refresh expired card details through network account updater services and choose, for each attempt, a moment with a statistically better chance of approval. That is real engineering, and it recovers real money. Notice the unit of analysis, though. The model optimizes a transaction: this card, this issuer, this amount, this hour. Its scoreboard is approval probability. It does not know, and was never built to know, whether approving this transaction is actually the right outcome for the subscription underneath it. A perfectly timed retry can still collect from a customer who emailed support yesterday asking to pause, or re-bill a card the customer replaced precisely because they wanted the old one to stop being used for this service. What it cannot see: stale in a different way Card data goes stale in two senses, and smart systems only fix one. They are good at the mechanical sense: a new expiry date, a reissued card number, a network token that survives reissuance. They are blind to the human sense. The card may be valid and still be the wrong card — a shared family card, a corporate card whose owner changed jobs, a debit card tied to an account the customer is closing this month. No issuer pattern reveals that. Only a conversation with the customer does, which is why a clear card-update request, sent at the right moment in plain language, recovers a class of failures that infinite silent retries never will. items.snippet: Kimberly-Clark is one of the most heavily shorted stocks in the S&P 500. At the October 15, 2026 settlement, 50.6 million of its shares were sold short, 15.2% of its shares outstanding, up from 8.3 million a year earlier. Read the usual way, that is a growing
items.content: Kimberly-Clark is one of the most heavily shorted stocks in the S&P 500. At the October 15, 2026 settlement, 50.6 million of its shares were sold short, 15.2% of its shares outstanding, up from 8.3 million a year earlier. Read the usual way, that is a growing crowd betting the Kleenex maker will fall. The timing says something else. The position started climbing in November 2025, right after Kimberly-Clark agreed to buy Kenvue and pay partly in its own shares. In a stock deal, arbitrage funds commonly buy the target and short the buyer, so the short position grows with the deal, not with a view on the company. So I checked how many of the most-shorted S&P 500 stocks have a reason like that written into their own filings. How I checked I took FINRA's short interest for every S&P 500 member at the October 15, 2026 settlement and ranked the 25 highest as a share of shares outstanding. For each, I searched SEC filings since October 2025 for the four standard sources of hedged short selling: a stock-for-stock deal or exchange offer, convertible or exchangeable notes, forward sales of new shares, and mandatory convertible preferred stock. I read every hit. Boilerplate mentions, such as debt covenants that refer to exchange offers in general, don't count. items.snippet: Introduction Colleges, universities, and training institutes are constantly searching for smarter ways to attract prospective students. Traditional outreach—phone calls, emails, and campus tours—still works, but it’s time‑consuming and often inconsistent. Ente
items.content: Introduction Colleges, universities, and training institutes are constantly searching for smarter ways to attract prospective students. Traditional outreach—phone calls, emails, and campus tours—still works, but it’s time‑consuming and often inconsistent. Enter AI calling agents : intelligent, voice‑enabled bots that can handle thousands of conversations simultaneously. By automating outreach, schools can nurture leads, answer questions, and guide applicants through the enrollment funnel with unprecedented speed and personalization. How AI Calling Agents Work AI calling agents combine natural language processing (NLP), speech recognition, and machine‑learning algorithms to simulate human conversation. Here’s a quick breakdown of the process: Data Integration – The system pulls prospect information from CRM platforms, inquiry forms, and social media ads. Voice Scripting – Using dynamic scripts, the AI tailors its dialogue based on the student’s interests (e.g., engineering, liberal arts, online programs). Real‑Time Interaction – When a call is placed, the AI detects tone, pauses, and intent, adjusting its responses on the fly. Actionable Follow‑Ups – After the conversation, the agent logs key details, schedules campus tours, or sends personalized email summaries. Because the technology learns from each interaction, the more it talks, the better it becomes at handling objections, providing program details, and even spotting enrollment barriers such as financial aid concerns. Benefits for Student Enrollment 1. Scalable Outreach One AI calling agent can manage dozens of calls per hour, freeing admissions staff to focus on high‑touch activities like counseling and scholarship interviews. This scalability means institutions can reach a larger pool of prospects without expanding the team. 2. 24/7 Availability Prospective students often research programs outside regular office hours. AI agents answer questions at any time, reducing missed opportunities and keeping the enrollment pipeline full. 3. Personalized Experience By leveraging data from previous interactions, AI agents can reference a student’s specific interests—“I see you’re interested in our cybersecurity certificate. Let me tell you about our upcoming information session.” Personalization drives higher conversion rates. 4. Data‑Driven Insights Every call is logged and analyzed. items.title: My ending remarks: Hacktoberfest 2026
items.snippet: October is over, and so is another Hacktoberfest. I'm writing this the monday after, while it's still fresh, because I have two things to say: one is a thank-you, and the other is a (friendly) complaint. What I got out of it I came into this year discovering a
items.content: October is over, and so is another Hacktoberfest. I'm writing this the monday after, while it's still fresh, because I have two things to say: one is a thank-you, and the other is a (friendly) complaint. What I got out of it I came into this year discovering a new community that shared in my newfound passion with open source in mind. A place that we can get challenged and share our creations with each other. Hacktoberfest 2026 gave me that. A habit. Having a month-long goal turned "What project should I work on today?" into "I'll finish this challenge tonight!" Better skills. Reading unfamiliar codebases, working with leading opensource tools, and responding to feedback without getting defensive about it. And learning all of that in a natural environment, not through YouTube tutorials. Confidence. Getting better control over what tool to use to what project and estimating the time scope of my projects. Connections. I talked to people I'd never have met otherwise. I'm taking my hat of for Jacklyn Biggin. Her engagement and friendly attitude were dangerously contagious. The community is the real prize The stickers are fun, but what I'll remember is the people. Fellow hackers who took time to leave kind, specific comments on a random project shared in the discord. Fellow attendees who answered questions in Discord at odd hours when the Hacktoberfest crew took their well earned rest. People who shared beginner-friendly resurces to other people's issues. Someone even went the extra mine bug-fix with them when someone got stuck. Hacktoberfest's new subject shift regarding AI in the open source space was a new take that even I, a newbie, felt some people in the comunity had a slight issue with. Me on the other hand thought this was a logical change considering how more and more AI takes a part in the day to day life, like it or not. So with having to deal with that and still welcoming newcomers to this experience must have taken some extra effort. If you've stayed somewhat open minded and helped around where you could: thank you. You made it a good experience for newbies like me. Shoutout to the hosts Fest hosts are the unsung heroes of this whole thing. They give up evenings and weekends to organize meetups, find venues, explaining the lay of the land to nervous first-timers, and keep the energy up when GitHub goes down from time to time. Events seems to be where Hacktoberfest turns from "me and my laptop" into a shared experience. Sitting in a room (or a call)

items.title: From one command to a live app on a $5 VPS
items.snippet: You own the server, the code and the data. Here is what the first ten minutes look like. Why the default path gets annoying You rent a backend and it works. The annoyance shows up later: on app number two, when you see what a second project costs, and on the d
items.content: You own the server, the code and the data. Here is what the first ten minutes look like. Why the default path gets annoying You rent a backend and it works. The annoyance shows up later: on app number two, when you see what a second project costs, and on the day you want to leave and find out what you can take with you. The database is yours in theory. In practice the export is a job you write yourself, the users sit in someone else's auth format, and the files live in a bucket you do not control. That is a trade, not a scandal, and it is worth seeing what the other side of it looks like. This post walks through one: a backend you create on your own machine, deploy to a server you rent, and can leave with one command. I build CrescoDB, so that is the tool in the examples, and I will say where it stops. Create the project You need Node 20 or newer. node --version Create the project: npm create crescodb@latest my-app This writes the project into my-app , installs the CLI inside it, starts it and opens the dashboard. The dashboard asks you to sign in to a CrescoDB account. The account is free and needs no card. Now add auth. Move into the folder and run the generator: cd my-app npx cresco create auth That command writes the auth code into your project as plain files: register.js , login.js , middleware.js and jwt.js , wired to the project database. Passwords are hashed with scrypt and sessions use JWT. Next to them sit schema.cresco , which describes your tables, and cresco.db , the SQLite file. It is a normal Node project. Open it in an editor and read the login route. Nothing in it is hidden behind a package you cannot open. Run it npm run dev The API starts on port 3000 and the dashboard is at http://localhost:3000/studio . The database is SQLite, so there is nothing to install and no Docker. For the store starter, the project's own page shows this output: ✓ schema.cresco · cresco.db · store starter ✓ shop is ready. REST API on :3000 Dashboard opened, connected to shop Your app is served too. cresco dev serves your project folder at http://localhost:3000/app and reloads the page when you save, so the frontend sits next to its API. The schema Everything comes from one file. A model looks like this: { "name" : "Order" , "fields" : [ { "name" : "id" , "type" : "uuid" , "primaryKey" : true }, { "name" : "total" , "type" : "number" , "required" : true } ], "access" : { "read" : [ "authenticated" ] } } From that, every model gets create, read, update and delete

items.title: Six predicates in this codebase are written twice, once in TypeScript and once in SQL
items.snippet: A campaign in Nakodo can be paused in three different ways: stop finding new creators, stop the email flow, or stop both. Nakodo can also pause a campaign itself, for instance when a Free account's month of contacts is used up, and our pricing page states a co
items.content: A campaign in Nakodo can be paused in three different ways: stop finding new creators, stop the email flow, or stop both. Nakodo can also pause a campaign itself, for instance when a Free account's month of contacts is used up, and our pricing page states a couple of those cases, including that extra campaigns are paused rather than deleted when a plan gets smaller. From that one product idea comes a question the code has to answer in two completely different places. A React component renders a status dot and needs to know whether this campaign is still searching. A background job runs a query that has to pick which campaigns' searches to claim out of everyone's. The first has one row in memory. The second must not load any rows to find out. So the rule is written twice, on purpose, and the two files sit next to each other. src/lib/pause.ts 51 lines, no imports at all, 16 importers src/lib/pause-sql.ts 29 lines, imports drizzle and the schema, 10 importers The same sentence in two languages // pause.ts export const isFinding = ( c : CampaignState ): boolean => c . status === " active " || pauseModeOf ( c ) === " emails " ; // pause-sql.ts const pausedByUser = and ( paused , isNull ( campaigns . pauseReason )); export const findingSql : SQL = or ( active , and ( pausedByUser , eq ( campaigns . pauseMode , " emails " ))) ! ; There are four pairs in these two files: finding, searching, emailing and starting conversations. Two more live elsewhere in the repo, and I will come to both. pause.ts has no imports, which is deliberate: it is used by client components, by server components, and by the schema's own types, so it cannot be allowed to drag a database client into a browser bundle. pause-sql.ts is the half that knows about columns, and its ten importers are all background work. Reading the two together is also how you find out what the product actually decided. isEmailing is true for a campaign Nakodo paused itself, because the conversations already started are allowed to finish, while startsConversations is false for the same row, because nothing new may begin. In SQL that is two expressions that differ by one or branch: export const emailingSql : SQL = or ( active , and ( paused , isNotNull ( campaigns . pauseReason )), and ( pausedByUser , eq ( campaigns . pauseMode , " finding " )), ) ! ; export const startingSql : SQL = or ( active , and ( pausedByUser , eq ( campaigns . pauseMode , " finding " ))) ! ; Where three-valued logic agrees with a default by

items.title: Designing photo-to-video workflows around roles, scenes and honest previews
items.snippet: Photo-to-video tools have a deceptively simple interface: upload a picture, pick an effect, and press Generate. The harder product question is what the uploaded picture is supposed to control. I maintain AI Baby Dance. Its Hotel Lobby, Tiny Desk AI and Vikas E
items.content: Photo-to-video tools have a deceptively simple interface: upload a picture, pick an effect, and press Generate. The harder product question is what the uploaded picture is supposed to control. I maintain AI Baby Dance. Its Hotel Lobby, Tiny Desk AI and Vikas Editor workspaces take three different approaches to that question. This is a walkthrough of their current workflows and the differences worth checking before generating a video. Start with the scene, then assign the photos A portrait is an identity reference, not a complete description of a performance. A useful interface needs to make the scene and the person's role explicit. In Hotel Lobby AI Video Generator , the two upload slots represent the left and right characters. Users choose among seven performance templates, including an orange recording booth, street rap, recording studio, rap battle, couple duo, grandpas duo and comedy roast battle. The recording studio accepts one or two photos; the other templates require two. The page includes playable template samples. The orange-booth sample shows two performers in front of a suspended microphone. The sample explains the intended setting, but it is not a preview generated from the user's uploaded faces. A group scene needs a casting interface Tiny Desk AI uses role-specific casting rather than treating a group photograph as five separately assigned identities. Users can provide one to five individual portraits. The roles are lead singer, saxophone player, keyboard player and two backing singers. With one photo, the user personalizes the singer and AI fills the remaining positions. With five, every performer has a separate reference. The page pairs one-, three- and five-photo examples with their generated band videos. That makes the difference between partial and full casting visible. The result is an original office-band scene, with bookshelves, microphones and AI-generated instrumental audio. It does not supply NPR concert footage or the original "Outstanding" recording. Both performance workspaces offer 5-, 10- or 15-second output in 720p, with vertical, square and landscape formats. Duration is also a spending decision: generation uses credits, and the interface displays the cost before submission. Leave room for an editable description A fixed performance template is useful when the scene is already defined. For broader visual changes, an editable prompt gives users another kind of control. items.title: WhatsApp Coexistence for Developers: History Sync, Message Echoes and Contacts Without Breaking Your Inbox
items.snippet: Most WhatsApp Cloud API integrations assume they own the number: every message in or out passes through your webhook and your send call. Coexistence breaks that assumption. A business keeps using the WhatsApp Business app on its phone and connects the same num
items.content: Most WhatsApp Cloud API integrations assume they own the number: every message in or out passes through your webhook and your send call. Coexistence breaks that assumption. A business keeps using the WhatsApp Business app on its phone and connects the same number to your platform, so messages now arrive from three directions at once: live customer messages on the normal messages webhook, a backfill of up to six months of old chats, and copies of whatever the owner types on their phone. Get the merge wrong and you get duplicate contacts, a chat list reordered by six-month-old messages, automations replying to history, and an inbox that says "you can reply" when WhatsApp won't deliver. This post covers what coexistence sends you, the decisions it forces, and a tested TypeScript implementation of each webhook, based on what we built and fixed in WAPGROWAI's own coexistence support. All Meta behaviour quoted here is from Meta's coexistence onboarding guide and its webhook reference pages. The snippets are small, self-contained versions of the patterns, and each was run against the cases shown. What changes when the app and the API share a number On a coexistence number, the business still uses the app for 1:1 chats, and your platform sees them. But plenty doesn't carry over to the Cloud API side. Meta's feature table marks these as not supported: group chats, disappearing and view-once messages, live location, broadcast lists (which become read-only), voice and video calls, the app's business tools (catalog, orders, status), its messaging tools (marketing messages, greeting and away messages, quick replies, labels), the business profile, and channels. Two limits matter for platform code: Throughput is fixed. Numbers "in use with both the WhatsApp Business app and Cloud API have a fixed throughput of 20 mps" (messages per second), instead of the usual 80 that can rise to 1,000. Campaign senders need to pace for 20. Offboarding happens in the app. The Deregister API can't be used on coexistence numbers. The business disconnects from the app's settings, and you get an account_update webhook with PARTNER_REMOVED . Four webhooks, three sources Subscribe to these fields for coexistence numbers: Webhook field What it carries Live or sync? messages Customers' messages, as usual Live history Up to 180 days of past 1:1 chats, in phases and chunks Sync smb_message_echoes Messages the business sends from the app or a linked device Live, but from the business smb_app_state

items.content: Short answer: in my check, dev.to, Substack and Gumroad allow GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, PerplexityBot and Google-Extended in robots.txt. Medium disallows GPTBot but allows the others. Indie Hackers disallows all four for the whole site. On dev.to the full post text is also in the raw HTML, so a crawler that does not run JavaScript still gets the article. Part of the run was interrupted, so anything I could not finish is left out. robots.txt, per host host GPTBot OAI-SearchBot PerplexityBot Google-Extended dev.to allowed allowed allowed allowed aicitationnotes.substack.com allowed allowed allowed allowed normbrytande.gumroad.com allowed allowed allowed allowed medium.com disallowed ( / ) allowed ( * ) allowed ( * ) allowed ( * ) indiehackers.com disallowed ( / ) disallowed ( / ) disallowed ( / ) disallowed ( / ) Notes: "Allowed" means robots.txt does not forbid it. Whether a CDN or WAF blocks the real bots is not verified. GPTBot is OpenAI's training crawler. OAI-SearchBot is the one used for ChatGPT search. Medium only blocks the first. dev.to serves a /llms.txt (200). It asks that AI-assisted articles set ai_disclosure_level accurately. Is the article text in raw HTML? curl -sL --compressed -A " " " $URL " dev.to: all 5 of my posts, full text present, 692 to 1,657 words each. Substack and Indie Hackers: full text present. Gumroad product pages: body text only inside an Inertia data-page JSON attribute, plus , meta description and Product JSON-LD. Exact-title lookups With a web search tool (backend not disclosed, so not tied to any specific engine): all 5 of my dev.to posts were found by exact title. None of my 6 Medium posts were found, and for three cross-posted ones the dev.to copy came up instead. What the two dev.to posts Perplexity cited had in common For "How do I check if ChatGPT recommends my product?", Perplexity cited two dev.to posts by other authors, both with 0 reactions. One has the question as its title and answers in the first sentence. The other has a near-question title and answers within 3 short paragraphs, then lists numbered steps. My posts open with a story. items.title: When agents invent APIs — make grep-first a merge gate
items.snippet: I keep catching agent PRs that call helpers that do not exist. Not typos — confident imports of fetchUserProfileV2 , useCheckoutMachine , formatMoneyLocale . Green TypeScript locally (because the agent also invented a stub), red in CI once the stub is gone, or
items.content: I keep catching agent PRs that call helpers that do not exist. Not typos — confident imports of fetchUserProfileV2 , useCheckoutMachine , formatMoneyLocale . Green TypeScript locally (because the agent also invented a stub), red in CI once the stub is gone, or worse: green forever with a hand-rolled fake that nobody asked for. The fix that stuck for me is boring: grep-first as a merge gate . Before the model writes a call site, it has to prove the symbol already lives in the repo — or stop and ask. The failure mode Agents optimize for “the feature works in this chat.” They do not feel the cost of a new private API. So they: Import a name that sounds like your codebase Add a 20-line util next to the feature instead of reusing the real one three folders away Duplicate a hook with a slightly different signature “Fix” missing exports by creating them, then leave the real module untouched Reviewers then spend time deciding whether the new thing is intentional architecture or hallucinations with types. Grep-first means what, exactly? In the prompt (and later in CI), I require: Search before invent — rg / IDE search for the intended symbol, path, or behavior Cite the hit — paste the file path + a one-line snippet that proves it exists Reuse or stop — if nothing matches, do not invent a public helper; either use a nearby existing pattern or stop with a short note: “no existing X; options are A/B” Inventing a local private function inside the file you’re already editing is fine. Inventing a shared API is not — that’s a separate decision. Paste this into the agent prompt ## API invent ban (HARD) Before you import or call any symbol outside the files you are allowed to edit: 1. Search the repo for an existing equivalent ( `rg -n "functionName|HookName|ModuleName"` ). 2. In your reply, cite at least one real path + line that you will reuse. 3. If search returns nothing: STOP. Do not create a new shared util/hook/service. List 2–3 options (reuse nearby pattern / extend existing module / new module needs human OK). 4. Allowed without search: private helpers scoped to the current file only (not exported). Do not invent `*V2` , `*New` , or parallel hooks “for clarity.” Do not add barrel re-exports to paper over a missing symbol. The STOP clause is the whole point. Without it, agents treat “prefer reuse” as vibes and keep typing. What I grep for (frontend patterns) I don’t only search the exact name the model wants. I search for behavior : Intent Grep seeds I actually try

items.title: Building HM360: Creating a Self-Hosted Hosting Management Platform with Node.js
items.snippet: Building software for the hosting industry is an interesting challenge because hosting businesses have many interconnected operations to manage. Customer accounts, domain registrations, hosting services, billing, invoicing, provisioning and DNS management are
items.content: Building software for the hosting industry is an interesting challenge because hosting businesses have many interconnected operations to manage. Customer accounts, domain registrations, hosting services, billing, invoicing, provisioning and DNS management are all important parts of running a hosting company. I have been working on a project called HM360 , a self-hosted hosting management and automation platform developed by the WingsHoster team. I want to share what we are building and some of the challenges involved in creating a platform for hosting businesses. Why I Started Building HM360 Running a hosting business requires more than server infrastructure. As a hosting provider grows, managing customers, products, orders, domains and billing becomes increasingly complex. I wanted to build a platform that brings these operational components together while allowing hosting providers to deploy and manage the software within their own infrastructure. That became the motivation behind HM360. What Is HM360? HM360 is a self-hosted hosting management platform designed for: Web hosting providers. VPS and dedicated server providers. Domain resellers. Hosting startups. Web development agencies. The objective is to provide a centralized environment for managing hosting business operations. Technology Behind the Project The HM360 backend uses a JavaScript-based technology stack, including: Node.js for server-side application development. Express.js for backend application services. MySQL for relational data management. Modern JavaScript frontend technologies. One of the important considerations when developing a platform like this is designing independent modules that can work together without creating unnecessary dependencies. Key Areas We Are Developing 1. Customer Management Managing customer accounts and maintaining relationships between customers, products and services. 2. Hosting Service Management Managing hosting products, customer orders and service provisioning workflows. 3. Domain Management Supporting domain registration, renewal, transfer and DNS management workflows through registrar integrations. 4. Billing and Invoicing Managing invoices, payments and financial workflows associated with hosting services. 5. Marketplace Supporting vendor marketplace functionality and associated business workflows. 6. Built-in CMS Providing content management capabilities within the platform. One Interesting Challenge: Domain Registration Workflows Domain registration

items.title: Kubernetes: un run ID para el correo de CI
items.snippet: Un test de CI que espera un email suele fallar con un mensaje poco util: “timeout esperando el correo”. En Kubernetes, el síntoma puede venir del navegador, del worker, de la cola o de la bandeja de prueba. Si cada capa registra un identificador diferente, el
items.content: Un test de CI que espera un email suele fallar con un mensaje poco util: “timeout esperando el correo”. En Kubernetes, el síntoma puede venir del navegador, del worker, de la cola o de la bandeja de prueba. Si cada capa registra un identificador diferente, el equipo termina repitiendo el job sin saber que evidencia mirar. Un patrón pequeño ayuda bastante: asignar un run_id al inicio del flujo y llevarlo por el job, el mensaje de prueba, los logs y los artefactos. No arregla una entrega lenta por sí solo, pero convierte una sospecha difusa en una investigación corta. Para un equipo SRE, esa diferencia importa mas que añadir otro reintento. El síntoma: un test de correo que parece aleatorio Imagina un despliegue efímero que crea un namespace, registra un usuario y espera un enlace de activación. A veces pasa en 20 segundos; otras veces expira. El reporte muestra que el pod del navegador sigue sano, pero no dice qué bandeja consultó ni desde qué momento empezó a buscar. Hay varios fallos parecidos que se mezclan: el test leyó un mensaje viejo de otra ejecución; el worker publicó el evento, pero el consumidor todavía no lo procesó; la consulta filtró por asunto y encontró una copia equivocada; el pod murió y su log, que era la única pista, desapareció con él. En incidentes así, “correo desechable” describe el dato de prueba, no el problema operativo. También aparecen nombres informales como temp mailid o temp org mail en tickets y notas. Es mejor no depender de esas etiquetas: el sistema necesita un identificador estable. Qué debe identificar un run de CI El run_id no tiene que ser una plataforma nueva. Puede ser el identificador de la ejecución de CI más un sufijo de intento, por ejemplo ci-1842-attempt-1 . Lo importante es que se genere una sola vez y que cada componente lo conserve. Como mínimo, guardaría estos datos: run_id y número de intento. Namespace y nombre del job. Instante en que se creó el usuario o se disparó el email. Identificador de la bandeja de prueba, sin imprimir credenciales. Mensajes observados durante el polling: hora, asunto normalizado y estado. Motivo final: recibido, expirado, rechazado o cancelado. No hace falta registrar el contenido completo del mensaje en cada log. Basta con un hash o un artefacto protegido cuando el equipo necesite revisar el cuerpo. Asi se reduce el riesgo de filtrar tokens en los logs y se mantiene una pista útil. Un contrato pequeño para el job de Kubernetes El contrato puede viajar como variables de entorno

items.title: How Research Collaborations Can Create Hidden IP Ownership Risks
items.snippet: Research collaborations are becoming an important part of innovation across industries. Businesses work with universities, independent researchers, technology companies and specialist laboratories to develop new products, test ideas and solve technical problem
items.content: Research collaborations are becoming an important part of innovation across industries. Businesses work with universities, independent researchers, technology companies and specialist laboratories to develop new products, test ideas and solve technical problems. These arrangements can accelerate research and reduce development costs. They can also create valuable intellectual property (IP). However, the ownership of IP created during collaborative research is not always straightforward. A project may involve several contributors, shared resources, external funding and confidential information. Each participant may have a different understanding of who owns the results and who can use them commercially. If these issues are not addressed early, disputes can emerge long after the research has been completed. Understanding the less visible ownership risks is essential for organisations seeking to protect their investment and make effective use of research outcomes. Why IP Ownership Can Become Complicated in Collaborative Research Research projects rarely follow a simple path from an idea to a finished product. A business may provide funding and technical equipment, while a university contributes research facilities and academic expertise. Individual scientists may develop methods, software or technical improvements during the project. Each contribution can raise a different ownership question. Funding a project does not automatically give a sponsor ownership of every invention or research output. Similarly, access to laboratory facilities does not necessarily establish ownership of the results. The legal position depends on the nature of the work, the applicable agreements, employment arrangements and relevant intellectual property laws. Problems arise when participants rely on informal expectations instead of clearly defining their rights. The Difference Between Existing IP and Newly Created IP One of the most common sources of uncertainty is the failure to distinguish between intellectual property brought into a project and IP developed during the collaboration. Existing IP may include patents, software, technical designs, research methods, databases, confidential processes and proprietary materials. This is often described as background IP. Newly developed IP may include inventions, improvements, research findings, prototypes and other outputs produced through the joint work. items.title: Is AI costing jobs outside tech? I read 4,335 S&P 500 earnings calls
items.snippet: I read 4,335 earnings calls from the S&P 500 companies outside the technology sector, held from January 2024 to 23 October 2026, looking for one thing: an executive saying AI was changing the company's headcount. It happened on 41 calls, by 26 companies. That
items.content: I read 4,335 earnings calls from the S&P 500 companies outside the technology sector, held from January 2024 to 23 October 2026, looking for one thing: an executive saying AI was changing the company's headcount. It happened on 41 calls, by 26 companies. That is about one call in a hundred. How I counted I searched every sentence that mentions AI for a link to jobs, headcount or hiring, then read each candidate by hand. A call counts when an executive said AI is reducing the company's headcount, or will, or that it lets the company keep headcount flat or grow it more slowly than the business. A broader count adds calls where AI is named next to job cuts, a hiring slowdown or a flatter structure without being given as the cause. I also counted denials, where an executive said the company is not using AI to cut jobs, and analyst questions about AI and headcount. A keyword filter would not get close. Executives mentioned AI on 61.2% of these calls in July to September 2026, and on most of them AI is a product or productivity story with no word about staff. Rare, but rising Year Non-tech calls AI tied to headcount Share Broader count Share 2024 1,576 8 0.51% 12 0.76% 2025 1,526 16 1.05% 31 2.03% 2026, to 23 October 1,233 17 1.38% 45 3.65% All 4,335 41 0.95% 88 2.03% The jump came in the second half of 2025, when the share tripled. Mostly hiring less, not layoffs Of the 41 calls, 22 were about growing without adding people and 5 about not replacing people who leave. Only 14 described cut roles or lower headcount. Banks describe the attrition version most plainly. A large bank loses thousands of people a year, so hiring fewer of them shrinks the workforce without a layoff. Bank of America's chief executive called it "let attrition be your friend" in April 2026. The cuts that do get named are often small and specific. United Airlines' chief financial officer said in October 2025 that "our management headcount is 4% lower than last year", with another 4% planned for 2026. Banks and a freight broker Financial services companies made 20 of the 41 claims, on 2.58% of their calls. Industrials made 15, and eight of those came from one company, C.H. Robinson, which tied AI to headcount on 8 of its 11 calls and reported average headcount down 12.3% from a year earlier in Q1 2026. items.snippet: Regulatory Architecture of China’s MOFCOM Announcement No. 48: A Technical Analysis The release of Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) Announcement No. 48 marks a critical inflection point in the global governance of artificial intelligence. By formalizing export co
items.content: Regulatory Architecture of China’s MOFCOM Announcement No. 48: A Technical Analysis The release of Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) Announcement No. 48 marks a critical inflection point in the global governance of artificial intelligence. By formalizing export controls on specific generative AI technologies, the Chinese government has transitioned from soft-law guidance to hard-law constraints on the cross-border transfer of model weights, inference architectures, and training methodologies. This article provides a technical dissection of the scope, enforcement mechanisms, and systemic implications of these controls, specifically focusing on how they intersect with existing international trade frameworks and the technical reality of model distribution. The Scope of Controlled Technologies Announcement No. 48 identifies several categories of AI technologies subject to export licensing requirements. These controls target the core intellectual property of the machine learning pipeline: generative algorithms, synthetic data generation, and the computational frameworks necessary for deployment. From a technical perspective, the controls focus on technologies that exhibit "generative" capabilities. The technical definitions provided by MOFCOM align with the parameters of Transformer-based architectures and their derivatives. Specifically, the regulation targets: Large-scale model training: Architectures capable of multi-modal data processing and autonomous content generation. Synthetic data generation: Technologies that automate the creation of high-fidelity data used to augment existing training sets. Model customization/fine-tuning: Tooling that modifies pre-trained base models for domain-specific applications, effectively acting as an export-controlled "instruction set." The control list functions by asserting state sovereignty over the intangible assets of the AI supply chain. Unlike traditional dual-use hardware controls—such as those governing semiconductor lithography or high-end GPUs—Announcement No. 48 governs the instructional output of the research and development process. items.snippet: Originally published at htpbe.tech . The version on htpbe.tech stays in sync with the latest detection algorithm — refer to it for the canonical text. You have a PDF in front of you – a bank statement from a tenant, a payslip from a candidate, an invoice from
items.content: Originally published at htpbe.tech . The version on htpbe.tech stays in sync with the latest detection algorithm — refer to it for the canonical text. You have a PDF in front of you – a bank statement from a tenant, a payslip from a candidate, an invoice from a supplier you have not paid before – and something about it bothers you. So you search for a fake document detector, and you get a page of tools that all claim to answer the same question. They don’t. Each tool in that list looks at a different part of the file, and each one misses things another would catch. Picking one without knowing which part it reads is how a document gets ‘checked’ and still gets through. Short answer: what a fake PDF detector actually does A ‘fake PDF detector’ is not one kind of tool. Some read the metadata fields, some look at the rendered page, some compare the text against expected values, and some examine the internal structure of the file for signs it was changed after it was created. None of them answers ‘is this document genuine?’ on its own – each answers a narrower question, and the useful choice is the one whose question matches what you need to know about the file. The six kinds of fake PDF detector Kind of tool What it inspects Good at Where it stops Metadata viewers Document properties: producer, creator, creation and modified dates A fast, free look at what the file says about itself Shows fields without judging them; fields can be rewritten Online ‘was this PDF edited’ checkers Varies by tool – often metadata, sometimes more A fast first answer, nothing to install Depth varies; ask what the result is based on Visual and image-forensics tools The rendered page and embedded images Spotting visual anomalies in how the page looks A cleanly edited PDF can look perfect OCR and content-consistency checkers The text and figures on the page Wrong totals, mismatched names, values that don’t add up Reads what the page says, not how the file was produced Manual review Everything a trained person can see and cross-check Context, judgement, calling the issuer Slow, inconsistent at volume, does not see how the file was built Structural forensics The PDF’s internal construction and revision record Whether the file itself was changed after it was created Says nothing about whether the content is true or who issued it The rest of this article takes each row in turn. items.title: Redis 8.12 RC2's SEXPIRE command cuts a set membership check from two round trips to one
items.snippet: A Redis set has always had one expiry for the whole key. If you wanted one member of a set to disappear on its own, say a session token in a set of active sessions, or a temporary grant in a set of permissions, you built a side index yourself: a sorted set wit
items.content: A Redis set has always had one expiry for the whole key. If you wanted one member of a set to disappear on its own, say a session token in a set of active sessions, or a temporary grant in a set of permissions, you built a side index yourself: a sorted set with the expiry as the score, checked on every read, swept by a cron job. Redis 8.12, currently at release candidate 2, adds that directly to the set type. I built it from source, since there's no Docker image for an RC yet, and measured what changes when the server does this instead of your application code. The new commands are SEXPIRE , SPEXPIRE , SEXPIREAT , SPEXPIREAT to set an expiry on specific members, SPERSIST to clear it, and STTL , SPTTL , SEXPIRETIME , SPEXPIRETIME to read it back. There's no official command reference page for any of them yet; I pieced the syntax together from COMMAND DOCS and the release notes. The headline number The actual value of this feature isn't in setting the expiry. It's in checking membership afterwards. Under the old pattern, "is this member still valid" means SISMEMBER plus a ZSCORE lookup against your own expiry index, compared against the current time client-side. Under the new one, SISMEMBER alone already reflects the TTL, because the server has removed the member once it expired. I populated two 2,000-member sets, gave every member the same TTL, then ran 2,000 validity checks against each pattern, three times: run old pattern (SISMEMBER + ZSCORE) new pattern (SISMEMBER alone) difference 1 997.7 ms 475.8 ms 52.3% faster 2 889.0 ms 444.6 ms 50.0% faster 3 994.3 ms 423.6 ms 57.4% faster That's one round trip removed from every single read, and it held steady across all three runs: roughly half the time, every time. On loopback, where a round trip is already cheap, that's still a 50% cut. Over a real network to a managed Redis instance, removing a round trip matters more, not less, though I only measured loopback here and I'm not going to claim a number I didn't run. The number that argues against it Setting the expiry doesn't get any faster. I benchmarked writing the TTL itself, 2,000 members, three runs, old pattern being a plain ZADD into a side index versus the new SEXPIRE call: run old pattern (ZADD to a side index) new pattern (SEXPIRE) difference 1 497.2 ms 506.7 ms 1.9% slower 2 430.0 ms 438.9 ms 2.1% slower 3 483.7 ms 599.7 ms 24.0% slower SEXPIRE was never faster to call than a plain ZADD , and in one run it was a quarter slower. That's not surprising

items.title: Why AI-Built Work Comes Back for Rework, and How to Cut It
items.snippet: The short version Rework is normal with AI coding agents, and most of it comes from a few repeatable causes rather than bad luck. The biggest cause is missing information: the agent cannot see decisions, rules and wishes that live only in your head. Give the a
items.content: The short version Rework is normal with AI coding agents, and most of it comes from a few repeatable causes rather than bad luck. The biggest cause is missing information: the agent cannot see decisions, rules and wishes that live only in your head. Give the agent a check it can run, such as a test or a screenshot to match, so it can catch its own mistakes before you see them. Changing your mind after building has started is the most expensive kind of rework, so settle open questions first. Keep rules that must always apply in writing in the project's instruction file, because long chats lose early instructions. If your AI coding agent keeps coming back with fixes, or redoes things it already called finished, that is common and usually explainable. Rework with AI agents mostly comes from missing information, no way for the agent to check its own work, and requests that change halfway through. You can reduce all three without writing any code. This guide explains where rework comes from, which kinds are cheap and which are costly, and what you can do about each. What does "rework" mean with an AI coding agent? Rework is any work done a second time. The agent builds a feature, someone finds a problem, and the agent goes back to fix it. Or a test fails after the work was called finished. Or you look at the result and say, "That is not what I meant." Human teams have rework too. The difference is that an AI agent redoes work quickly, so it can feel free. It is not. Every second pass takes time, and it also uses part of your plan's usage allowance or, on a pay-as-you-go setup, your money. Some rework is healthy. A reviewer catching a real flaw before release is the system working. The goal is not zero rework. The goal is to stop paying twice for problems you could have prevented. Why does the agent get it wrong in the first place? Claude Code's best-practices documentation says that when a session does not go the way you expected, it is almost always because Claude built something different from what you had in mind, or because it is missing information it cannot get from reading the project. Think of a very capable new contractor on day one. They can read everything in the building, but they cannot read your mind. Cause 1: facts that live only in your head The agent can read your project files. It cannot see a deal you made with a customer last week, a rule your legal team insists on, or the fact that "active user" means something specific at your company. The

items.snippet: Notifio is a desktop app that watches rental search pages and tells you when a new listing appears. The main process is about 7,000 lines of TypeScript, no bundler and no tree shaking, so an export that nothing imports does not get dropped anywhere. It just si
items.content: Notifio is a desktop app that watches rental search pages and tells you when a new listing appears. The main process is about 7,000 lines of TypeScript, no bundler and no tree shaking, so an export that nothing imports does not get dropped anywhere. It just sits there looking like part of the design. I counted them. The script is crude on purpose: find every export function , export const and export class , then count how many times that name appears in any other file plus any extra time it appears in its own. total exported symbols: 189 never referenced anywhere else: 14 Fourteen names, fifteen definitions, because one of the names is defined twice. Here is what they turned out to be, and which ones are telling me something. The one that is a product gap export const deactivateLicense = () => request { ok : boolean } > ( " /api/license/deactivate " , { method : " POST " }); That is in the renderer's API client, which is the layer whose entire job is to be called by a component. Nothing calls it. The route at the other end is not a stub either. It is the most careful handler in the local server: app . post ( ' /api/license/deactivate ' , ( req : Request , res : Response ) => { const cfg = loadConfig (); delete cfg . license ; saveConfig ( cfg ); monitor . stop (); // Drop the cached upgrade state too, so a different licence activated on // this machine can't inherit the previous one's entitlement. entitlement . clearCache (); res . json ({ ok : true }); }); Four steps in a deliberate order, with a comment explaining the one that is easy to forget. Somebody thought about what deactivation means on a machine where a cached entitlement is trusted for six hours . Then the UI for it was never built, so today the app can be activated and never signed out. It is not blocking anybody from using what they bought. The terms grant a licence to install on devices you own, so there is no device cap to free up, and nothing breaks by leaving a licence in place. What is missing is the answer to "I am selling this laptop": the only way to get your email address and token off the machine is the instruction in section 6 of the privacy notice , which is to delete the whole application data folder, taking your saved searches with it. One more detail in the same corner. items.title: From Script to Success: Writing Effective Dialogues for AI Calling Agents
items.snippet: Introduction In today’s hyper‑connected world, AI calling agents are reshaping how businesses engage with customers over the phone. Whether it’s confirming appointments, collecting feedback, or handling simple support queries, a well‑crafted dialogue can turn
items.content: Introduction In today’s hyper‑connected world, AI calling agents are reshaping how businesses engage with customers over the phone. Whether it’s confirming appointments, collecting feedback, or handling simple support queries, a well‑crafted dialogue can turn a routine call into a memorable brand experience. This guide walks you through the process of turning a raw script into a successful conversation that feels natural, efficient, and genuinely helpful. Understanding the Role of AI Calling Agents AI calling agents are more than automated voice responders; they act as the front‑line ambassadors of your brand. Unlike text‑based chatbots, voice interactions demand a higher level of empathy and timing. The AI must interpret tone, manage pauses, and adapt to interruptions—all while staying on message. Recognizing this responsibility is the first step toward writing dialogues that build trust and drive conversion . Key Principles of Effective Dialogue Writing 1. Keep It Conversational People speak in short, varied sentences. Avoid long, scripted monologues. Break information into bite‑size prompts and let the AI ask open‑ended questions that invite a response. 2. Prioritize Clarity Use plain language and avoid industry jargon. When you must mention technical terms, introduce them with a brief explanation. Clear dialogue reduces misunderstandings and shortens call duration. 3. Embed Intentional Pauses Silence is a powerful tool. Insert short pauses after questions to give callers time to think. In written scripts, denote pauses with “(pause)” or “...” so the voice engine knows when to breathe. 4. Personalize Whenever Possible Leverage available data—such as the caller’s name, recent purchases, or appointment details—to tailor the conversation. Personal touches make the AI feel less robotic and more human‑like. 5. Guide the Call Toward a Goal Every dialogue should have a clear objective, whether it’s confirming a booking, collecting a survey response, or routing to a live agent. Use transition phrases like “Let’s confirm your appointment” to keep the call focused. Step‑by‑Step: Crafting a Winning Script Define the Call Objective Write a one‑sentence statement of the desired outcome. Example: “Confirm the customer’s upcoming service appointment and collect a preferred time slot.” Map the Call Flow Sketch a simple flowchart: greeting → verification → main request → confirmation → closing. items.title: Queue vs Topic vs Log: Picking the Broker
items.snippet: Most broker decisions are made in a ten-minute conversation that ends with "we'll just use Kafka," or from the other side, "SQS is fine, it's cheap." Both sentences treat the broker as a throughput-and-price decision. It isn't. What you are actually choosing i
items.content: Most broker decisions are made in a ten-minute conversation that ends with "we'll just use Kafka," or from the other side, "SQS is fine, it's cheap." Both sentences treat the broker as a throughput-and-price decision. It isn't. What you are actually choosing is a contract : who owns a message after it is delivered, who tracks how far each consumer has read, and whether yesterday's events still exist tomorrow. Get the contract wrong and no tuning fixes it. A team that picks a queue and later needs a new service to bootstrap from the last 30 days of order events has nothing to replay. A team that picks Kafka for background jobs ends up owning partition planning, rebalances, and head-of-line blocking to get what a queue provides out of the box. Three primitives, three contracts QUEUE (competing consumers) TOPIC (fan-out) LOG (retained stream) producer ──▶ [ m3 m2 m1 ] ──┬▶ A producer ──▶ topic ──┬▶ [sub-A] ▶ A producer ──▶ [m1 m2 m3 m4 m5 …] └▶ B ├▶ [sub-B] ▶ B ▲ ▲ each message goes to ONE each subscription gets consumer X consumer Y consumer, then is deleted its OWN copy (offset 2) (offset 5) Queue Topic (pub/sub) Log Delivery model Competing consumers: one handler per message Fan-out: every subscription gets a copy Every consumer group reads the whole stream independently After consumption Deleted on ack Deleted per subscription on ack Retained until retention expires, regardless of reads Read position owned by Broker (visibility timeout / lock) Broker, per subscription Consumer (offset) Replay No No Yes, by rewinding offsets Failure handling Per-message retry and DLQ Per-subscription retry and DLQ None built in: a failing message blocks its partition The last row is where teams get surprised. In a queue, message 7 failing does not stop message 8. In a log, the consumer's offset means "everything before this is done" — a message that keeps failing stalls its partition unless you build retry topics yourself. On Azure, a topic subscription is a queue with its own lock, delivery count, and dead-letter sub-queue. items.content: Somewhere in Cameroon right now, a student is revising from a photocopy so faded that the numbers are hard to read, and an elder is telling a story that no book has recorded. Cameroon Open Data is a community project that collects this kind of knowledge, such as exam questions, proverbs, translations between our languages, laws and facts about our places, and stores it in an open and organised way so that students, researchers and the AI tools of the future can learn from it. You do not need to be a developer to help. You do not need to install anything, edit a file or learn Git. To contribute, you fill in a form on the GitHub website, the same way you would fill in any online form, and press Submit. A robot turns your answers into a properly formatted record and sends it to a reviewer. This guide shows you every click. You can find the project here: Cameroon Open Data on GitHub . Contents 1. Create a GitHub account 2. Star the repository 3. Open the Issues tab 4. Choose the right form 5. Fill in the form 6. Submit and see what happens A worked example Rules to follow If something goes wrong 1. Create a GitHub account GitHub is the website where the project lives, and creating an account is free. Open the GitHub sign up page , enter your email address, choose a password and a username, and follow the instructions. GitHub sends a code to your email to confirm that it is really you. Your username is the name that can appear next to your contribution, so choose one you are happy to see in public. If you already have an account, sign in and go to the next step. 2. Star the repository A repository, often shortened to "repo", is simply the project folder on GitHub. Starring it is like bookmarking and applauding at the same time. It costs nothing, it tells other people the project is worth a look, and it helps us find more contributors. Open the project page and click the Star button near the top right. The star turns yellow once it is saved. 3. Open the Issues tab On the project page, look at the row of tabs under the project name: Code, Issues, Pull requests, Actions and so on. Click Issues . Then click the green New issue button on the right. 4. Choose the right form GitHub now shows a list of forms, and each one has a short description. Pick the one that matches what you want to share.
