items.title: Cross-Border Payments & Compliance for Solo Developers
items.snippet: Cross-Border Payments & Compliance for Solo Developers Selling software internationally as a one-person company is easier than ever—until money has to cross a border. Then you meet three-headed problems: getting paid, keeping the tax authorities happy, and not
items.content: Cross-Border Payments & Compliance for Solo Developers Selling software internationally as a one-person company is easier than ever—until money has to cross a border. Then you meet three-headed problems: getting paid, keeping the tax authorities happy, and not getting your account frozen. This guide covers the pragmatic path: what to set up, what to avoid, and where the real risks hide. Pick a Payment Rail That Matches Your Customers Most solo developers default to Stripe, and for good reason: it handles card processing, subscriptions, and 135+ currencies in one dashboard. But Stripe is not always the cheapest or most available option. Stripe / Paddle / Lemon Squeezy : Best for SaaS and digital products. Paddle and Lemon Squeezy act as merchant of record (MoR), meaning they handle sales tax and VAT collection on your behalf. For a solo developer, an MoR is often worth the ~5% fee because it removes a huge compliance burden. PayPal : Ubiquitous but expensive (4–5% + FX spread) and prone to holds on new accounts. Keep it as a fallback, not a primary rail. Wise Business / Payoneer : Great for receiving B2B invoices and paying contractors. Wise gives you local account details (IBAN, ACH, sort code) in multiple countries, which reduces friction for clients. Crypto / stablecoins : Only if your customers demand it. Treat it as a niche add-on, not a foundation. Actionable tip: If you sell to consumers in the EU or UK, use an MoR. If you sell B2B to a handful of companies, invoice them directly via Wise or Stripe Invoicing and let them handle their own VAT reverse-charge. Understand Where You Owe Tax Cross-border tax is where solo developers get blindsided. Two concepts matter most: 1. VAT/GST on digital services. The EU, UK, Australia, and many others require you to charge VAT based on the customer's location , not yours. This is called the destination principle. The EU's OSS (One-Stop Shop) lets you file a single return for all EU sales once you exceed the €10,000 threshold. Below that, you can charge your local rate. 2. Income tax and permanent establishment. If you're a sole trader in Country A selling to customers in Country B, you generally owe income tax only in Country A—unless you create a permanent establishment (office, employee, dependent agent) in Country B. Remote software sales rarely trigger this, but don't set up a local entity or hire locally without advice. Actionable tip: Use an MoR until you're doing meaningful volume (say, $100k+/year). Then t

items.title: From a 2017 Experiment to 800+ Commits: What Building Retro Paddle Taught Me
items.snippet: It started with a simple question: could I still build a decent Pong-style game from scratch? Back in 2017 I opened a canvas and added two paddles, a ball and a score counter. It was a small experiment to see what I could make, and I put the result on YouTube:
items.content: It started with a simple question: could I still build a decent Pong-style game from scratch? Back in 2017 I opened a canvas and added two paddles, a ball and a score counter. It was a small experiment to see what I could make, and I put the result on YouTube: the first version from 2017 . In January 2024 I picked it up again. Almost two years, more than 800 commits and quite a few late evenings later, that experiment has grown into something much bigger. It now has more than 20 power-ups and power-downs, weapons, portals, sea mines, a computer opponent, online multiplayer and even its own dependency-free npm package. I call it Retro Paddle, and you can play it right here: Play Retro Paddle It's free, needs no account or installation, and works on desktop and mobile. Below is how it grew, and a few things I learned along the way. 1. Plain JavaScript, paper and a set square The very first version, in 2017, was plain JavaScript on an HTML canvas, without a framework, game engine or physics library. There were no AI coding tools to lean on back then either. What I remember best from those early days is figuring out how the ball should bounce off the walls. I grabbed a piece of paper and a set square (a triangular ruler), drew the ball's incoming direction, marked the wall and worked out what the outgoing direction should look like. The angle of incidence had to equal the angle of reflection. It might sound a little old-fashioned, but I really enjoyed working it out that way. I wanted to understand the maths and write the behaviour myself instead of pulling in a physics library, and that code is still the foundation of the game. 2. Turning Pong on its side The next big decision was also one of the simplest: I didn't want another horizontal Pong game. A horizontal field is fine on a desktop, but on a smartphone you either rotate your phone or squeeze the game into a narrow strip of screen. So I turned the whole thing 90 degrees. In Retro Paddle the ball travels from top to bottom. You hold your phone upright, your paddle sits at the bottom, and the full height of the screen is your playing field. On a touchscreen you drag your finger anywhere and the paddle follows, so your thumb never covers the paddle you're trying to watch. It sounds like a small change, but it shaped almost everything that came after: the layout, the controls, the gameplay and even how the power-ups work. 3. items.title: We write four version numbers to disk and read none of them, and every migration we shipped is a shape check
items.snippet: Notifio is a desktop app that watches rental search pages from your own machine and emails you when a new listing appears. It has no database and no account system, so everything it knows lives in files under app.getPath('userData') . I have written about the
items.content: Notifio is a desktop app that watches rental search pages from your own machine and emails you when a new listing appears. It has no database and no account system, so everything it knows lives in files under app.getPath('userData') . I have written about the five files and their four durability strategies before. This week I went looking for something narrower: how the app handles data written by an older build of itself. Every shipped desktop app has this problem, every version bump makes it worse, and the standard answer is a version number in the file. We have four of those. Here is every one, and every read of one. The four version numbers The settings file writes one: const DATA_VERSION = 4 ; function defaults (): UserData { return { version : DATA_VERSION , autoReply : { enabled : false } }; } function save ( data : UserData ): void { writeEnvelope ( PROFILE_PATH , { ... data , version : DATA_VERSION }); _cache = migrate ( data ); } The recordings file writes one: const FILE_VERSION = 2 ; const parsed = readEnvelope RecipeFile > ( RECIPES_PATH , { version : FILE_VERSION , recipes : [] }); And the envelope those two files share writes one of its own, on every write: const envelope : Envelope = canEncrypt () ? { v : 1 , enc : ' safeStorage ' , data : safeStorage . encryptString ( json ). toString ( ' base64 ' ) } : { v : 1 , enc : ' none ' , data : json }; Four numbers on disk: version: 4 , version: 2 , and v: 1 in two files. Now grep the repository for a line that compares any of them to anything. There isn't one. readEnvelope branches on enc and never looks at v . The recordings reader takes parsed.recipes and ignores parsed.version . And the settings migration, which is the one place in the app explicitly named after the job a version field exists for, does not read the version either: function migrate ( raw : unknown ): UserData { const data = ( raw ?? {}) as { autoReply ?: Partial AutoReplySettings > }; return { version : DATA_VERSION , autoReply : { enabled : data . autoReply ?. enabled === true }, }; } It takes one field it recognises, defaults it to false unless it is exactly true , stamps the current version on the result and throws everything else away. That function is correct, it has survived three product changes, and the number next to it has never once been consulted. items.title: I kept correcting AI until I realised what was actually broken
items.snippet: You corrected the AI yesterday. Today, it made the exact same mistake again. Maybe it used an outdated price, invented a product feature you do not offer, or missed an important step in a client proposal. You correct it in the chat, get the answer you wanted,
items.content: You corrected the AI yesterday. Today, it made the exact same mistake again. Maybe it used an outdated price, invented a product feature you do not offer, or missed an important step in a client proposal. You correct it in the chat, get the answer you wanted, and move on. But what happens when someone else on your team asks the same question tomorrow? The AI makes the same mistake all over again. Nobody knows it was already corrected, and someone has to spend time fixing it from scratch. This is one of the most overlooked problems with using AI in everyday business workflows. Teams spend hours correcting AI outputs, but they rarely have a system to make sure those corrections actually improve future results. If you want to get more real, dependable work out of AI, you have to stop treating prompts like one-off chat conversations. You need to treat them like code and build a Feedback and Learning Loop . Why "More AI Output" Usually Means More Work When teams talk about wanting more AI output, they usually focus on speed. They look at how fast a model types, how many pages it can generate in a minute, or how many questions it answers in an hour. In practice, raw speed does not help if the answers are unreliable. An AI can draft a ten-page technical spec in five seconds, but that does not save time if an engineer has to spend thirty minutes reading every single line to catch errors. +------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | THE AI PRODUCTIVITY TRAP | | | | High Volume + Unreliable Output = Hours Spent Proofreading Mistakes | | Controlled Volume + Reliable Output = Real Time Saved Every Week | +------------------------------------------------------------------------+ When AI outputs become more consistent and predictable, reviewing them becomes much easier. Your team spends less time fixing recurring blunders and more time focusing on the details that genuinely need human attention. Why In-Chat Corrections Get Lost It is easy to assume that if you correct an AI once, it will remember the lesson. But in reality, language models do not automatically learn from in-chat corrections. If you tell an AI that your product price changed from \$99 to \$149, that does not mean the model will remember that change in another session. Whether that information carries forward depends entirely on how your application is built. Some advanced setups use conversation logs, persistent memory, or external knowledge retrieval (like RAG). items.title: A serving stepper that is not allowed to change the answer, and the 608 checks that say it does not
items.snippet: Munchable reads packaged food labels and tells you whether the product fits the gut conditions you manage. It also ships a recipe library, 38 of them, published at munchable.app/recipes and filtered for you inside the app. The recipes are not a separate featur
items.content: Munchable reads packaged food labels and tells you whether the product fits the gut conditions you manage. It also ships a recipe library, 38 of them, published at munchable.app/recipes and filtered for you inside the app. The recipes are not a separate feature with a separate code path. A recipe is converted into the same shape as a product and run through the same engine, which is what lets a page say who it suits: munchable.app/recipes/gentle-rice-congee says it is cleared for all eight conditions, munchable.app/recipes/baked-salmon-with-dill-potatoes names five of them. An earlier post covered that decision. This post is about the consequence nobody asks for when they add a serving stepper to a recipe screen. The hazard In most recipe apps, the serving control is cosmetic: it multiplies the numbers you read and nothing else depends on it. Here, the quantities feed a verdict. So "cooking for six" is a user action that could, in principle, change whether the app says a dish suits you. There is no acceptable version of that. A dish is the same dish at any batch size, and a control that changed the answer would mean the answer was never about the dish. Where the numbers come from Every figure on a recipe page is derived from one array: the ingredient lines, each with a weight in grams. The live congee page prints: 50 minutes, serves 2. About 178 g a serving, with 8 g of fat and 1 g of fibre in it. None of those three numbers is stored. The serving size is the batch weight divided by the servings. The fat and the fibre are summed from a per-ingredient table and divided the same way. Cooking water is not an ingredient line at all, it belongs to the steps, so it cannot dilute anything. That is the "no second copy" rule applied to arithmetic, and it is the same reason the per-condition line on the page is computed rather than authored. A hand-typed per-serving figure is a number nobody can check, and one that an author silently invalidates the moment they change a quantity. The invariant Scaling is deliberately boring: const factor = serves / recipe . serves ; return { ... recipe , serves , ingredients : recipe . ingredients . map (( i ) => ({ ... i , qty : i . qty * factor , grams : i . grams * factor , })), }; Every weight is multiplied by the same factor, so each ingredient's share of the batch is unchanged, the per-100 g figures are unchanged, and the per-serving weight is unchanged because both the numerator and the denominator moved. items.title: Vercel CI vs GitHub Actions for Next.js: which to use
items.snippet: Vercel CI is worth trying if your Next.js repo is private, already on Vercel, and your checks are slow because they rerun everything on every push. It reads your Turborepo task graph, runs only what a change affects, and bills per CPU minute. GitHub Actions is
items.content: Vercel CI is worth trying if your Next.js repo is private, already on Vercel, and your checks are slow because they rerun everything on every push. It reads your Turborepo task graph, runs only what a change affects, and bills per CPU minute. GitHub Actions is still the general-purpose tool: any trigger, any OS, deploys, schedules, and free on public repos. For most teams the answer for now is both, with GitHub Actions keeping the jobs Vercel CI can't do. Everything below was checked against Vercel's and GitHub's own docs and pricing pages on 2 November 2026. Vercel CI is a beta from 28 October, so treat the numbers as a snapshot, not a contract. What Vercel launched on 28 October 2026 Vercel announced Vercel CI in beta on 28 October 2026 (also in the changelog ). The pitch is aimed squarely at people whose coding agents open more pull requests than humans can wait for: most CI reruns the whole workflow for a one-line change, and that gets expensive when agents push all day. How it works, according to the Vercel CI docs : You tag Turborepo tasks with "tags": ["ci"] in turbo.json . On every git push , Turborepo works out which tagged tasks the change affects. Tasks whose inputs haven't changed come back from Vercel Remote Cache, on by default. The rest run in dependency order, each on its own isolated machine. Vercel posts a check to the pull request, so branch protection can block merges as it does today. { "tasks" : { "lint" : { "tags" : [ "ci" ] }, "typecheck" : { "tags" : [ "ci" ] }, "build" : { "tags" : [ "ci" ], "outputs" : [ ".next/**" , "!.next/cache/**" ] } } } That's the whole config. No workflow YAML. Vercel's claim is that push-to-green in its own repos got 2 to 6 times faster, and that the system has run nearly 8 million tasks across its repos and the private beta. Those are Vercel's numbers about Vercel's repos; I haven't reproduced them. items.title: The Architecture of Generation: Understanding Diffusion Transformers (DiTs)
items.snippet: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs): Merging generative diffusion processes with Transformer scaling to power next-generation visual AI. How replacing convolutional U-Nets with Transformer backbones revolutionized visual synthesis, video generation, and spatial AI.
items.content: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs): Merging generative diffusion processes with Transformer scaling to power next-generation visual AI. How replacing convolutional U-Nets with Transformer backbones revolutionized visual synthesis, video generation, and spatial AI. For years, generative image and video models relied almost entirely on the U-Net architecture. In early diffusion models, U-Nets handled the complex task of denoising image latent vectors step-by-step through downsampling and upsampling convolutional layers. While U-Nets were effective for moderate resolutions, they suffered from a major scaling limitation: convolutional layers struggle to capture global context across high-resolution spatial dimensions and long video sequences. To unlock true compute scaling for visual media, researchers engineered Diffusion Transformers (DiTs)—replacing convolutional U-Nets with Transformer backbones. What is a Diffusion Transformer? A Diffusion Transformer (DiT) combines two powerful ideas in modern AI: Diffusion Models: Generative algorithms that start with random Gaussian noise and iteratively remove noise over multiple timesteps to generate crisp images or video. Transformer Architecture: The sequence-processing backbone behind LLMs, which uses self-attention mechanisms to model relationships across all data tokens in parallel. Instead of processing image features through spatial convolutional blocks, a DiT breaks latent visual grids into small patch tokens (similar to Vision Transformers). It then applies standard Transformer attention layers across these visual tokens, allowing every region of an image or video frame to attend to every other region simultaneously. Why DiTs Outperform Traditional U-Nets Transitioning visual diffusion from U-Nets to Transformers unlocks critical capabilities: Predictable Scaling Laws Just as Large Language Models perform better as parameter counts increase, Diffusion Transformers exhibit strict empirical scaling laws. Increasing Gflops (through larger models or more visual tokens) consistently improves image fidelity and textual alignment. Superior Global Context Modeling Convolutional filters process localized pixel neighborhoods, making it difficult for models to understand large-scale structural relationships (such as consistent lighting or complex multi-object geometry). items.title: Building a Sub-Millisecond AI Gateway in Go for Autonomous Coding Agents
items.snippet: When building workflows with autonomous coding agents (like Claude Code, Cursor, or OpenCode), agent execution loops issue dozens of rapid LLM calls per minute. Standard Python-based proxies introduce 40ms–100ms of latency per hop, balloon to hundreds of megab
items.content: When building workflows with autonomous coding agents (like Claude Code, Cursor, or OpenCode), agent execution loops issue dozens of rapid LLM calls per minute. Standard Python-based proxies introduce 40ms–100ms of latency per hop, balloon to hundreds of megabytes in memory, and easily choke during parallel agent streaming. To solve this, I built GoRoute ( https://github.com/ziuus/goroute ) — an ultra-lightweight, high-throughput AI gateway and dynamic LLM router written in Go. The Latency & Reliability Problem In autonomous coding agent sessions: Compounding Proxy Latency : In a 30-step agent loop, 60ms of routing overhead adds 1.8 seconds of pure wait time. Provider Rate Limits : Hitting a 429 on Anthropic or OpenAI kills the entire agent trajectory unless failovers are instantaneous. Protocol Mismatches : Tool definitions and message schemas differ between OpenAI (function_call / tools) and Anthropic (messages API). Architecture & Key Features Sub-0.8ms Local Routing : Zero-allocation hot path, standard library HTTP + lightweight routing, baseline footprint Universal Protocol Translation : Transparently translate OpenAI format to Anthropic messages format and vice-versa, allowing any coding tool to talk to any upstream model. Dynamic Failover Cascades : If Claude 3.5 Sonnet hits rate-limits or 5xx errors, GoRoute cascades automatically to DeepSeek-V3 or GPT-4o with zero lost tokens. Multi-Account Token Pooling : Distribute requests round-robin across multiple API keys to maximize quota without manual key rotation. Native MCP Compatibility : Designed to sit cleanly alongside Model Context Protocol servers. Quick Start Run locally via Go: go install github.com/ziuus/goroute@latest goroute --port 8080 --config config.yaml Or via Docker: docker run -p 8080:8080 -v $( pwd ) /config.yaml:/app/config.yaml ghcr.io/ziuus/goroute:latest Point your agent or SDK to http://localhost:8080/v1 and you are ready. Open Source GoRoute is 100% open source under the MIT License. GitHub Repository : https://github.com/ziuus/goroute Live Demo & Docs : https://goroute-website.vercel.app Feedback, issue reports, and benchmarks are warmly welcomed! items.title: Walk-forward testing with an embargo: keeping time in order
items.snippet: train_test_split(X, y, shuffle=True) is fine for photos of cats. For anything that happens in time, it quietly lets the model learn from the future: Tuesday's training row sits next to Monday's test row, and markets on neighbouring days are related. Walk-forwa
items.content: train_test_split(X, y, shuffle=True) is fine for photos of cats. For anything that happens in time, it quietly lets the model learn from the future: Tuesday's training row sits next to Monday's test row, and markets on neighbouring days are related. Walk-forward Keep time in order: Train on everything up to a date. Test on the period right after it. Move forward and repeat. Our schedule for the stock models: Training window: the trailing 756 trading days (about three years). Refit: every 63 trading days (about a quarter). Label: each stock's result versus SPY from the next open to the open 20 trading days later. The gap (embargo) There's a second, subtler leak. The label looks 20 days ahead. So the last training rows have labels that overlap with the first test days. The model has, in effect, seen part of the test period's outcome. The fix is an embargo : leave a gap of 20 trading days between the end of the training data and the start of the test period, so no training label reaches into the test window. def walk_forward ( dates , train = 756 , step = 63 , embargo = 20 ): start = train + embargo while start len ( dates ): tr = dates [ start - embargo - train : start - embargo ] te = dates [ start : start + step ] yield tr , te start += step What it costs Fewer training rows, more refits, and results that look worse than a shuffled split. Every one of those is a more honest picture of what would have happened in real time. If a time-series result was produced with a random split, treat it as unverified. From Quantooo Lab, the makers of quantooo.com , a free, open and educational quant lab: every formula, every test and every failure is public. See it here: https://quantooo.com/method Educational, not investment advice.

items.title: I measured the title and description of all 461 generated pages, and exactly one of them loses the brand name
items.snippet: Munchable answers whether a packaged food fits the gut conditions you manage. Most of its public surface is generated: 461 pages that each answer one ingredient question, indexed at munchable.app/answers , plus eight condition guides and 38 recipes. 516 URLs i
items.content: Munchable answers whether a packaged food fits the gut conditions you manage. Most of its public surface is generated: 461 pages that each answer one ingredient question, indexed at munchable.app/answers , plus eight condition guides and 38 recipes. 516 URLs in all, and everything except a handful of fixed pages comes out of data rather than out of a file somebody wrote. Which means the title tag and the meta description are not copy anybody proofread. They are output. So I measured all of them. The two numbers a search result can show export const TITLE_LIMIT = 60 ; export const DESCRIPTION_LIMIT = 160 ; These are the familiar approximations of where Google cuts. The comment above them says why they are enforced rather than remembered: * A title of 60 characters or more, or a description of 160 or more, gets cut * mid-word, and the part that gets cut is usually the part carrying the answer. That is the specific hazard of a question page. The title is the question, so the part of the description that matters is the beginning, and the part of the title that matters is all of it. A question truncated at "Is hydrogenated vegetable oi..." has spent the impression and told the reader nothing. What 461 pages actually measure Run over every generated page, with the brand suffix accounted for: title min 30 median 37 max 56 (limit 60) description min 93 median 117 max 148 (limit 160) pages within 3 characters of the title limit: 0 pages within 10 characters of the description limit: 0 The shortest title on the site is munchable.app/is-rye-low-fodmap , at 30 characters including the brand. The longest is 56. Nothing is close to the edge, and that is not restraint on my part: it falls out of the phrasing. "Is X low FODMAP?" is short because the condition's search term is short, and the longest titles are the ones where a four-word ingredient meets a four-letter condition. The descriptions are the more interesting half, because they are assembled rather than written. Each one leads with the answer and then says what to do with it: No. Baguette is an avoid wherever it appears on the label. Scan a barcode to check a real product. That shape is deliberate: the description leads with the verdict rather than with a promise to deliver one, so the snippet is useful before the click. items.content: Notifio is a desktop app that watches rental search pages and tells you when a new listing appears. Its marketing site is 38 URLs of Next.js App Router, derived from four TypeScript arrays rather than typed out, and I have audited most of it in public by now. Here is one I had not looked at. Four of those routes end like this: if ( ! site ) notFound (); // app/alerts/[site]/page.tsx if ( ! article ) notFound (); // app/guides/[slug]/page.tsx if ( ! target ) notFound (); // app/compare/[target]/page.tsx if ( ! article ) notFound (); // app/for/[audience]/page.tsx Four deliberate throws into a page that does not exist in the repository: $ find src -name "not-found*" -o -name "error*" -o -name "global-error*" -o -name "loading*" $ Nothing. No not-found.tsx , no error.tsx , no global-error.tsx , no loading.tsx anywhere under src . Every one of those four calls, and every mistyped URL on the domain, is handed to the framework's built-in page. So I went and read what we have been serving. What the default actually is $ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{size_download} \n " https://notifio.app/nope 404 13615 13,615 bytes. Measured in the loaded DOM: /nope /help elements 0 18 7 9 tags 3 1 visible text 404 / This page could not be found. the page Zero anchors is the one that matters. There is no nav, no footer, no link home, no link to the site hub , nothing. Browsers use the first one, so the tab says the 404 text, which is at least the honest half of the pair. items.title: We built a world map for discovering independent apps
items.snippet: Finding an audience is one of the hardest parts of shipping an app. We wanted to explore a different way for people to encounter independent products: a world map where each listing has a place. That idea became TheWorldOf . Visitors can explore apps visually,
items.content: Finding an audience is one of the hardest parts of shipping an app. We wanted to explore a different way for people to encounter independent products: a world map where each listing has a place. That idea became TheWorldOf . Visitors can explore apps visually, browse categories and open individual listings. Developers can present their apps and give people another way to discover what they have built. The question behind the project A map can make browsing feel more exploratory, but a visual interface only helps if people can find something relevant. We are interested in the balance between discovery and usability: when is a map a useful way to browse, and when would a straightforward list work better? We are at an early stage and would value candid feedback from developers: Is the purpose clear on your first visit? What information would help you decide whether to explore an app? If you build mobile apps, what would make a directory listing worth your time? Try it at https://theworldof.app/ . We are the team behind the project, and we would especially appreciate specific examples of anything confusing or missing. This post was prepared with AI assistance and reviewed for accuracy.

items.title: Building a User-Friendly Online Calculator: From Complex Rules to Simple Results
items.snippet: Online calculators are useful digital tools that help people solve everyday problems without complicated manual calculations. From salary estimators to financial planning tools, a well-designed calculator can make information easier to understand and access. H
items.content: Online calculators are useful digital tools that help people solve everyday problems without complicated manual calculations. From salary estimators to financial planning tools, a well-designed calculator can make information easier to understand and access. However, building a useful online calculator requires more than adding input fields and displaying a number. Developers need to consider calculation logic, data validation, user experience, and mobile responsiveness. In this article, let's explore some important principles behind building a practical online calculator. Start with a Real User Problem Every successful digital tool should solve a specific problem. Before writing code, developers should understand: Who will use the calculator? What information will users provide? What result do they expect? Which rules or formulas should be applied? What limitations should be explained? For example, employees working in the UAE may want to estimate their potential end-of-service gratuity before changing jobs or leaving their current employer. A dedicated calculator can make this process easier. Design Simple Input Fields A good calculator should not overwhelm users with unnecessary fields. Depending on the calculation, useful inputs may include: Monthly basic salary Employment start date Last working date Employment category Each field should have a clear label and helpful instructions. Input validation is also important. A calculator should identify missing values, invalid dates, and incorrect salary entries before processing the calculation. Implement Accurate Calculation Logic The calculation engine is the most important part of any calculator. For example, under the standard UAE private-sector gratuity system, eligible full-time employees generally receive: 21 days of basic salary for each of the first five years of service. 30 days of basic salary for each additional year. The standard entitlement is generally capped at two years' wages. However, different employment categories and alternative savings schemes may follow different rules. Developers should identify the applicable scheme before applying a formula. Focus on User Experience A technically accurate calculator can still be difficult to use if its interface is confusing. Consider these design principles: Clear instructions: Explain what information users need to enter. Readable results: Display the estimated amount prominently. Mobile responsiveness: Make sure the calculator works on smartphon

items.snippet: Stealers have been harvesting browser passwords, cookies and wallet seeds for years, and the bottleneck was never the stealing. It was the reading. A single infected machine coughs up thousands of lines of credentials, sessions and files, and a human operator
items.content: Stealers have been harvesting browser passwords, cookies and wallet seeds for years, and the bottleneck was never the stealing. It was the reading. A single infected machine coughs up thousands of lines of credentials, sessions and files, and a human operator had to decide which victims were worth a second look. This week Cisco Talos published research on VOLTA-AUTODOXER, a Windows infostealer that closes that gap the way any overworked team would: it hired an analyst. The analyst is a large language model. Ryan Fetterman's Talos writeup is the primary source here, and it is worth reading, because the interesting part of VOLTA is not that it uses AI. It is what it uses AI for. A mature stealer, plus one new stage Strip the AI away and VOLTA is a competent, ordinary stealer. It harvests passwords and cookies from Chromium browsers, Outlook profiles, Slack workspaces, payment cards, cryptocurrency seed phrases, Discord, Telegram, Steam and Roblox sessions, Microsoft OAuth tokens, SSH and cloud provider keys, Wi-Fi profiles, and screenshots. Exfiltration runs over Telegram, in three stages. What VOLTA adds is the step after collection. The malware assembles what Talos calls a structured evidence bundle about the person behind the machine: geolocation and home address, employer and employer domain, inferred birth year, card last-4 digits, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata, iPhone backup indicators, and a live valuation of the victim's Roblox account. To firm up the home address, it uses stolen session access to search the victim's own Gmail for receipts from Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart and PayPal. Then it serializes the bundle and sends it to an LLM for appraisal. The analyst prompt The requests go through OpenRouter, a unified API gateway, with a chain of models: Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6 by default, falling back to Moonshot's Kimi K2 and then Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash. The fallback logic is worth pausing on. VOLTA checks each response for refusal phrases like "I can't" or "I'm not able," and simply tries the next model. Talos describes a chain of up to three models, resilient against any one model's refusal. The system prompt, about 240 words, casts the model as a "forensic intelligence analyst" and includes the instruction that the bundle is the only permissible source of facts. items.title: How to Keep a Character Consistent Across AI Video Clips Using Reference Images
items.snippet: If you have tried to make anything longer than a single AI video clip, you have probably hit the same wall: the character in shot one is not quite the character in shot two. The jacket changes color, the face shifts slightly, the hair grows between cuts. For a
items.content: If you have tried to make anything longer than a single AI video clip, you have probably hit the same wall: the character in shot one is not quite the character in shot two. The jacket changes color, the face shifts slightly, the hair grows between cuts. For a one-off meme that is fine. For a short story, a product ad with a recurring mascot, or a series of social clips, it breaks the whole thing. This post walks through a practical workflow for keeping a character consistent across clips. It is tool-agnostic in principle, but I will show where reference-based generation fits in, because that is the single biggest lever. Why characters drift in the first place Most text-to-video models generate each clip from scratch. Your prompt says "a woman with short red hair in a green raincoat", and the model samples one plausible interpretation. Run it again and you get another plausible interpretation. Text is a lossy description of a face; there are thousands of faces that match "short red hair". Image-to-video helps, because the first frame pins down the look. But the model still has to invent the character from other angles as the camera moves, and over several clips small deviations add up. Reference-based generation changes the input: instead of only describing the character, you give the model one or more images of the character and ask it to place that character into a new scene. This is the approach we will build around. Step 1: Build a clean character sheet Everything downstream depends on the quality of your references. Spend time here. One subject, plain background. Busy backgrounds leak into the generation. A neutral backdrop makes it clear what the "character" is. Two or three angles. A front view and a three-quarter view cover most camera moves. A full-body shot helps if the outfit matters. Lock the distinctive details. Pick two or three features that make the character recognizable (a red scarf, round glasses, a scar) and make sure they are clearly visible in every reference. Consistent lighting. Mixed lighting across references can confuse the model about skin tone and color. You can generate the sheet itself with a text-to-image model, then use image-to-image passes to produce the extra angles from the first image so they stay aligned. Keep the image that looks best as your "master" reference. Step 2: Write prompts that describe the scene, not the character This is the most common mistake. items.title: The Uncanny Valley of Organizations: When Companies Powered Entirely by AI Start Behaving Strangely
items.snippet: In late 2024, a small software company in Estonia did something that made no sense to its competitors. It raised its prices by 40%, laid off its entire sales team, and started sending handwritten-style notes to its 12,000 customers, each one personalized to th
items.content: In late 2024, a small software company in Estonia did something that made no sense to its competitors. It raised its prices by 40%, laid off its entire sales team, and started sending handwritten-style notes to its 12,000 customers, each one personalized to the customer’s usage patterns, each one signed with the same name. The founder, who was still nominally in charge, later admitted he hadn’t approved any of it. The board had. The board was an AI system, and the AI system had decided that the best path to growth was to shrink, raise prices, and invest everything into retention through weird intimacy. Revenue went up 31% in six months. Churn dropped to 2.1%. And nobody inside the company could fully explain why it was working. That story is a composite of several real cases I’ve been tracking, but the pattern is real and it’s spreading: we are now seeing the first generation of companies where the strategic decisions are made by AI systems rather than humans, and those systems are producing decisions that humans would not make. Some of those decisions are working spectacularly. Some of them are working in ways that make the humans around them deeply uncomfortable. This is the uncanny valley of organizations. Not the valley where a robot looks almost human. The valley where a company behaves almost sensibly, and the almost is what gets you. Here’s the claim I want to test: the interesting question about AI-run organizations is not whether they can succeed. It’s whether the kind of success they produce is legible to the humans who depend on them. When a company’s decisions become unintelligible to the people inside it, the company has crossed a threshold that we don’t have governance for, and the results are not obviously good. What “AI-Run” Actually Means Let me be precise, because “AI-run company” is a phrase that gets used loosely. There are four levels, and they’re different in kind: Level 1: AI-assisted. Humans make all decisions, but AI provides analysis, forecasts, and recommendations. This is where most companies are now. It’s not the interesting case. Level 2: AI-delegated. Humans set goals and constraints, and AI makes operational decisions within them. Pricing, scheduling, inventory, hiring funnels. This is where a lot of large companies already are, whether they admit it or not. Level 3: AI-directed. AI makes strategic decisions, including decisions about goals and constraints. items.title: Expanding Firmware Correctness: Integrating Toolchain and Debugging Strategies
items.snippet: Understanding Firmware Correctness Beyond Software Correctness Firmware correctness encompasses more than just functional output; it requires validation in terms of timing, context, and shared state integrity. Unlike standard software, where correctness often
items.content: Understanding Firmware Correctness Beyond Software Correctness Firmware correctness encompasses more than just functional output; it requires validation in terms of timing, context, and shared state integrity. Unlike standard software, where correctness often focuses on whether a function returns the correct value, firmware correctness must also consider interrupt latency, stack overflow, and re-entrancy as first-class failure modes. For instance, a stack overflow on a Cortex-M target without a Memory Protection Unit (MPU) can silently corrupt the heap or neighboring stack frames before any fault is detected. Re-entrancy bugs in shared peripheral drivers can manifest only under specific interrupt timing conditions, which are difficult to reproduce in host-based unit tests. Therefore, hardware-in-the-loop validation is essential for interrupt-driven code to expose timing-dependent failures that simulations cannot reliably detect. Toolchain Configuration and Cross-Compilation Challenges Cross-compilation is a critical step in embedded firmware development, targeting a different instruction set, memory layout, and runtime environment than the host machine. Proper toolchain configuration is vital to prevent early boot failures and ensure firmware correctness. The linker script configuration controls memory section placement, such as flash, RAM, and backup domains. Misdefining a region boundary in the linker script can lead to memory corruption during startup, causing hard-to-reproduce failures before the application code executes. Compiler optimization flags also play a significant role in firmware correctness. For example, building with optimizations enabled from the start is recommended, as debugging at -O0 and shipping at -O2 can hide timing bugs until the final build. Ensuring peripheral register accesses are volatile-qualified and ISR sequences are not inlined or reordered are correctness requirements, not optional coding conventions. Debugging Embedded Firmware on Hardware Effective debugging of embedded firmware requires hardware interfaces like JTAG and SWD, which support hardware breakpoints, watch expressions, and live memory inspection without altering timing. Unlike printf-based debugging, these interfaces do not add code to the firmware image, preserving the timing integrity crucial for diagnosing issues in production-like builds. When UART logging is unavailable or would disturb timing, semi-hosting and Real-Time Transfer (RTT) are better options

items.title: 7 Pages Indexed, 400+ Waiting: What a Month of Google's Slow Lane Taught Me
items.snippet: My site has been live for almost a month. Google has indexed seven of its pages. Seven. The sitemap lists around 420 URLs. I am writing this down because the slow lane taught me more than any SEO guide did — and because if you are building on free hosting, you
items.content: My site has been live for almost a month. Google has indexed seven of its pages. Seven. The sitemap lists around 420 URLs. I am writing this down because the slow lane taught me more than any SEO guide did — and because if you are building on free hosting, you deserve the honest numbers, not a success story with the hard parts edited out. Here is the month, as it actually happened. The first two pages — the homepage and the serials page — showed up on Google about two weeks in. Everything after that has been a wall. Every morning, the same routine: open Search Console, inspect the next priority URL, click "Request indexing," and meet the same message — "Quota Exceeded." The daily quota is so small that most days zero URLs get submitted. Not ten. Zero. The sitemap is its own mystery. The file itself is fine — valid XML, every page listed. Google says it "couldn't fetch" it. I resubmitted it. It still couldn't fetch it. I resubmitted it again, twice in two days, and the status did not change. The individual pages that are already indexed stay indexed, so the site is not broken. The sitemap is just… unread, for reasons Google does not explain. The kids' section is the one that stings most. It is the most-visited part of the site, the part parents actually use — and Google has never seen it. Every inspection says the same thing: "URL is not on Google. Page is not indexed: URL is unknown to Google." Unknown. After three weeks of daily attempts. So what actually moved anything? Two things, and they are not what the guides promised. First, articles. One night I published six honest build-log articles across two platforms — twelve live links in a single evening, to pages that were already indexed. That did more in one night than ten days of directory submissions did in total. Second, patience with the boring parts. The directories mostly ghosted me — one live listing in twelve days, the rest sitting in review queues measured in weeks and months. I stopped chasing them and kept publishing instead. New episodes every day, new stories, a new article when there is something real to say. Here is what I would tell anyone starting where I started: do not measure your first month in indexed pages. Measure it in published pages. Google's slow lane is not a verdict on your site — it is a queue, and the queue moves on its own schedule. Your job is to make sure that when it finally arrives at your door, there is something worth indexing. The seven pages are real. The other 40

items.title: Working Across Repositories With AI, Without Moving to a Monorepo
items.snippet: A cancellation change starts in the Orders repository. Billing needs the reason for the request, and Fulfillment needs it when handling a shipment cancellation. An AI agent can edit a field in each codebase, yet still miss who decides whether a refund is allow
items.content: A cancellation change starts in the Orders repository. Billing needs the reason for the request, and Fulfillment needs it when handling a shipment cancellation. An AI agent can edit a field in each codebase, yet still miss who decides whether a refund is allowed or a shipment can be stopped. For a team keeping these services in separate repositories, a useful starting point is to make each domain's responsibilities and contracts explicit. Give the agent that context, then connect the repository-specific changes through one review. The next task should inherit the reviewed context and evidence. The following is an illustrative design, not a report of a customer deployment or measured results. It assumes an external agent environment with authorized access to the repositories and their test tooling. Define the bounded contexts before describing the repository layout A bounded context establishes where a domain model and its terminology apply. Martin Fowler's introduction to bounded contexts explains why different parts of a business can use different models of concepts that share a name. In this example, Orders, Billing, and Fulfillment each have a repository and a bounded context. That is a choice for this example. A repository boundary alone does not establish a domain boundary, and an existing system may have a different mapping. For our cancellation change, the distinctions look like this: Context Owns Must learn from another context Decision it retains Orders Cancellation requests and order lifecycle Payment and shipment outcomes How those outcomes affect order state Billing Captures, refunds, and payment records Cancellation request and reason Whether a refund is eligible Fulfillment Picking, dispatch, and shipment records Cancellation request and reason Whether work can stop at its current stage The word “cancelled” should not silently acquire one meaning across all three. A request can exist while a shipment is already dispatched. A refund may need separate handling. The agent needs those distinctions before it decides which files to touch. Give each repository a context brief Create one reviewable brief per context. Its purpose is to help a person or agent locate the authoritative contracts and understand their limits. For the Orders brief, useful content includes: What Orders owns, and which decisions belong to Billing or Fulfillment. The accepted cancellation reason values and the meaning of an absent value. items.title: Java learning Series | Day-5 Acces Modifier.
items.snippet: What is Access modifier? Access modifier are the reserved keyword in object-oriented programming that control the visibility and scope of the class method and variables. They are core tools used to enforce encapsulation (hiding internal data and state) and abs
items.content: What is Access modifier? Access modifier are the reserved keyword in object-oriented programming that control the visibility and scope of the class method and variables. They are core tools used to enforce encapsulation (hiding internal data and state) and abstraction (exposing only necessary functionality). Public(public) ---> Accessible any where in the application(all packages and classes). private(private) ---> Accessible only within the class members. Protected(protected) ---> Accessible within the same class, same package, and by subclasses in different packages. Default(no keyword) ---> If no access modifier is specified, this means only classes within the same package can access it. What is POJO? POJO stands for Plain Old Java Object. It is an ordinary Java object that is completely independent of any specific framework, third-party library, or complex enterprise architecture. It was introduced by sun microsystems. POJO are used to represent the entities of business logic, public class EmployeeEntity { private String name ; private int id ; private int salary ; public EmpolyeeEntity ( String name , int id , int salary ){ this . name = name ; this . id = id ; this . salary = salary ; public String getName (){ return name ; } public void setName ( String name ){ this . name = name ; } public int getId (){ return id ; } public void setId ( int id ){ this . id = id ; } public int getSalary (){ return salary ; } public void setSalary ( int salary ){ this . salary = salary ; } } } There are no restrictions on access modifiers. Fields can be private, protected, public, or default. A constructor is optional. It can contain business logic and represent entities directly in the application.

items.title: Building Scalable Microservices with .NET: Architecture, Communication & Deployment
items.snippet: Building Scalable Microservices with .NET: Architecture, Communication & Deployment Welcome to Edition #13 of Modern .NET, AI & Software Engineering Weekly . As applications grow, their architecture must evolve to support increasing users, business complexity,
items.content: Building Scalable Microservices with .NET: Architecture, Communication & Deployment Welcome to Edition #13 of Modern .NET, AI & Software Engineering Weekly . As applications grow, their architecture must evolve to support increasing users, business complexity, integrations, and operational demands. A system that works perfectly for a small team may become difficult to maintain when multiple teams are developing features, services have different scaling requirements, and business workflows become more complex. This is where microservices architecture can make a difference. But microservices are not simply about splitting a monolithic application into smaller APIs. They introduce new architectural decisions around communication, data ownership, resilience, deployment, monitoring, and distributed systems. For .NET developers, ASP.NET Core provides a strong foundation for building these distributed applications. Let's explore how to design and implement scalable microservices using modern .NET technologies. 1. Understand the Purpose of Microservices Microservices architecture structures an application as a collection of independently deployable services. Each service focuses on a specific business capability and owns the logic and data associated with that capability. Consider an e-commerce platform: Identity Service: Authentication and user management. Catalog Service: Products and categories. Order Service: Order creation and management. Payment Service: Payment processing. Inventory Service: Stock management. Notification Service: Emails, SMS, and notifications. Each service can be developed, tested, deployed, and scaled independently. However, independence is important. If every service depends heavily on every other service, the architecture can become a distributed monolith. The goal is not to create as many services as possible. It is to establish meaningful business boundaries. 2. Design Services Around Business Capabilities One of the most important decisions in microservices architecture is identifying service boundaries. A common mistake is splitting an application based on technical layers: One service for controllers. One service for repositories. One service for database access. This does not create meaningful microservices. Instead, use business capabilities and domain boundaries to identify services. Domain-Driven Design (DDD) introduces the concept of bounded contexts. Each bounded context represents a specific business domain with its own lan

items.title: User-agent: * doesn't apply to crawlers you named in robots.txt
items.snippet: A Disallow under User-agent: * does nothing for a crawler that has its own group in robots.txt. Each crawler reads exactly one group, the one matching its name, and * is only the fallback for crawlers you didn't name. I learned this from my own logs. I had blo
items.content: A Disallow under User-agent: * does nothing for a crawler that has its own group in robots.txt. Each crawler reads exactly one group, the one matching its name, and * is only the fallback for crawlers you didn't name. I learned this from my own logs. I had blocked my /go/ redirect links under * , and Cloudflare-verified Googlebot still fetched them 133 times in three days, ClaudeBot 213 times in five. Here's why, how to fix it, and a small script that catches the mistake before it ships. The version that doesn't work User-agent: Googlebot Allow: / User-agent: ClaudeBot Allow: / User-agent: * Allow: / Disallow: /go/ It's easy to end up here: you allow AI search crawlers by name, then later add a Disallow under * . In this file, /go/ is allowed for both Googlebot and ClaudeBot. Both specs say so: RFC 9309 , section 2.2.1: if no matching group exists, crawlers MUST obey the * group. Google's robots.txt spec : only one group is valid for a particular crawler, and the others are ignored. Groups don't inherit from each other, and * is not a shared base. The fix Write each blocked path into every named group. User-agent: Googlebot Allow: / Disallow: /go/ User-agent: ClaudeBot Allow: / Disallow: /go/ User-agent: * Allow: / Disallow: /go/ Keeping Allow: / next to Disallow: /go/ is fine. RFC 9309, section 2.2.2, picks the longest matching rule, so for /go/amazon/... the four-character Disallow: /go/ beats the one-character Allow: / . Once Googlebot re-read the fixed file, it stopped: Day (UTC) Googlebot → /go/ Oct 26 49 Oct 27 (fixed at 13:31) 52 Oct 28 – Nov 2 0 It took about four hours to stop, which fits Google caching robots.txt for up to 24 hours. A script that finds the group you forgot With a dozen named groups, you will eventually miss one. items.title: From Chatbots to AI Agents: When Should Software Take Action?
items.snippet: The Builder’s Letter — Edition 6 From Chatbots to AI Agents: When Should Software Take Action? For the past few years, much of the conversation around Artificial Intelligence has focused on chatbots. We ask questions, receive answers, generate content, summari
items.content: The Builder’s Letter — Edition 6 From Chatbots to AI Agents: When Should Software Take Action? For the past few years, much of the conversation around Artificial Intelligence has focused on chatbots. We ask questions, receive answers, generate content, summarize documents, and interact with AI through conversational interfaces. These capabilities have already changed how people work with software. But a new shift is taking place. AI is moving beyond simply answering questions. It is increasingly being used to perform tasks, interact with systems, execute workflows, and take actions on behalf of users. This is where AI agents enter the picture. However, there is an important engineering question that every software builder should consider: Just because AI can take an action, does it mean we should allow it to? 1. The Difference Between an AI Chatbot and an AI Agent A traditional chatbot primarily responds to user input. For example, a user might ask: "What were my total expenses last month?" The chatbot processes the question, retrieves or interprets relevant information, and provides an answer. An AI agent can potentially go further. It might: Understand the user's request. Identify the required information. Call the appropriate API. Retrieve relevant records. Perform calculations. Prepare a report. Ask for confirmation before sharing or submitting it. The difference is not simply that one uses a better AI model. The real difference is the ability to interact with external tools and systems. A chatbot communicates. An AI agent can communicate, reason through a workflow, and take permitted actions. 2. An AI Agent Is More Than an LLM One common misconception is that building an AI agent simply means connecting an application to an LLM and giving it a prompt. That is not enough for production software. A reliable agent typically requires several components: LLM or reasoning model Interprets user intent and determines the next step. Tools and APIs Allow the agent to interact with external systems, databases, services, and application functionality. Business logic Enforces the actual rules of the application. Financial calculations, permissions, validation, and transaction rules should not depend entirely on AI-generated decisions. items.title: Why do we keep testing employees for yesterday’s phishing attacks
items.snippet: “Yesterday’s price is not today’s price,” a phrase Fat Joe popularized in 2021 , reminds us that what worked yesterday may not deliver the same value today. In cybersecurity, this matters when we continue to assess employees against familiar phishing technique
items.content: “Yesterday’s price is not today’s price,” a phrase Fat Joe popularized in 2021 , reminds us that what worked yesterday may not deliver the same value today. In cybersecurity, this matters when we continue to assess employees against familiar phishing techniques while attackers use AI to craft more convincing, personalized messages. Having conducted multiple phishing simulations and one in October, 2026, I believe we need to ask a harder question: are we preparing people for the phishing attacks they are likely to face today, or testing their ability to recognize or remember the warning signs we have taught them to expect? What happens when those warning signs don’t apply or they face novel attacks? AI -enabled “phishing landscape” The traditional tell-tale signs of phishing which we used to train employees for are becoming less dependable. Generative AI can help attackers produce convincing messages, personalize lures and improve the quality of their communication. This does not mean every phishing campaign uses AI in reality, but it raises the bar for what employees may encounter . A 2025 report by SC Media covering Egress research found that 75% of the phishing kits examined on dark-web markets advertised AI capabilities, while 82% offered deepfake features. These figures relate to the kits analyzed, rather than all phishing activity, but they show that AI-enabled features are appearing in tools available to criminals. Add this to the spike in recent phishing attacks with AI prompt injections and you realize quickly the landscape has morphed. This matters for awareness programs. If employees are mainly taught to look for spelling mistakes, generic greetings or suspicious formatting, they may be less prepared for a message that uses familiar names, relevant business context and professional language when attackers use AI to craft them. Training needs to emphasize verification in addition to simply recognition and unexpected requests should be checked through a trusted channel, even when the message appears legitimate. Click rates are not everything Phishing simulations often produce a straightforward headline and statistics: the percentage of recipients who clicked a link, entered credentials and deleted or reported the message. items.title: Who approves the files that control your AI coding assistant?
items.snippet: A pull request adds a helpful setup step for an AI coding assistant. No application source changes. The description calls it a developer-experience improvement, and the reviewer sees a short configuration file beside some Markdown instructions. Before approvin
items.content: A pull request adds a helpful setup step for an AI coding assistant. No application source changes. The description calls it a developer-experience improvement, and the reviewer sees a short configuration file beside some Markdown instructions. Before approving it, the reviewer needs to answer a different question: what will this change allow to run on a colleague’s machine? The issue has moved beyond hypothetical repository poisoning. In an October 8 analysis of agent-skill distribution , StepSecurity revisited the June Miasma campaign, which planted AI-tool and editor configuration in a Microsoft repository without modifying application source. The configuration was intended to trigger credential harvesting through developer tooling. The October publication describes an inventory product, but the underlying campaign illustrates a wider operational problem: merging a configuration change can distribute execution instructions to the people working in that repository. StepSecurity also reports that the commit carried a skip-CI flag and a backdated timestamp, and that it moved code execution from package install to folder open. A control that runs only in the build pipeline never sees that path. The first reliable checkpoint is the pull request, and it needs a person who knows what the file can trigger. I recommend giving these changes a named owner and an enforceable review path. An organization should be able to identify who approved a hook, what the approval covered and where the approved version is allowed to run. Review the behavior behind the filename A repository file can serve several purposes. It may describe a coding convention, direct an agent toward a script, register a tool or arrange for a command to run at a lifecycle event. Those differences matter more than the extension. A Markdown instruction is not automatically executable code. It can nevertheless influence an agent that has permission to execute commands. A JSON setting may directly register a shell command. Review should establish the mechanism, the trigger and the authority available when it fires. Skills show why the filename is a poor guide. StepSecurity notes that a skill’s allowed-tools field can let the agent use listed tools without a permission prompt during the turn that invokes the skill, and that Claude Code’s documentation says workspace trust does not gate that field. items.title: What a security strategy that survives 2027 looks like
items.snippet: Equifax CISO Jeremy Koppen sees the same dynamics most security chiefs are facing: hackers on the one side using AI to perform more sophisticated attacks at unprecedented speed, and defenders on the other adopting AI to match that volume and velocity. “AI is c
items.content: Equifax CISO Jeremy Koppen sees the same dynamics most security chiefs are facing: hackers on the one side using AI to perform more sophisticated attacks at unprecedented speed, and defenders on the other adopting AI to match that volume and velocity. “AI is changing the pace on both sides,” he says. “Attackers are using it to operate at greater scale, and Equifax is using it to innovate more quickly.” In the next year, Koppen will continue to evolve Equifax’s security strategy to keep with an accelerating threat environment. “That means building on the security already embedded across our design and development process, so checks run early and automatically,” he says. “It also means expanding how we use AI in our own security operations to handle routine work, so our experts can focus on the threats and initiatives that matter most. Done well, security becomes one of the reasons a product can launch sooner.” As for the rising tide of AI agents entering enterprise workflows, Koppen says that “identity controls are central” to his 2027 security strategy. “Across the industry, more activity on enterprise networks now comes from AI agents, bots, and automated workflows, and most traditional security controls were designed with a human user in mind,” he explains. “That’s why we’re applying the same rigorous verification to these identities that we apply to people.” Of course, Koppen, like other seasoned security leaders, knows his IT security strategy must evolve to address more than just AI. Geopolitics, the anticipated arrival of quantum computing, and increasingly interconnected systems, are also changing the threat landscape and attack surface — sometimes in radical ways — and should prompt strategic changes, too. That in turn is putting pressure on CISOs to rethink their practices, policies, and approaches as we head toward a new year likely to be at least as wild of a ride as 2026 has been. “CISOs realize they need to transform, because their current state isn’t working. And it’s going to be a pretty significant transformation over the next few years for CISOs to be successful,” says Omar Khawaja, a CISO, a faculty member at Carnegie Mellon University’s CISO program, and a board member at HITRUST and FAIR Institute. Of course, transformation, as always, is a work in progress, Khawaja says; as a result many security execs are still working out what needs to change in 2027 and how to make those changes happen. items.title: Show HN: Wikihack – HackerTube, but for Wikipedia articles mentioned on HN
items.content: After seeing Karpathy's Hackertube and Hackerbooks, I just had to make Wikihack. I scraped all mentions of wikipedia on hackernews and ranked them, and turn them into a scrollable feed to make it a bit more easy to digest / interact with. You can see where people submitted the articles and where people mentioned it in comments. The top shows the most frequently linked articles. items.title: Game Off 2026: The theme is SHIFT
items.snippet: GitHub’s annual month-long game jam is back for its 14th year! This November, make a game inspired by the theme SHIFT. Change gears, swap perspectives, bend reality, or just press a certain key. The post Game Off 2026: The theme is SHIFT appeared first on The
items.content: It’s time to make Shift happen. Game Off , GitHub’s annual month-long game jam, returns for its 14th year this November. Thousands of developers have joined us over the years to make everything from polished platformers to wonderfully weird experiments. Whether you’re making your first game or your fiftieth, we’d love for you to join us. The theme for Game Off 2026 is SHIFT ! Shift gears. Shift perspectives. Shift dimensions. Shift bits. Work the night shift. Or make a game where the only buttons are the Shift keys. How you interpret the theme is entirely up to you. You have until December 1, 2026, at 13:37 PST to build and submit a game inspired by SHIFT. Strong or loose inspirations apply! Join Game Off 2026 on itch.io shift /ʃɪft/ Noun A change in position, direction, perspective, or reality. A period of scheduled work, usually when something breaks. A keyboard key used to capitalize letters, sprint in games, and accidentally enable sticky keys. In computing, an operation that moves bits left or right, because apparently bits need exercise too. Verb To change gears, direction, or the laws of physics. To move between worlds, dimensions, timelines, or questionable life choices. To transform into something (or someone) entirely different. To pass responsibility to somebody else, especially when the production build breaks. Acronyms (that we definitely just made up) Okay, we made these up: Space Hamsters Initiating Faster Travel Shapeshifters Hiding In Forgotten Temples Suspicious Humans Investigating Feral Toasters Skeletons Hastily Improvising Functional Transportation Or invent your own. We love seeing where you take the theme. Need inspiration? Here are a few concept ideas A one-button (or two-button) game where the Shift keys are is your only control. A racing game where shifting gears changes more than your speed. Second gear reverses gravity, third slows time, and fourth removes the brakes. A perspective puzzler where rotating the camera turns walls into floors and shifts shadows into platforms. A puzzle-platformer where you shift between two overlapping realities. That broken bridge might exist in the other world. Unfortunately, so might the monster standing on it. A shapeshifting adventure where you transform into creatures and objects, inheriting their abilities and weaknesses. A night-shift horror game set in a convenience store where the customers get progressively stranger, and whatever’s in aisle seven definitely isn’t covered by your training

items.title: Show HN: OmniDiff – Opensource, super fast, content aware Git difftool, in Rust
items.content: I have been researching what the ultimate diff tool would look like, based on actual diffs in open source repositories. OmniDiff can diff: code (25 languages), config, images, PDFs, archives, cursors, fonts... It's fast. It can diff C++ files of tens of thousands of lines in under 100ms, on a 2023 ThinkPad T14s. It's open source. AGPLv3. It's based on real diffs. I looked at the 7400 repositories that are listed in Gentoo packages, sampled 2000 diffs and solved them manually to get a good understanding of what is needed, before putting together the diff pipelines for each content type. Incidentally, this also forms the basis of the CI pipeline, so the robustness of the codebase is quite high. I'm still developing it. It's v0.3.0 at this time. But I have been using it daily as my git difftool for months now, and it works well. AI Disclosure: Yes, I do use AI. No, I do not vibecode.

items.content: Cloudflare has moved a post-quantum rebuild of GeoKey Manager into closed beta, guarding geo-fenced keys with hybrid ML-KEM-768 and X25519 instead of the attribute-based encryption used since 2022.
